title: Residual congestion and urinary sodium and chloride trajectories in acute heart failure.
abstract: Residual congestion remains frequent after initial treatment for acute heart failure (AHF), and its presence may not be adequately identified using individual clinical or biochemical markers. We investigated residual congestion using a multimodal approach and examined its relationship with changes in urinary sodium and chloride during the first 72 h of hospitalization. We prospectively included consecutive patients hospitalized for AHF who underwent congestion assessment at admission and 72 h. Clinical evaluation, NT-proBNP, and venous Doppler ultrasound (VExUS) were integrated to assess congestion. Residual multimodal congestion was defined by the presence of at least two of three criteria: VExUS score ≥ 1, < 30% reduction in NT-proBNP, and clinical congestion score ≥ 3. Urinary sodium and chloride were measured at admission and 72 h, and their changes over time were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models. Baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), worsening renal function, and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio were additionally characterized. Among 146 patients, 67 (45.9%) had residual multimodal congestion at 72 h. Urinary sodium and chloride concentrations were lower in patients with residual congestion. Both electrolytes decreased during the first 72 h (p < 0.001 for both), but their changes differed according to residual congestion status, with significant time-by-group interactions for sodium (p = 0.013) and chloride (p = 0.001). Patients with residual congestion also showed a trend toward poorer 180-day event-free survival, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (log-rank p = 0.078). Patients with residual congestion showed different early patterns of urinary sodium and chloride during treatment for AHF. Serial measurement of these electrolytes may complement clinical, biochemical, and venous ultrasound assessment when evaluating the response to decongestive therapy. These findings support their potential role in characterizing different decongestive profiles, although their clinical and prognostic value requires further evaluation.

title: The role of low muscle strength in predicting mortality in patients with liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Sarcopenia is a prevalent complication in chronic liver disease (CLD), traditionally assessed by muscle mass. Recent paradigm shifts focus to dynapenia as the primary determinant of adverse outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the role of dynapenia, as measured by handgrip strength (HGS) and ultrasound-derived diaphragmatic excursion, in predicting mortality in this population. This prospective study included consecutive outpatients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma history attending a tertiary hepatology unit. Muscle mass was assessed in subgroups using bioimpedance analysis (BIA) and computed tomography (CT). Associations between sarcopenia proxies and 24-month all-cause mortality were analyzed with adjusted Cox regression models, and survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves. Ninety-one patients were included (age 73.4 ± 8.1 years; 71 [78%] male); 20 (22%) had dynapenia. Twenty-two deaths occurred at two years (24.2%). Over 24 months, dynapenia (by HGS) and diaphragmatic excursion were associated with mortality in adjusted models (aHR 1.68, 95% CI 1.12-2.53, p = 0.012; aHR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.97, p = 0.042). In subgroups, they remained the only muscle parameters associated with mortality, while muscle mass indices were not significant. Finally, Kaplan-Meier estimates showed lower 24-month survival in dynapenic patients across groups (in overall population 65% vs. 79%, p = 0.05). Low muscle strength is a key prognostic parameter in patients with cirrhosis and HCC. In our small cohort, it was the only muscle-related measure significantly associated with mortality. These findings support further evaluation of muscle strength assessment as a potential tool for risk stratification in this population.

title: Diagnostic performance and timeliness of ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy for peripheral lymphadenopathy in Internal Medicine: a multicenter real-world study.
abstract: Background Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) is increasingly used for evaluating peripheral lymphadenopathy, but evidence regarding its implementation in Internal Medicine remains limited. We assessed its diagnostic performance, safety, and diagnostic timeliness in routine clinical practice. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included consecutive patients undergoing ultrasound-guided CNB of peripheral lymphadenopathy in five Internal Medicine departments between February 2021 and March 2026. The primary outcome was diagnostic performance. Secondary outcomes included safety, diagnostic timeliness, performance in lymphoma patients, and factors associated with obtaining a definitive diagnosis. Results A total of 413 patients were included (median age 62 years; 41.3% women). Lymphoma and carcinoma accounted for 44.1% and 23.7% of final diagnoses, respectively. The first CNB provided a definitive diagnosis in 85.7% of patients and a suggestive diagnosis in 8.0%, yielding an overall diagnostic yield of 93.7%. No major complications occurred. Median time from biopsy request to procedure was 1 day (IQR 0-2), and median time to definitive diagnosis was 10 days (IQR 6-16). Surgical biopsy was required in 9.4% of patients and was associated with longer diagnostic delays (42 vs 9 days; p < 0.001). Among 182 patients with lymphoma, overall diagnostic yield was 93.4%. Lower operator experience and hospital size < 500 beds were independently associated with a lower likelihood of obtaining a definitive diagnosis. Conclusions Ultrasound-guided CNB of peripheral lymphadenopathy performed by internists demonstrated high diagnostic yield, excellent safety, and short diagnostic timelines in a large multicenter real-world cohort. Operator experience and institutional context may influence diagnostic performance.

title: Impact of antithrombotic therapy on management and prognosis of patients hospitalized for upper gastrointestinal bleeding: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background Antithrombotic agents are frequently implicated in upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB), yet their impact on prognosis and management remains unclear. The aim of this study was to assess the impact of pre-existing antithrombotic therapy on the management and prognosis of patients hospitalized for UGIB. Methods This study used data from a retrospective, multicenter cohort of adult patients hospitalized for UGIB between January 2019 and December 2020 in Greater Paris University Hospitals. Patients were categorized into four groups according to their pre-existing antithrombotic treatment: antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulant therapy, both, or none. The primary outcome was thirty-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included endoscopy, endoscopic hemostasis, and blood transfusion within 7 days, and intensive care unit admission. Associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression and reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (95%CIs). Results Among 928 patients, 226 (24%) were on antiplatelet therapy alone, 154 (17%) on anticoagulant therapy alone, 61 (7%) on combined therapy, and 487 (52%) received no antithrombotic treatment. Thirty-day mortality was 6.9%: 8.4% in the no-antithrombotic group, 6.2% in the antiplatelet group, 4.5% in the anticoagulant group, and 3.3% in the combined therapy group. Compared with the no-antithrombotic group, anticoagulant therapy alone was associated with lower mortality (aOR=0.28, 95% CI 0.10-0.83), while antiplatelet therapy alone or combined therapy were not significantly associated (aOR=0.47, 95% CI 0.19-1.14 and aOR=0.12, 95% CI 0.01-1.11, respectively). Neither anticoagulant nor antiplatelet therapy was associated with secondary outcomes. Conclusions Antithrombotic therapy had no negative impact on the management or prognosis of patients hospitalized for UGIB.

title: Accuracy of deep learning in quantifying epicardial adipose tissue: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is significantly associated with cardiovascular disease and poor prognosis. Deep learning (DL) models have been explored for automatic EAT segmentation, but systematic evidence verifying their effectiveness is currently lacking. We conducted this meta-analysis to evaluate the accuracy of DL models for EAT segmentation and quantification, aiming to support the development of automated tools. We searched the Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore through February 20, 2026. Studies reporting DL-based quantitative EAT segmentation were included. Quality was assessed with QUADAS-2. The Dice similarity coefficient (Dice), correlation coefficient (R), and Bland-Altman bias were used to evaluate segmentation efficacy, the correlation between automated segmentation and reference standards, and consistency, respectively. A random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method pooled these measures. Thirty eligible studies were included, covering five image types. For non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), the pooled Dice was 0.888 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.853-0.924), and the pooled R reached 0.973 (95%CI: 0.958-0.982). The contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) subgroup performed best, yielding a Dice of 0.910 (95% CI: 0.881-0.939) and an R of 0.989 (95% CI: 0.976-0.995). This meta-analysis quantifies the accuracy of DL models for EAT segmentation and volume quantification. The findings indicate that DL achieves robust accuracy on both NCCT and CECT images. However, given that most current studies rely on internal validation, future work should prioritize large-scale, multicenter external validation to support the translation of these promising DL tools into robust clinical diagnostic systems.

title: Feasibility and durability of annular stabilization using an internal fixation ring in aortic valve repair: a computed tomography-based study.
abstract: Objectives Aortic annulus dilatation is a critical risk factor for late aortic insufficiency (AI) recurrence after isolated aortic valve repair. Durable annular stabilization remains technically challenging, and long-term data are limited. We evaluated the mid-term geometric stability of a novel "internal annular fixation ring" technique using an expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) ring and metallic holder. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 27 consecutive patients who underwent isolated aortic valve repair with internal annular fixation ring technique for significant AI between January 2015 and April 2024. Aortic root geometry was assessed using cardiac computed tomography (CT) and transthoracic echocardiography, preoperatively and during follow-up. The mean follow-up period for CT was 49.0 ± 38.2 months. The primary outcome was aortic annular stability assessed by agreement between the intended intraoperative annular diameter and the average annular diameter or area-derived annular diameter measured on follow-up CT. Secondary outcomes included freedom from aortic valve reintervention, echocardiographic and CT findings, late survival, and freedom from moderate AI. Results Overall, concomitant leaflet repair was performed in 74.1% of patients. The intended intraoperative annular diameter ((22 mm (22-24)) was not significantly different from the average annular diameter (22.2 mm (21.4-23.4), p = 0.49) or the area-derived annular diameter (22.2 mm (21.0-23.3), p = 0.15) measured on the follow up CT. Freedom from aortic valve reintervention was 92.3% at 7 years. Although no severe AI recurred, moderate AI developed in 7 patients (25.9%); however, no patient required hospitalization for heart failure during follow-up period. Conclusions The internal annular fixation ring technique provides feasible and durable aortic annulus stabilization in isolated aortic valve repair. Moderate AI recurrence highlights the need for further technical refinements.

title: Isolated surgical margin recurrence after segmentectomy for non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: We retrospectively reviewed patients undergoing segmentectomy for clinical stage I non-small cell lung cancer at two institutions in 2007-2015 who developed isolated margin recurrence. Among 240 segmentectomies, 17 patients developed margin recurrence; 16 received treatment. All underwent fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography; 13 had histological confirmation. Treatments comprised re-resection (n = 7), radiotherapy (n = 5), photodynamic therapy (n = 1), and epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors alone (n = 3). Re-resection resulted in one complication and no 90-day deaths. During a median follow-up of 53 months, subsequent progression occurred in none after re-resection, three after nonsurgical local therapy, and two after targeted therapy; five patients died. This series describes local and systemic treatment pathways. Although comparative efficacy could not be assessed, favorable local control was observed after re-resection in this selected cohort.

title: Early selective deep capillary plexus impairment at diagnosis in children with type 1 diabetes: an OCT angiography study.
abstract: Retinal microvascular dysfunction may precede clinically visible diabetic retinopathy in children with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), but whether it is detectable at diagnosis remains unclear. To evaluate retinal microvascular alterations at T1DM diagnosis using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) and assess associations between deep capillary plexus (DCP) vessel density and metabolic severity. This cross-sectional study included 50 children with newly diagnosed T1DM (100 eyes) and 50 age- and sex-matched controls (100 eyes). OCTA was performed using 6×6-mm macular and 4.5×4.5-mm optic disc scans. Vessel density (VD) was assessed in the superficial capillary plexus (SCP), DCP, and radial peripapillary capillary network. Foveal avascular zone metrics and retinal nerve fiber layer thickness were also analyzed. Linear mixed-effects models accounted for inter-eye correlation. Subgroup analyses were performed by HbA1c level and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) severity. SCP VD did not differ significantly between groups. DCP impairment is detectable at T1DM diagnosis before clinically visible diabetic retinopathy. OCTA may provide a sensitive, noninvasive biomarker of early retinal microvascular involvement in pediatric T1DM.

title: Achieving opioid-free anaesthesia.
abstract: Background Opioids have been central to anaesthetic practice for over a century, but they risk adverse effects including postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), ileus, respiratory depression, and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. These complicate recovery and contribute to the wider burden of opioid misuse, a growing concern in Irish healthcare. Opioid-free anaesthesia (OFA) supports Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) principles by removing opioid-related barriers to early mobilisation and functional recovery. Aims To review the rationale for OFA, how it is delivered, its limitations, and to assess how it fits into current perioperative practice in Ireland. Results OFA relies on combining agents that target multiple nociceptive pathways, such as N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists (ketamine, magnesium), alpha-2 adrenergic agonists (especially dexmedetomidine), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), paracetamol, intravenous lidocaine, and gabapentinoids. Where applicable, ultrasound-guided peripheral nerve blocks can reduce intraoperative analgesic requirements and extending postoperative analgesia. Evidence supports OFA across a range of surgical contexts. Benefits are most consistent in laparoscopic and major abdominal surgery, where faster return of bowel function, reduced length of stay, and lower rates of PONV are reported. Evidence on postoperative analgesia is less clear. Opioid consumption in the immediate post-anaesthetic period tends to be lower but is often comparable to a well-executed opioid-inclusive multimodal regimen thereafter. Conclusions Rigid opioid avoidance risks undertreating acute pain, so OFA is best applied selectively, guided by procedure type, patient comorbidities, and institutional resources. This review evaluates the rationale, implementation, and limitations of OFA, providing clinicians with a balanced appraisal of its role in modern perioperative care.

title: Current Role of Radiomics for Management of Soft Tissue Sarcoma.
abstract: Opinion statement Soft tissue sarcomas represent a diverse set of malignancies with equally diverse behavior, ranging from relatively indolent low-grade tumors to aggressive high-grade tumors with high metastatic potential. Initial diagnosis hinges on tissue biopsy for determining histologic subtype and grade, while conventional imaging plays critical roles in defining local tumor size and extent, staging, treatment response, and disease surveillance. However, conventional semantic interpretation of imaging studies overlooks much of the complex imaging data embedded in routine clinical studies. Radiomics encompasses the identification of novel disease biomarkers extracted from highly quantitative characterizations of tumor structure and heterogeneity and has shown promise in providing a deeper understanding of soft tissue sarcomas. Given the increasing usage of imaging in soft tissue sarcomas, particularly usage of MRI, it behooves both clinicians and radiologists to further the depth of understanding that may be gleaned from radiomics. These insights, although primarily experimental, represent a rapidly evolving landscape in soft tissue sarcoma diagnosis and management where radiomics will be increasingly integrated into clinical practice. The present work focuses on the latest updates with regards to the application of radiomics to the diagnosis, prediction of treatment response, assessment of treatment response, and prognosis of soft tissue sarcomas and how they may affect sarcoma management.

title: Image-Guided Ablative Options for Desmoid Fibromatosis: Contemporary Evidence and Guideline Integration.
abstract: Opinion statement Most patients with a newly diagnosed desmoid tumor should begin with multidisciplinary evaluation and active surveillance rather than immediate intervention, provided that symptoms are limited and further growth is unlikely to create irreversible morbidity. Treatment should be initiated when pain, functional limitation, sustained progression, or threatened critical structures make continued observation unacceptable. Percutaneous cryoablation is generally favored because the ice ball can be monitored directly, treatment can be personalized/tailored with the synergistic benefit of multiple probes, and the procedure can be repeated or staged when a complete margin would be unsafe. Complete ablation should be targeted when the entire tumor can be covered without jeopardizing skin, nerves, bowel, or other vulnerable structures; deliberate subtotal ablation is appropriate when the principal goal is pain relief or functional improvement and a safe circumferential margin is not achievable. Hydrodissection, skin warming, neural protection, and conservative treatment near critical anatomy are essential. Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound is an attractive incisionless alternative for tumors with a favorable acoustic window. Microwave or radiofrequency ablation should be reserved for carefully selected lesions and experienced operators; electrochemotherapy and chemical ablation remain investigational with some promising early evidence. Embolization can be useful for hypervascular tumors that are poorly suited to direct percutaneous treatment. Local and systemic therapy should not be viewed as mutually exclusive: systemic treatment is often preferable for diffuse, intra-abdominal, or anatomically hazardous disease, while ablation can address a dominant symptomatic focus, residual viable tumor, or focal progression. Further study into the benefits and sequencing of combining local therapy with systemic or targeted options will be helpful in the multi-disciplinary evaluation of this complex patient cohort.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Myocardial Perfusion Imaging with SPECT and PET in Liver Transplant Candidates: Physiologic Limitations, Current Evidence, and Future Directions.
abstract: Purpose of review Myocardial perfusion imaging with SPECT and PET is commonly used to assess coronary artery disease, but its role in liver transplant candidates remains incompletely defined. This review examines how cirrhotic physiology affects pharmacologic stress imaging and summarizes current evidence for the use of SPECT, PET, and quantitative perfusion measures in this population. Recent findings Hyperdynamic circulation, elevated resting myocardial blood flow, impaired chronotropic response, and attenuated vasodilator reserve may reduce the diagnostic performance of relative perfusion imaging. Reported SPECT sensitivity for coronary artery disease in liver transplant candidates is substantially lower than the general population. Quantitative PET, particularly myocardial flow reserve, has shown possible prognostic value, although evidence is limited to small observational cohorts. SPECT should be interpreted cautiously in higher-risk candidates. PET may offer additional physiologic and prognostic information, but transplant-specific thresholds and clinical pathways remain unvalidated. Whether improved perfusion-based risk stratification changes management and improves outcomes remains to be determined.

title: Neuroinflammation as a Final Common Pathway in Systemic Disease - How Systemic Disease Becomes Brain Disease.
abstract: Purpose of review This chapter reviews evidence that neuroinflammation constitutes a final common pathway linking systemic disease of diverse origin to a shared spectrum of CNS injury, and synthesizes its mechanistic, biomarker, and therapeutic implications. Recent findings Autoimmune, infectious, metabolic, malignant, and age-related diseases converge on five shared CNS mechanisms-blood-brain barrier disruption, microglial priming, complement-mediated synaptic injury, microvascular and thromboinflammatory injury, and autoantibody-mediated neuronal targeting-that interact as a self-perpetuating loop rather than a linear cascade, with meningeal lymphatic and glymphatic clearance governing whether the cycle resolves or persists. These processes are increasingly measurable with non-disease-specific fluid biomarkers (IL-6, IL-1β, neurofilament light chain, GFAP) and imaging biomarkers (TSPO PET, vessel-wall and permeability MRI), and several are now targets of mechanism-directed therapy-IL-1 inhibition, complement blockade, blood-brain barrier stabilization, microglial modulation, and precision immunotherapy timed to disease stage. Recognizing neuroinflammation as this final common pathway reframes diagnosis around shared biomarkers rather than disease labels, predicts cross-disease therapeutic benefit, and relocates the therapeutic window earlier-toward protecting a brain vulnerable long before overt neurological disease declares itself.

title: Cardiovascular Toxicity Across the Cancer Immunotherapy Spectrum: Mechanisms and Management in Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) and Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell (CAR-T) Therapy.
abstract: Purpose of review This review evaluates the evolving landscape of cardiovascular toxicities associated with two pillars of modern cancer treatment: immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. It examines their distinct immune-mediated pathophysiologies, clinical manifestations, and management frameworks. Recent findings While ICIs carry a clinical trial incidence for cardiotoxicity of approximately 1%, real-world data suggest rates of 3-5%, with myocarditis sometimes manifesting early as part of a high-mortality "Triple M" or overlap syndrome. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occur in nearly 50% of ICI-myocarditis cases. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) using the modified Lake Louise criteria, with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) detection sensitivity increasing from 21.6% to 72.0% when imaged after four days of symptoms. Conversely, CAR-T cardiotoxicity is predominantly driven by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which affects 49-93% of patients with currently licensed products. Severe CRS more than doubles the risk of cardiovascular events, including a 6-10% incidence of LVEF decline and a 4-18% incidence of arrhythmias. Recent advancements include machine learning models to predict MACE and structured screening programs to risk-stratify candidates. Cardiotoxicity remains a significant complication, highlighting the need for vigilant monitoring and early intervention. Management relies on baseline risk assessment and rapid deployment of targeted therapies, such as high-dose methylprednisolone for ICI-myocarditis and IL-6 inhibition (tocilizumab) for CAR-T-related CRS. A multidisciplinary cardio-oncology approach is essential to mitigate risks. With early diagnosis and appropriate immunosuppressive strategies in a multidisciplinary setting, these complications can be better managed, optimising oncological benefits whilst reducing treatment-related morbidity and mortality in majority of patients.

title: Therapeutics in Axial Spondyloarthritis: A Review of What Works - SPARTAN 2026 Annual Meeting Proceedings.
abstract: Purpose of review Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) encompasses a broad disease spectrum, and the management landscape has expanded considerably over the past two decades. This review synthesizes the current evidence on pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions in axSpA, addressing both symptom control and radiographic outcomes across drug classes and patient contexts. Recent findings NSAIDs remain the cornerstone of first-line therapy, with emerging long-term cohort data suggesting a dose-response relationship between NSAID exposure and reduced radiographic spinal progression in radiographic disease. TNF inhibitors retain the most mature evidence base regarding radiographic progression, with longitudinal data associating TNFi exposure with slower mSASSS progression and suggesting that this effect may be partially uncoupled from inflammation as measured by ASDAS, particularly with earlier treatment initiation. IL-17 inhibitors demonstrate robust symptomatic efficacy, while two-year structural data show low radiographic progression, although a treatment-specific structural effect has not been established. JAK inhibitors provide effective symptom control, and longer-term radiographic data are now available, but controlled evidence demonstrating inhibition of structural progression remains lacking. Exercise therapy, supported by a recent systematic review and meta-analysis, improves disease activity, function, mobility, pain, and fatigue, with subgroup analyses showing significant BASFI improvement only for sessions lasting ≤60 minutes. Obesity is associated with greater disease activity and poorer response to TNF inhibitors. Symptom control is achievable across all major drug classes in axSpA. Evidence regarding radiographic progression is most mature for TNF inhibitors, more limited for IL-17 inhibitors, context-dependent for NSAIDs, and currently insufficient to establish structural modification with JAK inhibitors. Effective management requires integrating pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies, including structured exercise as an evidence-based intervention, while recognizing obesity as a clinically relevant prognostic factor.

title: Imaging in Upper Tract Urothelial Carcinoma: Diagnostic Accuracy of Current Modalities for Local Tumor Staging.
abstract: Purpose of review To summarize current imaging modalities for upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) and evaluate their diagnostic performance for tumor staging and risk stratification. Recent findings CT urography remains the diagnostic standard with excellent accuracy for tumor detection, though its reliability for local staging is limited. MR urography shows promise for assessing muscle invasion but is operator dependent. FDG-PET demonstrates value in nodal and metastatic staging rather than primary tumor evaluation. Retrograde pyelography maintains a role in tumor diagnosis in circumstances where cross-sectional imaging is unable to be performed. Emerging approaches, including radiomics and machine learning, as well as novel modalities such as endoluminal ultrasound, optical coherence tomography, and contrast-enhanced ultrasound show encouraging preliminary results but lack large-scale validation. No single modality provides accurate clinical staging in UTUC. A multimodal approach integrating imaging with clinical and endoscopic data remains essential, while emerging technologies may improve future risk stratification.

title: Novel Imaging Techniques Prior to Surgical Management of Invasive Bladder Cancer: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Purpose of review To assess the diagnostic accuracy of novel imaging modalities in working up invasive bladder cancer prior to surgical management and their potential role in guiding treatment decisions. Recent findings Multiple new imaging modalities, including VI-RADS and Biparametric MRI have been developed to better guide management of invasive bladder cancer. There lacks a comprehensive review of these modalities and their diagnostic performance. We performed a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched through 2025. Studies reporting sensitivity and specificity of novel imaging for muscle invasion detection or nodal staging were included. Quality assessment used the QUADAS 2 tool. Thirty three studies encompassing 4,689 patients were included. Twenty three studies evaluated the Vesical Imaging Reporting and Data System for muscle invasion detection, achieving median sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 82% at a threshold of three or greater and 84% and 92%, respectively, at four or greater. Nine studies assessed positron emission tomography for nodal staging, with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography demonstrating superior sensitivity (23 to 81%) compared to conventional computed tomography (13 to 47%). Fibroblast activation protein inhibitor tracers showed the highest sensitivity (82 to 100%) with specificity of 82 to 90%. One radiomics study achieved 73% sensitivity and 84% specificity for lymph node detection. Novel imaging modalities demonstrate promising diagnostic accuracy for bladder cancer staging. The Vesical Imaging Reporting and Data System provides reliable muscle invasion assessment with threshold dependent performance. Positron emission tomography with fibroblast activation protein inhibitor tracers substantially improves nodal staging over conventional computed tomography. Integration of these modalities may optimize patient management, including use or omission of neoadjuvant therapy and consideration for organ sparing approaches. Prospective multicenter validation is needed.

title: The Role of Micro-Ultrasound in Prostate Cancer Detection.
abstract: Purpose of review To synthesize current evidence on the role of 29-MHz micro-ultrasound (microUS) in prostate cancer (PCa) detection and to define its position relative to multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) across the diagnostic pathway. We conducted a narrative review of prospective, comparative, and randomized studies, with clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection as the primary endpoint. Recent findings MicroUS provides ~ 70-µm axial resolution and enables real-time PRI-MUS-based risk stratification. Across head-to-head studies, microUS achieves diagnostic performance comparable to mpMRI. Evidence supports utility in biopsy-naïve patients, selected MRI-negative men with persistent clinical suspicion, repeat-biopsy settings, active surveillance, and local tumor staging, while combined mpMRI-microUS approaches have been shown to maximize yield of csPCa detection. Key limitations include operator dependence, interobserver variability, lack of validated biopsy-avoidance thresholds, and reduced sensitivity in anterior lesions. MicroUS is a practical, high-resolution platform that complements mpMRI and may enhance accessibility, efficiency, and precision in prostate cancer care.

title: Vascular Phenotyping with Photoacoustic and Ultrasound Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease: Recent Innovations.
abstract: Purpose of review Photoacoustic and ultrasound imaging together resolve vascular structure, wall biomechanics, blood flow, oxygenation, and tissue composition without ionizing radiation or iodinated contrast. This review summarizes what each modality can now measure in patients and asks which of these measurements are close enough to clinical use to inform cardiovascular management decisions. Recent findings Recent advances have expanded photoacoustic imaging toward faster, higher-resolution functional vascular phenotyping, including clinically relevant biomarkers and co-registered ultrasound imaging. Ultrafast and super-resolution ultrasound now quantify vascular biomechanics, hemodynamics, and microvasculature, with ultrasound localization microscopy entering clinical studies. Wearable ultrasound has also been validated for blood-pressure monitoring across diverse care settings, alongside increasingly quantitative feature extraction. Summary Ultrasound and photoacoustic imaging provide complementary vascular information: ultrasound offers depth, speed, and continuous access, while photoacoustic imaging adds compositional and oxygenation contrast. Despite limitations in quantitative accuracy, imaging depth, and system standardization, emerging patient studies now span super-resolution vascular mapping, functional biomarkers, and wearable monitoring. Their integration offers a potential route toward continuous, operator-independent vascular phenotyping for clinical decision-making.

title: Single-cell Transcriptomics in Autoimmune Diseases: Mechanistic Insights, Cross-disease Convergence, and Translational Challenges in Rheumatoid Arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Type 1 Diabetes, and Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Autoimmune diseases are characterized by loss of immune tolerance and substantial heterogeneity across patients, tissues, and disease stages. Although bulk transcriptomic studies have identified important inflammatory pathways, they cannot directly resolve rare, transitional, and tissue-contextualized cell states that may be relevant to disease mechanisms and therapeutic response. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables transcriptomic profiling at cellular resolution, while complementary multimodal, receptor-repertoire, epigenomic, and spatial approaches can link cellular states to protein phenotype, clonal architecture, regulatory programs, and tissue context. This review critically examines recent single-cell studies in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis, type 1 diabetes, and multiple sclerosis. Rather than providing a descriptive catalogue of published studies, we assess the strength of available evidence by distinguishing independently replicated findings from observations supported by limited studies, and cross-sectional associations from longitudinal, treatment-response, and functional evidence. Across the selected diseases, studies repeatedly report inflammatory programs involving interferon signaling, chemokine-mediated immune recruitment, and stromal-immune interactions; however, evidence for convergence at the cell-state and regulatory-network levels remains limited, and the extent to which shared signatures represent common pathogenic mechanisms rather than inflammatory context remains uncertain. We evaluate the translational potential of scRNA-seq for biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and treatment response prediction, while considering evidence from related tissue-based molecular stratification approaches, including the R4RA randomized trial in rheumatoid arthritis. R4RA provides prospective randomized evidence that synovial molecular features can enrich for differential therapeutic responses, but its use of bulk synovial transcriptomics and histopathology does not constitute prospective validation of single-cell-derived biomarkers. We further highlight cohort biases, reproducibility challenges, dissociation artifacts, computational ambiguity, and privacy concerns that constrain immediate clinical implementation. Together, these advances position single-cell profiling as a mechanistic discovery platform with substantial translational promise, contingent on standardization, validation across diverse cohorts, and integration with functional perturbation approaches.

title: Bone marrow adipose tissue in cardiometabolic disease: marrow niche remodeling, inflammatory hematopoiesis, and vascular pathology.
abstract: Bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) is increasingly recognized as a metabolically active, endocrine, and immunomodulatory component of the marrow niche rather than a passive fat depot. This narrative review synthesizes biological, imaging, epidemiological, and therapeutic evidence linking BMAT and marrow metabolic activation with cardiometabolic disease. BMAT arises from marrow stromal progenitors and exhibits depot-specific heterogeneity, endocrine activity, insulin responsiveness, and context-dependent expansion during aging, diabetes, obesity, menopause, osteoporosis, and chronic kidney disease. Mechanistically, experimental studies indicate that marrow adipocytes and adipocyte-lineage niche cells can influence hematopoiesis through metabolic and local signaling, whereas trained immunity is established primarily in HSPCs, myeloid progenitors, and monocyte/macrophage populations. Human MRI/MRS studies characterize BMAT quantity and composition, whereas 18 F-FDG PET reflects non-BMAT-specific marrow activation associated with vascular inflammation and early atherosclerosis; direct BMAT-cardiovascular evidence remains limited. Emerging population imaging and genetic analyses support BMAT as a disease-associated phenotype, particularly for osteoporosis and fractures. Interventions affecting metabolic, inflammatory, skeletal, or marrow pathways have differing degrees of BMAT-related evidence, and none has established that modifying BMAT improves cardiovascular outcomes. This review identifies BMAT as an emerging research phenotype while emphasizing that its causal, prognostic, and therapeutic relevance to cardiovascular disease remains unresolved.

title: Graph Neural Network Reveals the Cortical Morphology of Local Brain Aging in Normal Cognition and Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Estimating brain age (BA) from T 1 -weighted magnetic resonance images (MRIs) provides a powerful framework for quantifying anatomical brain aging. Whereas global BA (GBA) summarizes overall brain health, local BA (LBA) provides cortically specific patterns of aging at the subject level. Although previous studies have examined anatomical contributors to GBA, to our knowledge, no framework has been established to estimate LBA using cortical morphology. To address this gap, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) that uses morphometric features-cortical thickness, surface area, curvature, gray/white matter intensity ratio (GWR), sulcal depth-to estimate LBA across the cortical surface at high spatial resolution (mean inter-vertex distance = 1.37 mm). Trained on cortical surface meshes extracted from the MRIs of cognitively normal (CN) adults (N = 14,423), our model achieves better test-retest performance than the existing state-of-the-art, while identifying more biologically plausible patterns of aging in Alzheimer's disease (AD) on the ADNI dataset. Association cortices emerge as primary sites of morphometric aging in CNs, whereas mild cognitive impairment is characterized by widespread aging that is pronounced in the parahippocampal gyrus. AD subjects demonstrate significant aging across the entire cortex, particularly within medial temporal regions and associated cortical networks. Feature ablation highlights curvature and GWR as preferentially sensitive to AD pathology. Regional LBA gaps are significantly associated with neuropsychological measures of AD-related cognitive impairment, linking cortical aging patterns to clinical outcomes. These results demonstrate that GNN-based modeling of cortical morphometry enables biologically interpretable mapping of local brain aging with greater fidelity than prior work.

title: A Visual Support System for Stent-Assisted Treatment of Cerebral Aneurysms Using 3D Imaging and Augmented Reality.
abstract: Precise visualization of vascular structures is crucial for planning and performing stent-assisted interventions in cerebral aneurysms. Traditional 2D imaging frequently lacks sufficient spatial information, which restricts clinicians' ability to evaluate vessel morphology, branching patterns, and how stents would interact with the vessel wall. This paper introduces an integrated visual support platform that unites workflow-driven medical image processing, numerical simulation of stent deployment, and augmented reality (AR) visualization via Microsoft HoloLens. The platform features a configurable workflow engine to handle medical data processing covering: vessel segmentation, medial-axis computation, mesh creation, and region-of-interest definition, followed by interactive simulation of stent expansion using computationally efficient approximation techniques. The resulting 3D models of the vasculature and stent are displayed in a dedicated AR environment that supports gesture-based interaction, real-time stent adjustment, and immersive navigation inside the vessels. This system provides intraoperative decision support by enabling clinicians to analyze stent placement, aneurysm coverage, and possible geometric limitations, and it also supports replay of simulations for training and educational purposes. The work shows that integrating 3D imaging, numerical modeling of stent-vessel interactions, and augmented reality can markedly improve precision, safety, and situational awareness in neurointerventional procedures.

title: Quantified Brain Atrophy and Risk of Severe Mass Effect in Acute Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Background Large middle cerebral artery (MCA) infarctions can result in life-threatening cerebral edema. Quantitative brain atrophy may improve risk stratification for severe edema. We examined whether quantitative brain atrophy is associated with severe midline shift after large ischemic stroke and whether incorporating atrophy improves prediction beyond established clinical and radiographic predictors. Methods This was a retrospective observational cohort study of patients with greater than or equal to half MCA ischemic infarction, presentation within 24 h of last known well time, and at least one follow-up head computed tomography (CT), admitted to two academic hospitals with comprehensive stroke centers between 2006 and 2024. The study was approved by the institutional review boards of both centers. Brain atrophy was quantified as the inverse of standardized brain volume on admission head CT. The primary outcome was severe radiographic mass effect, defined as midline shift ≥ 5 mm on follow-up CT. The secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Multivariable regression models assessed associations between quantified atrophy and outcomes. Incremental prognostic value was evaluated by comparing models with and without atrophy using measures of goodness of fit, calibration, and discrimination. Results Among 565 patients (mean age 67.5 ± 15.7 years; 49.9% female), 223 (39.5%) developed severe mass effect. Greater atrophy was associated with lower odds of midline shift ≥ 5 mm [odds ratio (OR) 0.44, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.34-0.58], but not with in-hospital mortality. Incorporation of atrophy improved prediction of severe mass effect compared with the baseline model [likelihood ratio test χ 2 (1) = 41, p < 0.001; Akaike information criterion (AIC) 703 vs. 741; Bayesian information criterion (BIC) 733 vs. 767; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) 0.68 vs. 0.60]. Conclusions Quantified brain atrophy is independently associated with a reduced risk of severe mass effect after large MCA stroke and improved the performance of established predictive models. Incorporation of this imaging biomarker may enhance early risk stratification, monitoring, and intervention planning for patients at risk of life-threatening cerebral edema.

title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Value of Sonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter in Patients with Ischemic Stroke or Hypertensive Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Background Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a critical complication in nontraumatic brain injury, yet invasive monitoring carries significant risks, and noninvasive alternatives remain undervalidated. Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) ultrasonography represents a promising bedside technique, but data in nontraumatic populations are limited. This study evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic value of ONSD in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage. Methods This prospective observational cohort study enrolled 100 neurocritical intensive care unit (ICU) patients with acute nontraumatic brain injury [ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage; Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) < 9] who underwent admission computed tomography (CT) and bedside ONSD ultrasonography. Sixty age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers were enrolled exclusively to provide descriptive reference values for physiological ONSD and were not included in the primary diagnostic or prognostic analyses. CT-based radiologic ICP surrogates were the reference standard. Exploratory analyses evaluated inter-eye variability, adjusted models, and in-hospital survival. Results ONSD increased stepwise across healthy controls, patients with negative CT, and patients with positive CT (4.62 ± 0.33, 5.52 ± 0.51, and 6.50 ± 0.51 mm, respectively). Among neurocritical patients, a cohort-derived cutoff of ≥ 6.00 mm yielded 86.7% sensitivity, 85.0% specificity, 89.7% positive predictive value, 81.0% negative predictive value, 86.0% accuracy, and 0.901 area under the curve (AUC). Above-threshold ONSD remained independently associated with CT-positive elevated ICP after adjustment for age, body mass index (BMI), GCS, and systolic blood pressure (SBP) in exploratory multivariable analysis. Exploratory survival analysis showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality in patients with ONSD above the cohort-derived threshold (log-rank p = 4.77 × 10 -13 ). Conclusions Bedside ultrasonographic ONSD measurement appears clinically useful for early triage and longitudinal bedside surveillance in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly when invasive monitoring is unavailable or delayed.

title: High Postoperative Perihematomal Edema Trajectory after Endoscopic Evacuation for Supratentorial Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Background and objective The clinical relevance of perihematomal edema (PHE) after endoscopic evacuation of supratentorial intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is uncertain. We examined a longitudinal postoperative PHE phenotype and its association with 90-day functional outcome. Methods This two-center retrospective cohort included 136 patients who survived beyond 72 h after endoscopic evacuation of supratentorial ICH and had complete serial computed tomography (CT) and 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) assessment. CT windows were 0-24 h (T1), 48-72 h (T2), and day 5-7 (T3). Before outcome-model fitting, high postoperative PHE trajectory was defined as T3 PHE ≥ 36.6 mL or continuous increase across T1-T2-T3 with a T3-T1 change ≥ 7.7 mL; both thresholds were cohort-derived upper quartiles. Center-adjusted logistic regression examined associated factors and poor 90-day outcome (mRS score 3-6). Results High postoperative PHE trajectory occurred in 51 patients (37.5%). Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) severity (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.11 per category, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09-4.09), residual hematoma volume (aOR 1.75 per mL, 95% CI 1.35-2.27), and fever duration within 72 h (aOR 1.20 per h, 95% CI 1.08-1.34) were associated with this trajectory. Adding trajectory to the outcome model increased apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) from 0.846 to 0.905; trajectory was associated with poor outcome (aOR 25.21, 95% CI 6.13-103.60). Among 131 paired observations, mRS score 0-2 occurred in 71/131 (54.2%) at 90 days and 76/131 (58.0%) at 12 months (two-sided exact McNemar P = 0.125). Conclusions In this selected cohort of early postoperative survivors, IVH severity, residual hematoma volume, and fever duration were associated with high postoperative PHE trajectory, which was associated with poor 90-day functional outcome. This cohort-derived imaging phenotype warrants external validation as a candidate prognostic marker after endoscopic evacuation.

title: Resistance Phenotypes and Treatment Sequencing After Immune Checkpoint Blockade in MSI-H/dMMR Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Review.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed microsatellite instability-high or mismatch repair-deficient metastatic colorectal cancer, but clinically relevant progression still occurs and treatment after progression remains undefined. We performed a clinically oriented narrative review, updated August 8, 2026, and separated direct prospective evidence, retrospective post-ICI evidence, extrapolation from general metastatic colorectal cancer trials, case-level evidence, and biological rationale. In the absence of prospective post-dual-ICI sequencing studies, we propose an evidence-informed conceptual framework. Apparent early progression should prompt confirmation of MSI/MMR status and exclusion of pseudoprogression before classification as early global progression, late systemic progression, or oligoprogression. BRAF V600E is common in MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer and is not an absolute predictor of ICI failure, but it is a major treatment-defining branch after progression. Repeat tissue biopsy or circulating tumor DNA profiling should be selective, used when findings can alter management and without delaying urgent therapy. ctDNA-based molecular residual disease is prognostic after curative-intent colorectal cancer resection, including metastasectomy, but is not validated to direct treatment of radiographically evident post-ICI progression. Oligoprogression warrants multidisciplinary consideration of local therapy, while ICI rechallenge remains investigational. Most recommendations are retrospective or extrapolated; transparent evidence boundaries and prospective post-dual-ICI studies are essential.

title: Neoadjuvant and Perioperative Immunotherapy for Resectable Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Current Evidence, Endpoints, and Clinical Integration.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are being investigated across curative-intent treatment pathways for resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Randomized studies show that programmed cell death-1 blockade can increase pathological complete response (pCR) when added to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, while immunochemoradiotherapy can produce high pathological response rates. This structured narrative review summarizes current evidence for neoadjuvant and perioperative immunotherapy in ESCC within the context of established chemotherapy and chemoradiotherapy backbones. Particular attention is given to randomized ICI trials, the role of radiotherapy, interpretation of pathological and survival endpoints, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), postoperative therapy, perioperative safety, clinical response assessment, and regional applicability. pCR is a useful early activity endpoint and may carry prognostic information within individual regimens, but definitions and pathological assessment vary and trial-level surrogacy for overall survival has not been established. Longitudinal ctDNA is promising as a complementary measure of molecular residual disease but remains investigational for treatment adaptation. When radiotherapy is combined with ICI, established thoracic organ-at-risk constraints and careful monitoring for overlapping pulmonary and esophageal toxicity remain important because ICI-specific normal-tissue constraints have not been validated. Clinical complete response assessment also requires multimodal evaluation; post-treatment inflammatory changes can limit CT and PET-CT specificity. Overall, current data support continued phase III evaluation of ICI-containing strategies with mature event-free and overall survival endpoints and with comparators appropriate to regional treatment standards.

title: The impact of intratumor heterogeneity on outcome and resistance to therapy in primary breast cancer: a systematic review.
abstract: Intratumor heterogeneity (ITH), the coexistence of diverse subclones within a single tumor, may pose a major challenge to effective chemotherapy in breast cancer. This cellular diversity contributes to treatment failure, residual disease, and early relapse by enabling tumor adaptation and therapeutic resistance. Although increasingly recognized as a critical feature of breast cancer biology, it remains under-investigated and has not yet been integrated into routine clinical care. This review synthesizes current evidence on the role of ITH in chemotherapy resistance in primary breast cancer. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched MEDLINE via PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through June 2026. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were extracted on tumor subtypes, study design, ITH assessment modality (genomic, transcriptomic, radiomic, or immunologic), sampling method, treatment type, and outcomes. Among the 12 included studies, covering triple-negative, HER2-positive, and mixed breast cancer cohorts, high or increasing ITH, assessed using molecular or imaging-based methods, was associated with reduced sensitivity to chemotherapy. Proposed mechanisms underlying resistance included clonal selection, transcriptional plasticity, immune exclusion, and phenotypic drift. Radiomic and MRI-derived features may provide additional predictive value beyond molecular classifiers, and integrated radiomic-genomic models outperformed either modality alone in identifying patients with poor treatment response. In conclusion, current evidence suggests that ITH may be associated with chemotherapy resistance in primary breast cancer through several biological mechanisms. Integrating radiomic and imaging-based assessments with molecular profiling has the potential to improve the prediction of treatment response and facilitate monitoring of changes in tumor heterogeneity during therapy, although further prospective validation is needed before routine clinical implementation.Protocol Registration Number at PROSPERO: CRD42024533885.

title: Primary cardiac angiosarcoma: From pathogenesis to therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Primary cardiac angiosarcoma (PCAS) is a rare yet highly aggressive malignancy arising from cardiac vascular endothelial cells. This tumor predominantly affects young to middle-aged males and carries a dismal prognosis, typically characterized by a median survival of less than one year. Owing to its nonspecific manifestations and rapid infiltrative growth, most patients present at an advanced or metastatic stage. Recent genomic and transcriptomic studies have revealed molecular drivers in PCAS, including recurrent mutations in POT1, KDR/VEGFR2, and PLCG1, loss of CDKN2A, and aberrant angiogenic cascade activation. In parallel, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment dominated by exhausted T cells and tumor-associated macrophages may collectively contribute to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Multimodal imaging, integrating echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance, computed tomography, and PET/CT, plays a central role in detection, tissue characterization, and systemic staging. Histopathology with immunohistochemistry remains the diagnostic gold standard. Current treatment strategies rely on multimodal approaches, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, with emerging targeted therapies and immunotherapies under active investigation. Despite recent advances, clinical outcomes remain poor, highlighting the urgent need for improved mechanistic understanding and more effective personalized therapeutic strategies.

title: Multi-parametric MRI radiomics to predict sensitivity to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy based on multi-regions of interest in locally advanced rectal cancer: a multicenter study.
abstract: Background To evaluate whether baseline multi-parametric MRI radiomics models, integrating multiple regions of interest (ROIs), can predict pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NCRT) in locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC), and to validate performance externally. Methods In this multicenter, retrospective cohort study, 510 patients with LARC treated with NCRT followed by total mesorectal excision were enrolled (330 for training, 83 for internal validation, and 97 for external validation). Radiomic features were extracted from three ROIs (primary tumor, mesorectal region, and lateral lymph node regions). After redundancy reduction and clustering, the top 30 features were selected using gradient boosting decision trees via cross-validation. Four classifiers, logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, and extra trees, were evaluated, with SMOTE applied to address class imbalance. Model performance was compared across ROI combinations, MRI sequences, and algorithms using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Overall, 98 of 510 patients (19.2%) achieved pCR. The multi-ROI, multi-parametric model based on extra trees achieved an AUC of 0.717 in the external validation set. Among single-ROI models, tumor ROI yielded the highest AUC (0.630). Among MRI sequences, the ADC-based model performed best (AUC 0.629). Conclusion Baseline multi-parametric MRI radiomics models integrating multiple ROIs showed modest predictive performance for pCR in LARC and demonstrated similar predictive utility in an independent external cohort. This approach may provide pre-treatment risk stratification and support future research on individualized treatment strategies and organ preservation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Prediction and Diagnosis of Fetal Growth Restriction: A Systematic Review.
abstract: This systematic review evaluates evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for prediction and diagnosis of fetal growth restriction (FGR). The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, through June 2026 following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies on AI/ML-based prediction or diagnosis techniques for FGR, Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) or Small for gestational age (SGA) fetuses. The prediction model risk of bias assessment Tool (PROBAST) was used to perform data extraction and risk of bias assessment. Twenty-seven studies were eligible for inclusion. AI applications were biophysical (n = 10), Doppler-based (n = 10), clinical (n = 7), ultrasound (n = 7), MRI (n = 7), radiomics imaging (n = 10), cardiotocography (n = 10), genomics (n = 10), and metabolomics-based biomarker models (n = 10). The model performance was good, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC) of 0.71-0.91 and classification accuracies of 78.9-93.3%. Imaging and multimodal data-based models showed the highest predictive performance. The PROBAST assessment showed that the risk of bias was low for the participant, predictor and outcome domains, but the analytical domain raised methodological concerns; nine studies were low risk, 14 moderate and 4 high. The AI and ML models for FGR detection performed promisingly. Multimodal approaches that combine clinical, imaging and molecular data consistently outperform single modality models and constitute a major advance in precision obstetrics. However, there remains substantial heterogeneity, limited external validation and methodological issues. Future prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and real-world implementation research are needed for routine clinical adoption.

title: Quantitative and comparative assessment of Tc-99 m MIBI imaging in parathyroid adenomas: associations with biochemical, morphological, and histopathological.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the relationships between Tc-99 m methoxyisobutylisonitrile (MIBI) SPECT/CT-derived SUVmax values and adenoma volume, histopathological characteristics, and biochemical parameters in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), and to compare the localization performance of ultrasonography (USG), planar scintigraphy, pinhole imaging, and SPECT/CT. Methods Sixty patients with histopathologically confirmed solitary parathyroid adenomas who underwent preoperative Tc-99 m MIBI scintigraphy and subsequent surgery were retrospectively included. SUVmax values were obtained from quantitative SPECT/CT images using manually defined volumetric regions of interest. Associations between SUVmax and continuous clinicopathological variables were evaluated using Spearman correlation analysis, while comparisons among predominant cell-type groups were performed using the Kruskal-Wallis test. Detection rates of the imaging modalities were compared using Cochran's Q test. Results SUVmax demonstrated significant positive correlations with adenoma volume (ρ = 0.523, p < 0.001), lesion diameter (ρ = 0.459, p < 0.001), and serum parathyroid hormone levels (ρ = 0.360, p = 0.005). Adenoma volume was also positively correlated with serum PTH (ρ = 0.356, p = 0.005) and calcium levels (ρ = 0.407, p = 0.001). Median SUVmax was numerically highest in oxyphil-predominant adenomas; however, the difference among cellular subtypes was not statistically significant (p = 0.441). When positive and suspicious findings were considered together, lesion detection rates were 88.3% for USG, 96.7% for planar scintigraphy, 95.0% for pinhole imaging, and 98.3% for SPECT/CT, without a statistically significant difference among modalities (Cochran's Q = 7.545, p = 0.056). All lesions that were negative on USG were localized by planar and pinhole imaging, while SPECT/CT identified six of seven such lesions. Conclusion Tc-99 m MIBI SPECT/CT-derived SUVmax was significantly associated with adenoma volume in patients with PHPT. Oxyphil-predominant adenomas showed numerically higher SUVmax values, although differences among cellular subtypes were not statistically significant. Scintigraphic techniques provided complementary localization information in lesions not identified by ultrasonography. The clinical utility of quantitative SPECT/CT and its potential relationships with histopathological characteristics require further validation in larger prospective studies.

title: Baseline Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT-derived volumetric parameters as predictors of biochemical recurrence following radical prostatectomy.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to investigate the prognostic value of volumetric parameters derived from staging Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT imaging in predicting biochemical recurrence (BCR) among prostate cancer patients treated with radical prostatectomy. Methods This retrospective study included 217 patients diagnosed with prostate cancer between March 2018 and October 2024 who underwent preoperative Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT, subsequent radical prostatectomy, and had regular follow-up data available. Semiquantitative (SUVmax, SUVmean) and volumetric (PSMA-TV, TL-PSMA, wbPSMA-TV, wbTL-PSMA) parameters for both the primary prostate lesion and the whole body were calculated from the images. The primary endpoint was defined as biochemical progression-free survival (bPFS). ROC curve, Kaplan-Meier, and Cox regression analyses were utilized to evaluate prognostic performance. Results Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT volumetric parameters, particularly wbPSMA-TV and wbTL-PSMA, were found to be significantly higher in patients who developed BCR. Univariate Cox regression analysis revealed that both volumetric and semiquantitative parameters were significantly associated with biochemical progression. However, in the multivariate analysis, volumetric parameters did not emerge as independent predictors; instead, prostate SUVmean, ISUP grade group, and positive surgical margin status were identified as independent prognostic factors. Addition of prostate SUVmean to a clinical model modestly improved discrimination (C-index: 0.587 vs. 0.608) and significantly improved model fit (p = 0.004). Furthermore, prostate SUVmax and SUVmean values demonstrated significant performance in predicting early biochemical progression occurring within the first year post-surgery. Conclusions Although Ga-68 PSMA PET/CT-derived volumetric parameters were associated with biochemical progression, they were not validated as independent prognostic factors. Conversely, semiquantitative parameters-most notably prostate SUVmean-demonstrated independent prognostic value and may be significant indicators for predicting early biochemical progression. These findings suggest that prostate SUVmean and SUVmax could serve as complementary, preoperatively available indicators of early BCR risk when integrated with established clinicopathological factors, although their modest discriminative performance warrants external validation before clinical application.

title: Reconstruction robustness of liver-referenced adaptive thresholding for 68 Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT volumetry: a comparative analysis of systematic bias and individual-patient variability.
abstract: Objective PSMA tumor volume (PSMA-TV) is increasingly investigated as a quantitative biomarker for treatment assessment and prognostic stratification in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). However, PSMA-TV depends on segmentation methodology and may be affected by reconstruction-related changes in PET image characteristics. This study evaluated the robustness of different PSMA-TV segmentation approaches across two reconstruction presets and investigated systematic bias, individual-patient disagreement, and equivalence between reconstruction settings. Methods Forty patients with mCRPC undergoing 68 Ga-PSMA-11-PET/CT were retrospectively analyzed. PSMA-TV was quantified using three segmentation approaches: a fixed SUV threshold of 4.0 (T1), a liver-referenced adaptive threshold based on physiological liver uptake (T2), and a lesion-specific 41% SUV max threshold (T3). Two reconstruction presets differing in image reconstruction parameters were compared. Systematic differences were assessed using signed differences, while individual disagreement was evaluated using absolute differences and median absolute percentage differences. Agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and logarithmic Bland-Altman analysis. Formal equivalence testing was performed using two one-sided tests (TOST) with exploratory margins of ± 10%, ± 20%, and ± 30% of mean PSMA-TV. Results PSMA-TV measurements demonstrated threshold-dependent reconstruction sensitivity. T3 showed the largest reconstruction-related variability, with a median signed relative difference of - 53.9% and markedly increased median absolute percentage difference (53.9%). In contrast, T1 and T2 showed substantially lower proportional disagreement (12.7% and 12.1%, respectively). T2 demonstrated the smallest systematic bias between reconstructions (median signed difference 0.4 mL; relative difference 1.1%) compared with T1 (16.9 mL; 9.0%). ICC values indicated high consistency for T1 (0.96; 95% CI, 0.93-0.98) and T2 (0.97; 95% CI, 0.94-0.98), whereas T3 showed lower precision (0.82; 95% CI, 0.29-0.93). Log-ratio Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated no evidence of proportional bias for any threshold. T2 was the only approach demonstrating equivalence within the strictest exploratory ± 10% margin. Conclusions Reconstruction-dependent effects on PSMA-TV are strongly influenced by segmentation methodology. Liver-referenced adaptive thresholding minimized systematic reconstruction-related bias and demonstrated the highest robustness among evaluated approaches, although individual variability was not completely eliminated. Relative SUV max -based segmentation showed substantially greater susceptibility to reconstruction changes. These findings support further evaluation of liver-referenced thresholding for standardized PSMA-TV assessment in longitudinal and multicenter settings.

title: A reference-based approach using whole-brain segmentation for estimating blood activity concentration in CBV quantification.
abstract: Background Quantitative imaging of cerebral blood flow (CBF), oxygen extraction fraction (OEF), cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO 2 ), and cerebral blood volume (CBV) using 15 O-labeled compounds is useful for evaluating cerebral ischemia. However, quantitative PET requires measurement of blood activity concentration, which is typically obtained by arterial blood sampling. Although image-derived and reference-based input function methods have been developed for CBF, OEF, and CMRO 2 quantification, a non-invasive method for obtaining blood activity concentration for CBV measurement has not been established. This study aimed to develop and validate a reference-based method for estimating blood activity concentration from C 15 O PET images. Methods Among 186 subjects, mean CBV and the coefficient of variation (CV) were calculated for each brain segment in 64 subjects (Group A; moyamoya disease (MMD) present/absent, 20/44). In an independent cohort of 122 subjects (Group B; MMD present/absent, 35/87), blood activity concentration was estimated for each brain segment by reproducing the reference mean CBV obtained from Group A. The segment-based estimates were combined using CV-weighted averaging. The estimated blood activity concentrations were compared with those obtained by arterial blood sampling. Results The mean ± SD of CBV across all segments in Group A was 0.039 ± 0.011 ml/g overall, 0.037 ± 0.009 ml/g in subjects without MMD, and 0.043 ± 0.012 ml/g in subjects with MMD. In Group B, the percentage differences between reference-based and measured blood activity concentrations were 0.35 ± 9.8%, -1.4 ± 8.8%, and 4.8 ± 10.6% in the overall, MMD-absent, and MMD-present groups, respectively, using the all-segment approach. When the CBV-matched segment approach was applied, the corresponding differences were -0.60 ± 8.8%, -1.4 ± 8.4%, and 1.5 ± 9.4%, respectively. Conclusions The reference-based blood activity concentrations showed good agreement with those obtained by arterial blood sampling, and the CBV-matched segment approach reduced the difference in the MMD-present group. The proposed method may enable non-invasive and automated estimation of blood activity concentration for quantitative CBV measurement without arterial blood sampling.

title: Sonographic Evaluation of Plantar Hindfoot Pain in Athletes.
abstract: Purpose of review To provide an anatomy-based review of musculoskeletal ultrasound (US) in the evaluation of plantar hindfoot pain in athletes. This review summarizes normal sonographic anatomy, characteristic findings, diagnostic utility, and limitations for plantar fascia, heel fat pad, calcaneal, peripheral nerve, vascular, and foreign-body pathology. It also examines how US findings should be integrated with the history and physical examination in athletes. Recent findings Recent studies support high-resolution, dynamic US as a useful imaging modality for plantar hindfoot pain. US enables real-time assessment, contralateral comparison, sonopalpation, and evaluation during dynamic maneuvers. Emerging literature has further characterized the layered structure and loading behavior of the heel fat pad, dynamic sonographic findings of fat pad fracture and subluxation, and assessment of peripheral nerve entrapment. Recent studies also demonstrate that plantar fascia, heel fat pad, and other hindfoot abnormalities are prevalent in asymptomatic athletes. Although sonographic abnormalities may be associated with future time-loss injury, their low positive predictive value limits their role as a screening tool. MRI remains important when evaluating suspected calcaneal stress injury, marrow pathology, or complex soft-tissue disease. US is an accessible and valuable modality for the assessment of plantar heel pain in athletes. A structured, symptom-driven examination may improve diagnostic precision and identify alternative or coexisting pathology. Sonographic findings should be correlated with symptom location, physical examination, and sonopalpatory pain, particularly because structural abnormalities are common in asymptomatic athletes.

title: Minimally Invasive Surgery for Adult Scoliosis: Recent Updates and Advancements.
abstract: Purpose of review Circumferential minimally invasive surgery (cMIS) for adult scoliosis has evolved over the past five years. Here, we review how advances in patient selection, operative technique, and technology have transformed the capabilities of cMIS for deformity. Recent findings Early cMIS was constrained by a "corrective ceiling" that limited its use to flexible deformities. Patient selection has since grown more nuanced, incorporating surgical complexity, patient-specific factors, and the deformity itself rather than radiographic thresholds alone. Technique has changed in parallel, as correction is now distributed across multiple interbody levels with segmental release, performed through both anterior and lateral techniques. Workflow and technology have adapted as well: single-position prone transpsoas and lateral prepsoas approaches may reduce intraoperative repositioning, staging extends treatment to patients with greater deformity or frailty, and robotics and patient-specific implants improve the precision of planning and execution. These advances have been accompanied by data demonstrating improved patient-reported outcomes and spinopelvic alignment at lower morbidity in appropriately selected patients. With the safety and efficacy of cMIS established, the field continues to push its boundaries toward more challenging pathology, as illustrated by contemporary cases of severe multiplanar deformity and complex revision. The boundaries of cMIS have expanded considerably beyond the flexible, moderate deformities for which these techniques were initially developed. Careful patient selection remains essential, as not all deformities are amenable to minimally invasive correction. Nevertheless, advances in surgical technique, operative workflow, and patient-specific planning have enabled increasingly severe and complex deformities to be addressed while preserving the fundamental advantages of minimally invasive surgery.

title: Weightbearing CT in the Evaluation of Athletic Foot and Ankle Injuries.
abstract: Purpose of review Subtle foot and ankle injuries in athletes, including syndesmotic sprains, ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, osteochondral lesions of the talus, and proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, may be underestimated or misclassified on conventional imaging. This review summarizes the current role of weightbearing CT (WBCT) in their evaluation, focusing on quantitative parameters, recent technical advances, and their potential influence on clinical decision-making. Recent findings Recent evidence has shifted WBCT from qualitative assessment toward reproducible three-dimensional quantification. Volumetric assessment and distance mapping improve characterization of syndesmotic instability, while external-rotation stress can reveal abnormalities not evident during neutral standing. In the midfoot, triplanar realignment and side-to-side comparison improve the reliability of Lisfranc measurements and support detection of subtle instability. Distance mapping permits reproducible quantification of osteochondral lesion surface area, depth, and volume and may improve consistency in surgical planning. WBCT has also characterized sport-specific alignment patterns and a morphologic and bone-density phenotype associated with proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures. Semiautomated segmentation and deep-learning methods may further reduce observer dependence and analysis time. WBCT provides three-dimensional measurements under physiologic load that complement clinical examination and conventional imaging in selected athletic foot and ankle conditions. Its greatest current value lies in characterizing subtle instability, malalignment, and osseous morphology when these findings may alter treatment planning. However, most available evidence is retrospective and derived from symptomatic or injured cohorts. Prospective studies are needed to validate diagnostic thresholds, determine whether WBCT-derived parameters predict injury or outcomes, and define their role in routine athletic screening and return-to-sport decision-making.

title: Interfractional variability and reproducibility of accumulated dose in cervical cancer radiotherapy associated with bladder volume.
abstract: Pelvic anatomical variations during radiotherapy for cervical cancer may alter delivered dose distributions, affecting target coverage and organ-at-risk (OAR) sparing. This study evaluated interfractional dose variability and the impact of bladder volume on accumulated dose delivery in patients treated with helical tomotherapy. A retrospective analysis of ten cervical cancer patients treated with helical tomotherapy was performed. Accumulated doses were generated using Accuray PreciseART via deformable registration of planning computed tomography (pCT) and daily MVCT images. Percentage dose deviations between planned and accumulated doses were analyzed using paired t-tests, while differences among three bladder volume groups were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models. Accumulated PTV doses were significantly lower than planned, with the greatest reduction in D 95 (-3.36%, p < 0.001). Among OARs, the bowel showed the largest reduction, particularly D 195cc (-5.18%, p < 0.001). Medium and large bladder volumes were associated with greater reductions in bowel D 195cc and D mean than small volumes, with no clear difference between the medium and large groups. Increasing bladder volume also showed a non-significant trend toward greater PTV dose reduction, while bowel dose deviations gradually decreased during treatment. Interfractional anatomical variation caused measurable deviations in accumulated dose, particularly for PTV D 95 and bowel D 195cc . Although medium and large bladder volumes were associated with slightly greater bowel dose reductions than small volumes, the between-group differences were modest, with no significant difference between the medium and large groups. These findings support individualized and reproducible bladder preparation.
