title: Venous wash-out at contrast-enhanced ultrasound for the identification of hematologic splenic lesions: an exploratory real-world substudy.
abstract: Purpose Splenic lesions are a relatively rare but clinically relevant finding in internal medicine practice, particularly when hematologic or lymphoproliferative disorders are suspected. The aim of this exploratory subanalysis was to evaluate the role of CEUS perfusion patterns, with particular attention to venous wash-out and its timing, in discriminating between hematologic and non-hematologic disease in a real-world Internal Medicine cohort. Methods An exploratory retrospective subanalysis was conducted on patients included in the intervention arm of a multicenter Quality Improvement study evaluating a structured contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS)-based diagnostic pathway in newly identified splenic lesions. Consecutive adult patients with newly detected splenic lesions identified on B-mode ultrasound who underwent CEUS as part of the initial diagnostic evaluation were included. CEUS perfusion patterns were qualitatively classified according to arterial wash-in, venous wash-out, and wash-out timing. The diagnostic reference standard consisted of histologic and/or cytologic examination when available, or integration of clinical, laboratory, and imaging follow-up data within 90 days. In patients without histologic confirmation, non-hematologic classification required clinical and laboratory stability or improvement, stability or resolution of the splenic lesion on follow-up imaging, identification of an alternative non-hematologic diagnosis when present, and absence of a hematologic diagnosis during the 90-day follow-up. In line with the parent study, one patient in the intervention-arm cohort did not receive a definitive lesion-specific etiologic diagnosis within 90 days; however, no patient remained indeterminate for the prespecified binary endpoint because classification as hematologic versus non-hematologic was possible in all cases. The study endpoint was binary diagnostic classification (hematologic vs non-hematologic). Results Fifty patients were included, of whom 11 (22%) had a hematologic diagnosis and 39 (78%) had a non-hematologic diagnosis. In univariable analysis, multiple lesions, systemic symptoms, and especially venous wash-out were associated with hematologic diagnosis. Venous wash-out was present in 10/11 hematologic cases and in 3/39 non-hematologic cases. In hematologic cases, wash-out was almost always early (< 60 s), whereas in the few non-hematologic cases with wash-out it was late. In the exploratory multivariable model, venous wash-out was the only variable independently associated with hematologic diagnosis. Because of the small number of hematologic events, this association should be interpreted as statistically unstable and hypothesis-generating. Venous wash-out showed a sensitivity of 90.9%, specificity of 92.3%, positive predictive value of 76.9%, negative predictive value of 97.3%, and accuracy of 92.0%. Conclusion In patients with newly identified splenic lesions, venous wash-out at CEUS, particularly if early, was the pattern most strongly associated with hematologic diagnosis in this cohort. The absence of wash-out was associated with a low probability of hematologic disease, suggesting a possible utility of CEUS in diagnostic rule-out in real-world Internal Medicine settings. However, diagnostic performance estimates, particularly negative predictive value, should be interpreted cautiously in view of the low prevalence of hematologic disease and the exploratory sample size. These findings require confirmation in larger cohorts.

title: Ultrasonography after adult living donor liver transplantation: a review of vascular and biliary complications.
abstract: Living donor liver transplantation expands access to transplantation but introduces vascular and biliary reconstructions that require specific ultrasound assessment. Ultrasonography provides repeatable bedside evaluation without ionizing radiation, allowing early recognition of impaired flow and comparison with the postoperative baseline. This review examines how graft type and reconstruction affect Doppler interpretation in adult recipients, particularly after modified right-lobe transplantation. It addresses arterial, portal venous, hepatic venous, and biliary complications, with attention to measurement technique, transient postoperative changes, and limitations of diagnostic thresholds. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography helps resolve uncertain arterial patency and perfusion. Computed tomography, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, and invasive studies are selected according to the suspected complication and need for treatment.

title: Utility of ultrasonography for articular cartilage assessment in knee osteoarthritis: a comparative study with clinical scores and magnetic resonance imaging.
abstract: Objective To assess the utility of ultrasonography in evaluating femoral articular cartilage in knee osteoarthritis and to determine the relationship between sonographic cartilage abnormalities and clinical pain scores. Methods A prospective study was conducted on 63 clinically diagnosed knee osteoarthritis patients (126 knees) and 30 age-matched controls (60 knees). All participants underwent clinical evaluation and ultrasonography by two reviewers. Cartilage thickness and morphological abnormalities were assessed using a semi-quantitative sonographic grading system. Pain severity was evaluated using the visual analogue scale (VAS), and the relationship between sonographic cartilage grade and clinical pain was statistically analysed. A subgroup of 18 knees also underwent MRI for exploratory comparison of cartilage grading. Results Cartilage abnormalities were detected by USG in 97% of OA knees compared to 50% of controls (p < 0.001). Its affordability, safety, and dynamic capabilities make it a valuable adjunct for initial assessment and monitoring in routine clinical practice.

title: Performance of AI-based models in prenatal detection of trisomy 21 via ultrasonography: a systematic review.
abstract: Objective To systematically evaluate the performance, strengths, and limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) models for trisomy 21 classification and risk prediction, and for enabling ultrasound tasks, using fetal ultrasound. Methods PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception through October 2026, supplemented by manual screening of reference lists. Original, peer-reviewed studies that developed or validated AI models for trisomy 21 classification or risk prediction, or for enabling ultrasound tasks (nuchal translucency and facial marker measurement, segmentation, and plane recognition), using human fetal ultrasound images or ultrasound-derived measurements and reporting quantitative performance metrics were eligible. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias with PROBAST (prediction-model studies) and QUADAS-2 (enabling-task studies), resolving disagreements by consensus. Studies were categorized by primary task and synthesized narratively, without meta-analysis. Results Nineteen studies published between 2015 and 2026 were included: eight image-based classifiers, seven marker-based risk models, and four enabling-task studies. Image-based classifiers reported accuracies of 84-98.3% and AUCs of 0.95-0.985. Marker-based models reported AUCs of 0.84-0.983; detection rates of 90-100% at false-positive rates of about 3.6-3.9% came from one research group, whereas the largest cohort reported a sensitivity of 84% at a false-positive rate of 2.28%. Enabling-task studies were evaluated with task-specific metrics and were not compared with classification performance. Ten of fifteen prediction-model studies were at high risk of bias, mainly in the analysis domain; seven reported only image counts, and leakage between training and test data was likely in six. Most studies were retrospective with limited external validation. Conclusion Reported performance of AI models for trisomy 21 is high but comes mostly from retrospective, internally validated studies, and benefits for screening performance, invasive testing, or operator dependence have not been demonstrated. No study compared AI with cell-free DNA screening, so the role of these tools within current screening pathways remains undefined. Prospective, multicenter validation with karyotype-confirmed outcomes and standardized reporting is needed before clinical integration can be supported.

title: Sequential Pleural Fluid and Serum Biomarker Measurements in Patients Undergoing Medical Thoracoscopy for Persistently Undiagnosed Pleural Effusion: A Pilot Study from a TB-Endemic Tertiary Centre.
abstract: Introduction Pleural effusion remains diagnostically challenging when standard thoracentesis does not establish an aetiology. This pilot analysis described sequential biomarker measurements in patients proceeding to medical thoracoscopy and explored their associations and discrimination across final diagnostic classifications. Methods Prospectively collected data from a single-centre tertiary referral cohort were analysed. Pleural-fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) and serum complement components 3 and 4 (C3 and C4) were obtained on day 1, whereas pleural-fluid cancer antigen 125 (CA125) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) were obtained at the day 7/thoracoscopy evaluation. Final classifications were based on a composite reference standard integrating thoracoscopy, histopathology, microbiology, cytology, imaging, and clinical follow-up. Analyses were exploratory. Results Amongst 75 patients, 6 (8.0%) were classified as tuberculous pleural effusion (TB-PE), 33 (44.0%) as malignant pleural effusion (MPE) and 36 (48.0%) as other non-tuberculous, non-malignant pleural effusions. ADA differed across groups (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.002; Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.010) and showed exploratory discrimination for TB-PE (area under the curve [AUC] 0.934; bootstrap 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.855-0.995). At the conventional ≥ 40 U/L threshold, sensitivity was 83.3%, specificity 93.4%, positive predictive value (PPV) 55.6%, negative predictive value (NPV) 98.3%, positive likelihood ratio (LR+) 12.7, and negative likelihood ratio (LR-) 0.18. CA125, LDH, C3 and C4 did not show significant omnibus group differences after reanalysis. In a post hoc sensitivity analysis excluding 26 patients retained as non-specific pleuritis (n = 49), ADA remained significantly different across groups (P = 0.004; q = 0.022). Conclusions In this selected thoracoscopy cohort, day 1 pleural-fluid ADA showed the clearest exploratory signal, including after exclusion of non-specific pleuritis, but estimates were based on only six TB-PE cases and do not establish stand-alone utility or a role in avoiding thoracoscopy. The remaining biomarkers showed no robust aetiology-specific signal. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06159179.

title: Using a fully automated deep reasoning and learning model to distinguish bone health on computed tomography for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) and non-AIS patients: a pilot study.
abstract: Purpose Accurate evaluation of spinal bone density is essential for assessing bone health, particularly in preoperative planning for spine surgery patients. Conventional manual methods for measuring bone density are time-consuming and rely on a single slice, limiting precision and consistency. We hypothesize that a deep reasoning and learning-based (DR-AI) model can fully automate volumetric spinal bone density assessment, differentiating clinically favorable versus poor bone quality. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using preoperative low-dose CT scans from 20 patients: 10 with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) with favorable intraoperative bone quality assessment (Grade A) and 10 with neuromuscular (NM) scoliosis or neurofibromatosis (NF) demonstrating poor intraoperative bone quality (Grade D). The DR-AI model segmented and quantified volumetric Hounsfield Units (vHU) for each vertebra from T1 to L5. Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA), adjusted for age and gender, was used to compare vHU values between the cohorts. Polyserial correlations assessed association between surgeon-assigned grades and vHU measurements. Results MANOVA demonstrated differences in vHU between AIS and non-AIS cohorts from T3 to L5 (all p < 0.05). On average, AIS patients had higher mean vHU values (251.1 ± 37.9) than non-AIS patients (190.6 ± 54.9). vHU values demonstrated moderate-to-very strong correlations with surgeons' intraoperative assessment, ranging from ρ = 0.5 at T2 to ρ = 0.9 at L5. Conclusions The DR-AI model may represent a promising tool for preoperative planning, offering a faster, more objective approach for automated volumetric evaluation of vertebral bone characteristics through vHU. Future research should validate this technology in larger, more diverse cohorts. Level of evidence Level IV-Cross sectional study.

title: Development of new formulas for sex determination by three-dimensional analysis of the maxillary sinus on CBCT.
abstract: Purpose This study was designed to assess the validity of the maxillary sinus for sex determination using CBCT. Methods This study analyzed 230 CBCT scans of patients aged 18 to 50 years. The patients' CBCT records were obtained from the archives of the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology, Faculty of Dentistry, Ain Shams University. Linear and volumetric analyses of the maxillary sinus were performed using the OnDemand 3D software program. Linear analysis involved measuring the height, width, and depth of the maxillary sinus on coronal and axial views, while volumetric analysis was conducted by the software. Results Using volume for prediction achieved an accuracy of 96.5%, while height reached 92.6%. Depth, the least effective predictor, achieved an accuracy of 84.5%. There was a strong inter-observer and intra-observer agreement. Conclusion The results demonstrated that the volume of the maxillary sinus was the most significant differentiator of sex, followed by height as the next most effective variable. In contrast, the width and depth of the maxillary sinus were identified as the least reliable predictors.

title: Artificial intelligence in orthodontics: clinical maturity, evidence gaps, and emerging applications-a narrative review.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming orthodontics by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, supporting clinical decision-making, and facilitating digital workflows. This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of current AI technologies and their applications in orthodontics, including diagnostic imaging, treatment planning, treatment monitoring, patient communication, education, and emerging generative AI tools. The available evidence indicates that automated cephalometric landmark detection and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) segmentation have among the most advanced technical and external-validation evidence bases in orthodontic AI, whereas digital-model analysis has demonstrated high technical performance but more limited independent validation. However, no application met the predefined criteria for higher clinical maturity because prospective clinical effectiveness remained insufficiently established. Other emerging or experimental applications include AI-assisted treatment planning, remote monitoring, large language models (LLMs), and robotic systems, for which evidence remains predominantly retrospective, technical, feasibility-based, or early clinical. However, much of the current evidence is derived from retrospective studies, technical validation investigations, and proof-of-concept reports, with limited prospective clinical data demonstrating improvements in treatment quality, efficiency, or long-term patient outcomes. Important challenges remain regarding data quality, algorithmic bias, external validation, explainability, patient privacy, and regulatory oversight. Overall, AI should currently be regarded as a clinician-supervised decision-support tool rather than a replacement for professional expertise. Future progress is likely to depend on robust prospective clinical trials, transparent reporting, and responsible integration of AI into evidence-based orthodontic practice and the broader digital transformation of dentistry.

title: Estimation of 3D tracheal volume using regression analysis on multidetector computed tomography and quantitative deviation analysis at two different anatomical levels.
abstract: Purpose This study sought to streamline 3D tracheal volume (3D TV) assessment using routine multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) based estimation rather than time-consuming segmentation, while defining regional deviation dynamics for clinical planning. Methods 3D Slicer software was used to analyze thoracic multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) images from 147 healthy adults (71 women, 76 men) aged 18-83 years. The researchers measured tracheal length (TL), anterior-posterior diameter (TAPD), transverse diameter (TTD), subcarinal (SCA) and interbronchial (IBA) angles, and 3D TV. The magnitude of deviation was calculated in millimeters at the subcricoid (cervical) and carina (thoracic) levels. Results 3D TV (males: 34.39 ± 7.15 cm³, females: 23.89 ± 7.10 cm³), TL (males: 11.03 ± 1.12 cm, females: 9.82 ± 1.41 cm), TAPD (males: 20.89 ± 3.22 mm, females: 16.49 ± 3.08 mm), and TTD (males: median 16.97 mm, females: median 14.00 mm) were significantly higher in males (p < 0.001). Conversely, SCA was wider in females (85.98° ± 13.41°) than males (79.66° ± 12.33°) (p = 0.004). Age had no significant effect on 3D TV and deviation (p > 0.05). Rightward thoracic deviation predominated (70.75%), being significantly greater than cervical deviation (median 4.20 mm, Z = -9.25, p < 0.001). Horseshoe-shaped morphology correlated positively with thoracic deviation (r = 0.300, p = 0.019). The developed multiple linear regression model including age, sex, TL and TAPD explains 53.5% of the variance of 3D TV, with TL, sex and TAPD as significant predictors (adjusted R² = 0.535, p < 0.001). Conclusion This model allows for personalized airway assessment via two routine linear measurements and sex without requiring volumetric segmentation. The age-independent rightward thoracic deviation represents a frequently observed anatomical orientation, and these objective morphometric baseline data may inform procedural planning during invasive airway interventions.

title: Morphometric analysis and three-dimensional reconstruction of sphenoid sinus: Associations of linear dimensions and volume with pneumatization patterns and neurovascular relationships.
abstract: Background The sphenoid sinus (SS) shows morphological variability relevant to endoscopic endonasal skull-base access. This study examined associations of SS volume and linear dimensions with pneumatization patterns, extensions, and neurovascular anatomy. Methods This retrospective study included 253 adult sinus computed tomography (CT) examinations. Μaximum anteroposterior (AP max), laterolateral (LL max), and craniocaudal (CC max) dimensions were measured, and SS volume was calculated by semi-automated three-dimensional contouring with manual refinement. Pneumatization patterns and relationships with the internal carotid artery (ICA), optic nerve (ON), and Vidian nerve (VN) were examined using exploratory univariable logistic regression, supplemented by separate age- and sex-adjusted models for neurovascular outcomes. Results Mean SS volume was 11.12 ± 4.50 cm³. Males had greater volume (p = 0.001) and AP max (p = 0.013) than females. Volume correlated strongly with LL max (r = 0.791) and AP max (r = 0.705) (both p < 0.001). Each 1-mm increase in AP max was associated with posterior extension (OR = 1.57, 95% CI 1.40-1.76) and ICA (OR = 1.22), ON (OR = 1.13), and VN (OR = 1.24) protrusion and/or dehiscence. Each 1-mm increase in LL max was associated with lateral extension (OR = 1.39, 95% CI 1.28-1.52) and VN protrusion and/or dehiscence (OR = 1.24, 95% CI 1.18-1.31) (p < 0.001). Greater SS volume was associated with protrusion and/or dehiscence of all three structures, and remained associated with these neurovascular outcomes after adjustment for age and sex. Conclusions SS volume and linear dimensions provide complementary quantitative information on the magnitude and direction of pneumatization. AP max and LL max were associated with specific extension patterns and with neurovascular protrusion and/or dehiscence.

title: Comparison of Integrated Versus Sequential Artificial Intelligence-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis Systems in Breast Ultrasound: A Prospective Pilot Study on Examination Time, Reproducibility, and Diagnostic Performance.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To compare integrated and sequential artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis (AI-CAD) systems in terms of examination time, reproducibility, and diagnostic performance in breast ultrasound (US). Materials and methods This prospective single-center study included women who underwent breast US at a breast imaging center between February and March 2025. Two real-time AI-CAD systems were evaluated: an integrated system providing simultaneous lesion detection and diagnosis during scanning, and a sequential system in which lesion detection and diagnostic assessment were performed separately. Examination time was assessed in patients who underwent paired breast US examinations with both AI-CAD systems during the same visit, with randomized examination order. Reproducibility was assessed by applying both systems twice to the same breast lesions. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Examination time analysis included 97 patients and showed longer examination time with sequential AI-CAD than with integrated AI-CAD (P < .001), regardless of examination order. Reproducibility analysis included 145 patients with 215 lesions and showed almost perfect agreement between the first and second acquisitions for both systems (integrated vs. sequential: κ = 0.81 vs. 0.83). For the comparison between the first and second acquisitions, κ values for the integrated versus sequential systems were 0.92 versus 0.76 for malignant lesions, 0.79 versus 0.84 for mass lesions, and 1.00 versus 0.75 for nonmass lesions. However, agreement patterns varied across other scan-plane comparisons. Diagnostic performance analysis included 242 patients. Integrated AI-CAD showed higher sensitivity (integrated vs. sequential: 87.6% vs. 76.9%; P < .001), whereas sequential AI-CAD showed higher specificity (integrated vs. sequential: 74.2% vs. 90.0%; P < .001). AUC did not differ between the two systems. Conclusion Integrated and sequential AI-CAD systems showed complementary strengths in breast US. Integrated AI-CAD favored shorter examination time and higher sensitivity, whereas sequential AI-CAD favored higher specificity, with reproducibility differing according to lesion type.

title: CT Radiomics of Epicardial Adipose Tissue for Predicting Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia, affecting 1-2% of the general population. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) may contribute to AF through its proximity to the myocardium and coronary vessels, as well as its vasocrine and paracrine functions. Previous studies linked EAT thickness and volume with AF incidence. This review consolidates evidence on the correlation between radiomic analysis of EAT and the incidence of AF. Material and methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). Embase, PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for primary studies using CT-based EAT radiomics to predict AF. Case reports, animal studies, pediatric populations, and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)/ultrasound studies were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST, and methodological quality with the Radiomics Quality Score. Results Ten studies, including 2952 patients (53.8-81.4% male; mean age range 42.2-74.1 years), met eligibility. Six were retrospective, and four were prospective. The studies evaluated postoperative AF, AF recurrence after catheter ablation, AF detection, and AF subtype classification. Reported machine learning models included random forest, logistic regression, Cox regression, and Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). Performance metrics ranged from AUC 0.73-0.92, sensitivity 0.50-0.90 and specificity 0.53-0.98. Segmentation methods and feature extraction varied, and external validation was rare. Conclusion Machine learning models using EAT radiomic features show promise for AF prediction. However, this heterogeneity limits generalizability and precludes immediate incorporation into clinical practice.

title: Prediction of Double-Expressor Lymphoma in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Using a Non-invasive Model Based on [ 18 F] FDG PET/CT and Stacking.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To develop and validate an interpretable multimodal model integrating deep learning radiomics with clinical data using baseline [ 18 F] FDG PET/CT for non-invasive identification of the double-expressor lymphoma (DEL) in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Materials and methods The histopathological reference standard for DLBCL diagnosis and DEL subtyping was immunohistochemistry according to the 2016 WHO. Patients from January 2019 to July 2025 were retrospectively enrolled and randomly divided into training and test sets at 7:3, and a patient-level analysis was performed. Clinical, radiomics and deep learning features were extracted. After LASSO selection, individual and fusion models were constructed. Statistical analyses were performed using Python (3.6), and p-value < 0.05 was considered significant. Model performance was assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC), calibration and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHAP and a nomogram were used for interpretation. Results A total of 143 patients (82 males, 61 females, median age 61.5 years) were enrolled. ViT_KNN model achieved a test AUC of 0.936 (95%Cl 0.856-1.000), outperforming clinical (AUC 0.857, 95%Cl 0.722-0.993) and radiomics (AUC 0.706, 95%Cl 0.547-0.865) models. Late fusion, especially Stacking_LR, achieved the best performance (AUC 0.948, 95%Cl 0.865-1.000, accuracy 95.3%, specificity 100%, sensitivity 88.2%). Calibration and DCA confirmed clinical net benefit. SHAP analysis highlighted deep learning features as most influential. The Stacking_LR nomogram offers an intuitive clinical tool. Conclusion Deep learning radiomics based on baseline [ 18 F] FDG PET/CT enables effective non-invasive identification of DEL. The stacking ensemble strategy enhances multimodal fusion and provides a highly accurate, interpretable tool for DLBCL risk stratification.

title: Assessment of Pulmonary Vascular Stent Morphology Using Intra-procedural Cone-Beam CT in Fibrosing Mediastinitis: Imaging Agreement and Clinical Implications.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Percutaneous Pulmonary Vascular Stent Angioplasty (PPVSA) is a key treatment for pulmonary vascular stenosis in Fibrosing Mediastinitis (FM). This study evaluated the added value of intraoperative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) beyond conventional angiography for post-stenting assessment during PPVSA. Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included 54 consecutive FM patients who underwent PPVSA between August 2021 and May 2024, comprising 114 stents (99 arterial and 15 venous). All patients underwent intraoperative CBCT, angiography, and follow-up computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for assessment of stent geometry. Agreement between imaging modalities was evaluated using correlation, Bland-Altman, and reproducibility analyses. Associations between CBCT-derived parameters, hemodynamic outcomes, and stent patency were further explored. Results Among 54 patients (57.26 ± 11.47 years; 17 females [31.48%]), CBCT demonstrated excellent correlation with first follow-up CTPA. For maximum stent diameter, the correlation between CBCT and CTPA was r = 0.99, compared with r = 0.94 for angiography. For minimum stent diameter, the corresponding correlations were r = 0.99 and r = 0.85, respectively (all p < 0.001). Bland-Altman analysis showed smaller measurement bias and narrower limits of agreement for CBCT than for angiography. During a median imaging follow-up of 614.50 days, in-stent restenosis occurred in 15.79% of stents, whereas complete stent occlusion occurred in 1.75% of stents. Stents with a minimum-to-maximum diameter ratio <80% showed higher restenosis rates than those with a ratio ≥80% (24.00% vs. 9.38%, p = 0.017). In addition, among pulmonary arterial stents, a CBCT-derived stent relief index was positively correlated with trans-lesional systolic pressure gradient reduction (r = 0.249, p = 0.033). Conclusion Intraoperative CBCT provides reliable assessment of stent geometry during PPVSA. In addition to demonstrating strong agreement with first follow-up CTPA, CBCT-derived morphologic parameters may be associated with procedural hemodynamic improvement and may provide supplemental information regarding subsequent stent patency and long-term outcomes.

title: Ultrasound-Based Habitat Radiomics for Differentiating Phyllodes Tumor from Breast Fibroadenoma.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Phyllodes tumors (PTs) and fibroadenomas (FAs) have overlapping ultrasound (US) appearances. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an interpretable machine-learning model integrating US radiomics, habitat features, and clinical variables. Materials and methods This retrospective multicenter study included 1950 pathologically confirmed lesions (1029 FAs and 921 PTs) divided into training (n=918), validation (n=474), and test (n=558) cohorts. Nineteen voxelwise features were used for K-means habitat segmentation. The number of clusters was selected from K=2-10 in the training cohort and evaluated across 50 random seeds. Whole-lesion, habitat, and combined habitat-radiomics (HR) signatures were developed using a train-only feature-selection pipeline, and ExtraTrees was selected as the classifier. The final combined model was built by probability-level late fusion of the ExtraTrees HR model and a logistic clinical model based on age, lesion size, and orientation. Results K=3 yielded the highest Calinski-Harabasz index (200,927.01). Clustering was stable across 50 random seeds, with mean adjusted Rand indices of 0.9942, 0.9948, and 0.9941 in the training, validation, and test cohorts, respectively. Feature selection retained 39 whole-lesion features and 34 habitat features (habitats 1-3: 1, 14, and 19). The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.921 (95% CI, 0.904-0.939), 0.797 (95% CI, 0.754-0.835), and 0.844 (95% CI, 0.813-0.877) in the training out-of-fold, validation, and test cohorts. Conclusion In this multicenter cohort, a model integrating US habitat radiomics with age, lesion size, and orientation differentiated PTs from FAs with consistent discrimination across data partitions. Shapley additive explanations analysis provided global and case-level explanations of the combined prediction.

title: Retrospective Evaluation of the D-Dimer in Patients Undergoing CTPA for PE Evaluation.
abstract: Objective Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) is the choice imaging modality for diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE). Studies have demonstrated more appropriate use of CTPA following implementation of the Wells or Revised Geneva scores and/or D-dimer level thresholds into clinical frameworks. During the study period, these measures were not required prior to ordering a CTPA at our institution. The aim of this study was to retrospectively evaluate the institutional utilization and ordering patterns preceding CTPA for evaluation of PE, with focus on the laboratory D-dimer test. Methods This retrospective chart review included patients that underwent CTPA for suspected PE between January 1, 2022 and December 31, 2022. Data included clinical factors, D-dimer levels, CTPA results, and subspecialty of ordering providers. Statistical analyses were performed via SAS v9.4. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Results A total of 660 patients were included in this study, with 54 positives for PE (8.2%). title: Early Prediction of Insufficient Response to Ursodeoxycholic Acid: A Multimodal Model Based on Radiomics and Clinical Indicators.
abstract: Rationale and objectives This study aimed to integrate two-dimensional ultrasound (2D-US) radiomics and clinical indicators to develop a prediction model for early identification of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) patients with insufficient response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) at 6 months. Materials and methods 136 PBC patients were enrolled. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression was applied to select key features and construct a radiomics model. Six machine learning algorithms were compared using 5-fold nested cross-validation. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression were performed to identify independent clinical predictors and construct a clinical model. By combining the radiomics score and significant clinical factors using multivariate logistic regression analysis, a combined model was subsequently developed. Model performance was evaluated by AUC, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis. Results The support vector machine (SVM) algorithm achieved the highest mean AUC (0.696 ± 0.028) and the lowest coefficient of variation (4.055%) in nested cross-validation. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and platelet count (PLT) were independent predictors of insufficient response to UDCA. The combined model achieved an AUC of 0.865 in the test set, higher than those of the clinical model (0.778) and the radiomics model (0.833). The response status at 6 months was highly consistent with that at 12 months (kappa = 0.809). The model showed generally consistent predictive performance across different UDCA response criteria and histological fibrosis stages. Conclusions A noninvasive multimodal model based on pretreatment 2D-US radiomics features, ALP, and PLT can accurately predict the insufficient response to UDCA in PBC patients at an early stage.

title: Validation of Automated 3D MRI Knee Cartilage Measurements.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To assess the agreement between automated cartilage thickness measurements derived from three-dimensional (3D) dual-echo steady-state (DESS) magnetic resonance imaging and manual radiologist measurements. Materials and methods In 111 patients, cartilage thickness measurements across 21 knee subregions were compared between an automated segmentation software and manual radiologist measurements on 3D DESS and proton density (PD) fat-suppressed sequences. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis, Pearson correlation, and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). A post-hoc calibration approach was applied to both comparisons. Intersequence variability between PD manual and DESS manual measurements served as a benchmark. Results The automated method showed a systematic overestimation relative to the PD manual (bias +0.7 mm) and the DESS manual (bias +0.9 mm). After calibration, bias was eliminated. Postcalibration ICC improved substantially (PD: from 0.29-0.61; DESS: from 0.18-0.67), reaching levels comparable to the intersequence benchmark (ICC = 0.73). Per-region analysis revealed the greatest variability in patellar and lateral tibial subregions. Conclusion Following a simple global calibration, automated cartilage thickness measurements achieve overall acceptable agreement with manual reference measurements that is comparable to inherent intersequence variability. This supports the clinical acceptability of the automated approach as an efficient and reproducible alternative to manual segmentation.

title: A Multicenter Ultrasound Habitat Radiomics Framework For Diagnosing Tuberculous Lymphadenitis And Stratifying Rifampicin Resistance Risk.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To develop and validate an ultrasound-based habitat radiomics framework for the hierarchical differentiation of tuberculous lymphadenitis (TBLN) from non-tuberculous lymphadenopathy, and to noninvasively predict rifampicin resistance risk using an independently collected cohort of patients with confirmed TBLN. Materials and methods In this multicenter retrospective study, 618 patients with superficial lymphadenopathy who underwent ultrasound examination between January 2022 and December 2025 at four tertiary hospitals were included. Among them, 530 patients with definitive diagnoses were used for diagnostic differentiation and were divided into a model-development (training) cohort and an external validation cohort, while 236 patients with confirmed tuberculous lymphadenitis (TBLN) were included for rifampicin resistance risk assessment. Based on standardized B-mode ultrasound images, we developed a 2-stage ultrasound habitat radiomics framework that first differentiated tuberculous from non-tuberculous lymph nodes. Rifampicin resistance risk was assessed within the confirmed TBLN cohort using nested cross-validated out-of-fold predictions. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA), and model interpretability was assessed using SHAP-based methods. Results For differentiating tuberculous from non-tuberculous lymph nodes, the habitat-based model demonstrated strong discriminative performance, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.83 in the training cohort and maintaining consistent performance in the external test cohort. Using nested cross-validated out-of-fold predictions within the confirmed TBLN cohort, the habitat-based model achieved an AUC of 0.83 for predicting rifampicin resistance, outperforming conventional radiomics and demonstrating superior clinical net benefit. Spatial visualization revealed that high-risk habitats were localized to specific intralesional regions, underscoring the importance of spatial heterogeneity in both disease diagnosis and drug resistance assessment. Conclusion Ultrasound-based habitat radiomics provides an interpretable and clinically applicable framework for hierarchical diagnosis of tuberculous lymphadenitis and for rifampicin resistance risk assessment in an independent patient cohort, supporting precision imaging-guided management of tuberculosis.

title: Development and Validation of an Interpretable Machine Learning Model Based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI for Evaluating Small HCC (≤2 cm): A Multicenter Cohort Study.
abstract: Rationale and objectives This study aims to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine-learning model that integrates gadolinium ethoxybenzyl diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics, qualitative MRI features, and clinical data to accurately distinguish small (≤2 cm) hepatocellular carcinomas from benign hepatic lesions. Materials and methods This retrospective, multicenter cohort included 296 lesions (Center A: 209 [146 training, 63 internal test]; Centers B + C: 87 external validation). Three feature categories were extracted and integrated. A multistep feature selection and model tuning pipeline was performed exclusively within the training set using nested cross-validation to prevent data leakage. Seven machine learning (ML) algorithms were compared. In the external validation set, a reader study was performed to compare the diagnostic performance of the fusion model against that of radiologists. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was employed to interpret the optimal model. Results The fusion model combining three feature categories achieved the best diagnostic performance. In the internal test set, the fusion model yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.913, compared to 0.791 for the radiomics-only model. Its discriminative ability remained robust in an independent external validation cohort (AUC = 0.824), and remained stable after mitigating interscanner variability with ComBat harmonization (AUC = 0.806). The fusion model showed numerically higher performance than junior radiologists and performed comparably to senior radiologists. SHAP analysis identified hepatitis B virus status, alpha-fetoprotein, and specific hepatobiliary phase-derived radiomics features as key predictors. Conclusion An interpretable ML fusion model demonstrates robust discriminative ability for evaluating small HCCs. Although its numerical advantages over the radiomics-only model and junior radiologists did not reach statistical significance because of the limited external sample size, this noninvasive tool holds significant potential as a reliable diagnostic adjunct with future dynamic threshold optimization.

title: Echogenic Rind as an Independent Diagnostic and Prognostic Marker of Malignancy.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Echogenic rind has been incorporated into the BI-RADS v2025 ultrasound lexicon as an associated feature of masses; however, its utility as an independent diagnostic and prognostic marker of malignancy has not been well established. This retrospective study compares the imaging and phenotypic features of biopsy-proven malignant masses with and without an echogenic rind to assess its utility as an imaging marker. Materials and methods Consecutive patients with biopsy-proven malignant masses were placed into separate cohorts based on the presence/absence of an echogenic rind. An echogenic rind was defined as an ≥1 mm echogenic band that surrounded at least 25% of the mass circumference and disrupted adjacent tissue. Imaging characteristics (size, shape, margins, orientation), tumor type (ductal carcinoma in situ [DCIS], invasive ductal carcinoma, and invasive lobular carcinoma), receptor status, and Nottingham grades of masses in both cohorts were compared using Fisher's exact test and multivariate analysis. A separate cohort of consecutive patients with biopsy-proven DCIS presenting as masses was then reviewed to assess the proportion of masses with an echogenic rind and upgrade to invasive malignancy on surgical pathology. Results Masses with an echogenic rind were associated with invasive breast cancer (P = 0.001) and had higher upgrade rates when core biopsy revealed DCIS (P = 0.04). Masses in both cohorts did not vary by size (P = 0.41), shape (P = 0.44), or margin (P = 0.62), or demonstrate significant differences in receptor status (P = 0.98) or Nottingham grade (P = 0.85). Conclusion Presence of an echogenic rind surrounding a mass is associated with invasive malignancy and correlates with upgrade of DCIS to invasive cancer on surgical pathology but otherwise offers minimal additional diagnostic or prognostic utility to radiologists.

title: Multimodal Carotid Ultrasound-based Artificial Intelligence Model for Predicting Acute Ischemic Stroke Risk in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are at high risk of acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet accurate risk stratification remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and validate a multimodal model based on carotid ultrasound for improved AIS risk prediction. Materials and methods In this multicenter retrospective study, a total of 480 patients with T2DM who underwent carotid ultrasound were recruited from two centers, with one center (n=394) used for model development and the other (n = 86) for independent external testing. A dual-scale deep learning framework based on a Swin Transformer was developed to capture both local plaque features and surrounding vascular context. Deep learning features were integrated with radiomic and clinical features to construct a multimodal model. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), along with calibration and decision curve analysis. Results The multimodal model achieved AUCs of 0.952 (95% CI: 0.910-0.984) in the internal cohort and 0.939 (95% CI: 0.838-0.996) in the external cohort, showing improved performance compared to single-modality models. In the reader study, AI-assisted interpretation improved diagnostic performance across all readers, with AUC increases ranging from 0.760 to 0.857 and from 0.868 to 0.929 for senior readers, and from 0.450 to 0.700 and from 0.548 to 0.659 for junior readers. Generalized estimating equation analyses showed significant improvements in diagnostic correctness among both senior and junior readers, with P values of 0.00235 and 0.000343, respectively. Conclusion A multimodal framework integrating carotid ultrasound with clinical, radiomic, and deep learning features enables improved AIS risk stratification in patients with T2DM.

title: Intratumoral and Peritumoral Ultrasoundomics Models for Preoperative Prediction of Pathological Complete Response to Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy in Breast Cancer.
abstract: Rationale and objectives This study investigated the clinical utility of a machine learning (ML) model based on ultrasoundomics features (UFs) from primary foci to predict pathological complete response (pCR) in patients with breast cancer (BC) undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). Materials and methods Ultrasound images from 333 patients with BC treated with NAC were retrospectively analyzed. Patients in the internal training cohort and external validation cohort were from two different hospitals, respectively. Tumor regions of interest (ROI) were delineated, and outward segmentation of the peritumor area was performed, using the ROI edge as a baseline and expanding it by 3 mm and 5 mm, respectively. This resulted in three distinct segmentation images: ROI (intratumoral region), ROI (intratumoral region + 3-mm peritumoral region), and ROI (intratumoral region + 5-mm peritumoral region). Three sets of UFs were extracted, normalized using the Z-score method, and further refined through Spearman correlation analysis and LASSO for feature selection. Eight ML models (R0), based on key UFs in ROI (intratumoral region), were compared: support vector machine, K-nearest neighbor, random forest, Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, AdaBoost (AB), multilayer perceptron, and light gradient boosting machine learning. The optimal ML models were evaluated using diagnostic performance metrics, including AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. The best-performing algorithm was then applied to construct ML models (R3 and R5) incorporating ROI (intratumoral region + 3-mm peritumoral region) and ROI (intratumoral region + 5-mm peritumoral region). Predictive efficacy and clinical utility were assessed through decision curve analysis (DCA) and Shapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP), which quantified feature importance and facilitated model visualization and interpretation. title: Multicenter Comparative Validation of an nnU-Net-Based Automated CT Radiomics Workflow for Acute Pancreatitis Severity Prediction.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Computed tomography radiomics has shown potential for predicting acute pancreatitis (AP) severity, but conventional workflows depend on labor-intensive expert pancreatic segmentation. This study evaluated a no-new-Net (nnU-Net)-based automated segmentation-radiomics workflow against an expert manual-segmentation workflow, using AP severity classification as the downstream task, and assessed the automated workflow externally. Materials and methods This retrospective multicenter study included patients with AP from Center A (n = 214), Center B (n = 56), and Center C (n = 42). Expert manual pancreatic masks served as reference annotations for nnU-Net training and as the comparator for the radiomics workflow. After selecting the optimal nnU-Net configuration, radiomics features were extracted separately from manual and automated regions of interest, and AP severity classifiers were developed using the same analytical framework. Discrimination between the two workflows was compared in the independent internal test cohort using the area under the curve (AUC) and the paired DeLong test, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) and Bonferroni corrections applied to P values. Results In the internal test cohort, the Light Gradient Boosting Machine classifier achieved AUCs of 0.799 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.683-0.915) and 0.733 (95% CI, 0.593-0.873) with manual and automated segmentations, respectively. The absolute AUC difference was 0.066, and the paired DeLong comparison was not statistically significant after FDR correction (FDR-adjusted p = 0.360; Z = 1.1755, unadjusted p = 0.2398). The automated workflow achieved AUCs of 0.784 (95% CI, 0.653-0.915) in Center B and 0.715 (95% CI, 0.559-0.871) in Center C. The selected 2D nnU-Net achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.798 during five-fold cross-validation and 0.726 in the independent internal test cohort. Conclusion The nnU-Net-based automated segmentation-radiomics workflow showed no significant difference in discrimination compared with the expert manual workflow in the internal test cohort. It also maintained moderate discrimination across two external cohorts. These findings support the feasibility of reducing dependence on manual pancreatic segmentation, although the present analysis does not establish formal equivalence or interchangeability.

title: Added Value of CT Bone Reading Software in the Detection of Subtle Bone Metastases From Breast Cancer: Comparison with Standard Thorax CT.
abstract: Rationale and objectives The aim of this study is to evaluate the additional diagnostic value of CT Bone Reading software in detecting rib metastases on thoracic computed tomography in patients with breast cancer and to examine its effectiveness on lesion detection, evaluation time, and inter-reader agreement. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 110 patients with breast cancer and bone metastases who underwent both thoracic computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography-CT scans between January 2022 and January 2026. For lesion-level assessment, suspected rib lesions were also evaluated using available longitudinal follow-up imaging. Two radiologists independently evaluated conventional CT and CT Bone Reading images in separate reading sessions at least 2 weeks apart. Inter-reader agreement was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Cohen's κ statistic. Results In lesion-based analysis with conventional CT, Reader 1 detected 510 lesions (81.6%) and Reader 2 detected 577 lesions (92.3%), while CT Bone Reading allowed for the detection of an additional 115 (22.5%) and 48 (8.3%) lesions for Readers 1 and 2, respectively. The additionally detected lesions demonstrated a non-uniform distribution, with a marked predominance in the mid-rib region (levels 5th-8th). CT Bone Reading-assisted evaluation enabled the detection of significantly smaller lesions compared to routine CT for both readers (Reader 1: 8.0 mm vs 5.0 mm; Reader 2: 7.0 mm vs 5.0 mm; P < 0.001 for both). Evaluation time was significantly decreased from 129.22 ± 27.22 s to 64.94 ± 17.16 s for Reader 1 and from 122.99 ± 26.04 s to 64.44 ± 18.71 s for Reader 2 (P < 0.001 for both). Inter-reader agreement was excellent for measurements obtained by CT Bone Reading-derived evaluation (ICC ≥0.965; κ ≥0.947). Conclusion CT Bone Reading software increases the detection rates of rib lesions, reduces interpretation times, and demonstrates excellent inter-reader reproducibility compared to conventional CT assessment, with less experienced readers achieving the highest incremental throughput. By providing a comprehensive and continuous view of the ribs, this technique has the potential to improve diagnostic performance without additional radiation exposure, particularly in anatomically complex regions such as the mid ribs. Ultimately, this approach can enhance workflow efficiency during routine clinical practices.

title: Implementation of a Structured Peer Learning Program and Missed Critical Findings in a Large Integrated Radiology Practice: A Baseline Retrospective Analysis.
abstract: Rationale and objectives The American College of Radiology (ACR) defines peer learning as nonpunitive, education-centered case review, separated from individual performance evaluation. We describe a program designed against ACR criteria in a large integrated practice and report first-cycle metrics, including missed critical findings-a narrow subset of major misses. Materials and methods This retrospective analysis spanned 283 radiologists across more than 100 sites between March 30 and May 14, 2026. Cases entered through voluntary worklist submission, risk-event referral, and departmental escalation, and were adjudicated by a fellowship-trained coordinator. A missed critical finding (MCF) required both a finding on the institutional critical results list (provider notification within 30 minutes) and a 4B classification, with agreement between two independent reviewers. Exact (Poisson) 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Results Of 702 submissions, 489 (69.7%) were Learning Opportunities, 187 (26.6%) Great Calls, and 26 (3.7%) Agrees. Of 283 radiologists, 182 (64.3%) submitted at least one case, and 213 (75.3%) received feedback; two conferences were held. Of 17 candidates, reviewers concurred on 7 at initial review; the 10 discordant were resolved by consensus, none meeting criteria. Across 409,122 interpreted studies, the confirmed MCF rate was 0.017 per 1000 (95% CI 0.007-0.035). Seven radiologists (2.5%) had one event; none had more. No confirmed event had been independently filed as a safety event. Conclusion The MCF rate reflects a narrow, time-critical subset ascertained with unmeasured sensitivity against a diluted denominator. It is a conservative internal baseline, not a measure of diagnostic accuracy or individual performance.

title: Hyperintense Vessel Sign on High-Resolution Vessel Wall MRI and Perfusion Decompensation in Intracranial Atherosclerotic Disease: Burden Versus Proximal Extent.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To investigate the relationship between hyperintense vessel sign (HVS) on high-resolution magnetic resonance vessel wall imaging (HR-VWI) and cerebral perfusion decompensation in patients with intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion. Materials and methods This retrospective cohort included 128 patients with unilateral intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion undergoing HR-VWI and computed tomography perfusion. HVS was scored by vessel count and classified by extent (type 0, none; type 1, M3-M4; type 2, M1-M2); local collaterals were assessed on time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography. Prespecified Firth-penalized regression, bootstrap-validated threshold modeling, hierarchical likelihood-ratio tests, and collateral-phenotype analysis compared grade 2 versus grade 1. Results The study cohort comprised 128 patients (92 males, 36 females), with a mean age of 55.08 ± 10.58 years. 85 patients were grade 1, 43 grade 2. HVS score was independently associated with decompensation (odds ratio [OR], 1.09, P = 0.04), with an exploratory cutoff at 8 (bootstrap 95% confidence interval [CI], 6-8; adjusted OR, 6.93, P < 0.01). Grade-2 proportions differed across type 0/1/2 (25.00%/22.67%/63.64%); type 2 exceeded type 1 (adjusted OR 8.06, P < 0.01). Classification, not the score, added incremental value (likelihood ratio P < 0.01 vs reverse P = 0.15). Type 1 with collateral present marked compensation (5.88%; negative predictive value 0.94); type 2 with collateral absent marked decompensation (66.67%; adjusted OR = 33.90, P < 0.01). Score ≥8 gave 0.65 sensitivity and 0.80 specificity; combined-model area under the curve was 0.83 (95% CI, 0.75-0.90; optimism-corrected 0.79). Conclusion HVS score provides an exploratory screening cutoff, whereas proximal HVS extension into M1-M2 is strongly associated with decompensation; distal-limited HVS with local collateral formation marks compensation. Prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Open-Weight Large Language Models for Pathological Brain MRI Reports Classification: From Prompts to a Fine-Tuned Model.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Automated semantic classification of radiology reports can enhance clinical workflows and research, but often relies on language- and task-specific models, limiting scalability. This study aims to evaluate and improve the 0-shot baseline performance of open-weight large language models (LLMs) in the semantic classification of free-text magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reports. Materials and methods A corpus of 1385 reports from a single neuroradiology center was used to assess four LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-Small-2509, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) of comparable scale (∼20-35B parameters). The brain MRI reports were labeled as Pathological or Non-Pathological, with the Pathological ones further classified into five diagnostic categories (Neoformation, Vascular, Inflammation/Infection, Neurodegenerative, Other). The LLMs were evaluated using zero- and few-shot prompting with majority-vote aggregation. Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning was then applied to the best-performing model across multiple configurations. Performance was assessed using Macro F1, Micro F1, Precision, Recall, and Exact Match Accuracy. Results The binary classification task achieved a Macro F1 score of 0.84 on the best-performing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B model, while multilabel classification reached 0.81. Majority voting (MV) outperformed individual-set predictions. QLoRA fine-tuning yielded a Macro F1 score of 0.83 on the multilabel task; the improvement over the 0-shot baseline was statistically supported for Macro F1, Micro F1, Macro Precision, and Exact Match, whose bootstrap 95% confidence intervals excluded zero, but not for Macro Recall. Fine-tuning and few-shot prompting strategies are complementary, with neither consistently outperforming the other. Error analysis showed that the models struggled with borderline annotation cases and often missed secondary labels. Conclusion Open-weight LLMs demonstrate strong capability for neuroradiology report classification without extensive task-specific training. Fine-tuning further improves performance, supporting integration into scalable semantic radiology data pipelines. However, the present evidence comes from a single Italian center without external validation, and the fine-tuning gain was estimated on a small held-out test set, for which the Macro F1 improvement, though statistically significant, has a confidence interval with a lower bound close to zero. In this light, the approach is best positioned as an internal indexing and semantic-retrieval tool, supporting faster report retrieval, structured cohort identification, internal audit, and scalable phenotyping for neuroradiology research and data warehousing, as well as efficient active-learning strategies, with broader generalizability requiring additional external multicentre validation before clinical deployment.

title: Mammography and Ultrasonography for Symptomatic Male Breast Lesions: A PRISMA-DTA Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Male breast disease is uncommon, but symptomatic men require reliable differentiation between benign conditions and lesions warranting biopsy or oncologic management. This PRISMA-DTA (Preferred Reporting Items for a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies) systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility, and evidentiary limitations of mammography and ultrasonography for malignant versus benign male breast lesions. Materials and methods PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 30, 2026. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO before journal submission (CRD420261429183). Eligible reports evaluated mammography or ultrasonography in male breast disease and provided extractable 2 × 2 diagnostic data. Methodological quality was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2. Diagnostic accuracy was synthesized separately for each modality using bivariate random-effects modeling and summary receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results Thirteen eligible reports were included. Seven mammography datasets and five ultrasonography datasets were available for quantitative synthesis. Mammography showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.840 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.705-0.921) and a specificity of 0.951 (95% CI, 0.884-0.980), whereas ultrasonography showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.775-0.941) and a specificity of 0.958 (95% CI, 0.869-0.987). Although pooled specificity estimates were high, their magnitude may have been influenced by heterogeneous diagnostic thresholds, differential verification, variable follow-up, and sparse malignant case counts. Nine of 13 reports were judged to have an overall high risk of bias, and consistent paired head-to-head data were lacking. Conclusion Current evidence supports mammography and ultrasonography as complementary tools in risk-stratified assessment of symptomatic male breast lesions. Pooled estimates should be interpreted cautiously because the evidence base is small and methodologically limited. Current data do not establish direct modality superiority, do not justify biopsy avoidance when clinical-imaging discordance persists, and do not determine the incremental value of routine combined imaging.

This PRISMA-DTA (Preferred Reporting Items for a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies) systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility, and evidentiary limitations of mammography and ultrasonography for malignant versus benign male breast lesions.

PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 30, 2026. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO before journal submission (CRD420261429183). Eligible reports evaluated mammography or ultrasonography in male breast disease and provided extractable 2 × 2 diagnostic data. Methodological quality was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2. Diagnostic accuracy was synthesized separately for each modality using bivariate random-effects modeling and summary receiver operating characteristic analysis.

Results

Thirteen eligible reports were included. Seven mammography datasets and five ultrasonography datasets were available for quantitative synthesis. Mammography showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.840 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.705-0.921) and a specificity of 0.951 (95% CI, 0.884-0.980), whereas ultrasonography showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.775-0.941) and a specificity of 0.958 (95% CI, 0.869-0.987). Although pooled specificity estimates were high, their magnitude may have been influenced by heterogeneous diagnostic thresholds, differential verification, variable follow-up, and sparse malignant case counts. Nine of 13 reports were judged to have an overall high risk of bias, and consistent paired head-to-head data were lacking.

Conclusion

Current evidence supports mammography and ultrasonography as complementary tools in risk-stratified assessment of symptomatic male breast lesions. Pooled estimates should be interpreted cautiously because the evidence base is small and methodologically limited. Current data do not establish direct modality superiority, do not justify biopsy avoidance when clinical-imaging discordance persists, and do not determine the incremental value of routine combined imaging.

title: CT-based Multimodal Model for Early Severity Prediction in Hyperlipidemic Acute Pancreatitis: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To develop and validate a multimodal model integrating pancreatic parenchymal and peripancreatic fat radiomics with independent clinical predictors for early severity stratification in hyperlipidemic acute pancreatitis (HLAP). Materials and methods This retrospective multicenter study included 356 patients with HLAP from three centers. HLAP was defined as acute pancreatitis (AP) with serum triglycerides ≥11.3 mmol/L or 5.65 to 11.3 mmol/L, accompanied by lactescent serum after exclusion of other etiologies. Patients from Center 1 were assigned to the training (n = 193) and internal validation (n = 83) cohorts, whereas patients from Centers 2 and 3 formed the external test cohort (n = 80). One noncontrast abdominal computed tomography examination acquired within 72 hours of symptom onset was analyzed per patient. Clinical, radiomics, and fusion models were developed using four machine-learning algorithms. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, decision curve analysis, and DeLong tests. Results The cohort included 107 patients with severe AP and 249 with nonsevere AP. The median age was 37.0 years (interquartile range, 31.75-45.0), and 268 patients (75.3%) were male. The final pancreatic parenchyma-peripancreatic fat-clinical combined model achieved AUCs of 0.947 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.897-0.986) and 0.846 (95% CI, 0.735-0.940) in the internal validation and external test cohorts, respectively, with external sensitivity and specificity of 0.611 and 0.871. DeLong testing showed significant improvements over the pancreatic parenchyma radiomics, 15 mm peripancreatic fat radiomics, and clinical models in internal validation (all p < 0.05), but not in external testing (all p > 0.05). Conclusion The proposed multimodal model showed good discrimination and interpretability for early HLAP severity stratification and may support individualized clinical decision-making.

title: Full-Cohort Organ Dose Assessment from Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening in the National Lung Screening Trial.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Organ-specific dose estimates are needed to characterize radiation exposure from repeated low-dose computed tomography (CT) lung cancer screening in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). The objective was to estimate study-level doses and participant-level cumulative doses in the NLST CT screening cohort. Materials and methods This retrospective dosimetry study included 25,051 NLST CT screening participants from the Lung Screening Study and American College of Radiology Imaging Network components after excluding participants with any examination lacking a valid manufacturer-appropriate tube current-time input. Image-series metadata were linked with age, sex, height, and weight, and then valid records were grouped into 69,601 study-level screening examinations. Organ absorbed doses and effective dose were calculated using the National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for Computed Tomography with sex- and body-size-specific adult phantoms. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was assessed with 50 stochastic simulations. Results Participants underwent a mean of 2.78 study-level screening examinations; the median study-level volume CT dose index was 3.30 mGy. Median (interquartile range) study-level lung, breast, heart wall, active marrow, and effective doses were 3.93 (3.13-4.96), 3.94 (3.14-5.04), 3.94 (3.14-5.01), and 1.26 (0.99-1.60) mGy, and 2.07 (1.65-2.59) mSv, respectively. Corresponding cumulative participant-level doses were 11.30 (8.89-14.50), 11.39 (9.01-14.75), 11.41 (8.93-14.66), and 3.63 (2.79-4.66) mGy, and 5.94 (4.69-7.64) mSv. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was greatest for thyroid dose (mean coefficient of variation, 21.1%) and low for in-field organs. Conclusion Using NLST low-dose CT screening data, we estimated participant-level cumulative organ and effective doses and characterized variation across organs and body-size groups.

title: Ultra-High Gradient Thin-Slice Oblique Coronal Zoomed DWI for Perihilar and Distal Cholangiocarcinomas: Improved Tumor Depiction for Precise Surgical Planning.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Accurate preoperative assessment of extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (eCCA) remains challenging with conventional imaging. This study aimed to investigate the value of thin-slice oblique coronal zoomed diffusion-weighted imaging (OC-Z-DWI) on an ultra-high gradient system for eCCA (including both perihilar and distal subtypes) assessment. Materials and methods This prospective study enrolled 93 patients with pathologically diagnosed eCCA (54 males, 66.8 ± 9.0 years; 62 perihilar and 31 distal) and 43 patients without eCCA (19 males, 62.9 ± 11.8 years). All patients underwent conventional magnetic resonance imaging and OC-Z-DWI on an ultra-high gradient system (200 mT/m amplitude). Image quality of OC-Z-DWI was evaluated, and diagnostic performance and lesion sizing were compared between the conventional protocol and one incorporating OC-Z-DWI. Results OC-Z-DWI showed good scoring in noise, artifacts, and overall image quality (mean 3.83 ± 0.41, 3.65 ± 0.56, and 3.80 ± 0.43, respectively). Adding OC-Z-DWI to the conventional protocol significantly improved lesion edge sharpness (3.89 ± 0.31 vs 3.60 ± 0.53, P < 0.001), lesion conspicuity (3.94 ± 0.25 vs 3.75 ± 0.46, P < 0.001), diagnostic confidence (3.86 ± 0.38 vs 3.58 ± 0.65, P < 0.001), and diagnostic performance (AUC 0.917 vs 0.869, P = 0.018). Lesion size measurements with the OC-Z-DWI-based protocol demonstrated strong pathological correlation (r = 0.822), with lower pathological-imaging diameter discrepancy than the conventional protocol (median 4.0 mm vs 7.0 mm, P < 0.001). These improvements were consistent across both perihilar and distal subgroups. Furthermore, R0 resection patients exhibited a stronger imaging-pathology sizing correlation than R1 patients (r = 0.891 vs 0.528, P = 0.021). Conclusion Ultra-high gradient thin-slice OC-Z-DWI provides high-quality images for eCCA characterization. Adding OC-Z-DWI to the conventional magnetic resonance protocol enhances lesion delineation, diagnostic performance, and tumor sizing accuracy, delivering more precise preoperative information to optimize surgical planning.

title: Retrospective Lung-RADS v2022 Characterization of Fatal Lung Cancer Cases in the National Lung Screening Trial.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Persistent lung cancer mortality despite screening is multifactorial. Characterizing computed tomography (CT) findings preceding fatal lung cancer may identify imaging features and screening challenges that warrant further study. Materials and methods We conducted a retrospective, outcome-enriched case series nested within the 26,722-participant low-dose computed tomography arm of the National Lung Screening Trial. Among 359 participants who died of lung cancer within the prespecified interval, exclusions for positive baseline screening (n = 186), incomplete screening (n = 28), withdrawal/declined screening (n = 19), unavailable CTs (n = 6), or three negative screens followed by death 2+ years after the final screen (n = 29) yielded 91 participants. Screening CTs were retrospectively assessed using the Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) v2022. Four thoracic radiologists independently reviewed visible-in-retrospect nodules and adjudicated whether they met criteria for suspicion. Results Of 91 participants, 22 (24%; 95% confidence interval (CI), 17%-34%) had visible-in-retrospect nodules considered suspicious under Lung-RADS v2022 ("missed"), 16 (18%; 95% CI, 11%-27%) had visible nodules not meeting suspicion criteria ("not callable"), 50 (55%; 95% CI, 45%-65%) had no visible-in-retrospect nodule, and 3 (3.3%) were inconclusive. Missed nodules were frequently juxtapleural (41%), obscured (50%), or irregularly bordered (68%); not-callable nodules were frequently <6 mm (75%), juxtapleural (56%), or irregularly bordered (56%). Conclusion In this selected fatal-case series, small and juxtapleural nodules were common among visible nodules not meeting Lung-RADS v2022 suspicion criteria. These findings warrant evaluation in representative screening populations and should not be interpreted as estimates of population-level Lung-RADS performance.

title: A Hybrid Human-AI Workflow for Ultrasound Report Quality Control: A Multicenter Performance and Efficiency Evaluation.
abstract: Rationale and objectives This study evaluated a hybrid human-AI workflow for ultrasound report quality assurance using multicenter retrospective data. Materials and methods 786 anonymized ultrasound reports covering 22 examination categories were collected from four hospitals. Reports containing naturally occurring or implanted errors were matched across arms. GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 performed initial screening before review by six human reviewers (HRs). HR with blinded expert over-reading (HR-ex) served as control. Accuracy, false-positive (FP) and false-negative (FN) rates, and review time were compared. Supplementary validation compared HR and DeepSeek-assisted review using 1680 consecutive reports without implanted errors. Results Hybrid workflow (HYB) accuracy was comparable to HR (4o-HYB 80.2%, v3-HYB 82.5%, HR 82.3%) but lower than HR-ex (87.3%). Both HYBs showed higher FN rates than HR-ex (4o-HYB 34.2% and v3-HYB 27.3% vs HR-ex 16.9%, both p < 0.001). Severity assessment did not indicate preferential omission of clinically significant errors. Human verification reduced LLM-generated FNs and FPs. Median review time decreased substantially from 51.0 s (HR-ex) to 11.0 s (4o-HYB) and 12.0 s (v3-HYB). In supplementary validation (error prevalence, 9.6%), v3.2-HYB and HR showed FN rates of 22.6% and 24.3%, FP rates of 7.7% and 10.0%, and median review times of 15.4 and 24.3 s, respectively. Conclusion The LLM-assisted HYB achieved accuracy comparable to single-physician review while substantially reducing audit time. These findings require prospective real-world validation before routine clinical implementation.

title: Development and Multicenter Validation of a Hybrid Radiomics-Deep Learning Model for Risk Stratification of O-RADS 4 Adnexal Masses.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To develop and validate an artificial intelligence-driven hybrid model integrating ultrasound radiomics, deep learning (DL) signatures, and clinical predictors for differentiating benign from borderline/malignant Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System (O-RADS) 4 adnexal masses, and to evaluate its utility as a radiologist decision-support tool. Materials and methods This multicenter study retrospectively enrolled 653 patients from four centers (521 from Center A [training, n = 405; internal validation, n = 116]; 132 from Centers B-D [external validation]), and prospectively enrolled 126 patients from Center A. Pathological results served as the gold standard. Radiomics features were extracted to generate a Rad-score using machine learning classifiers. A transfer learning-based DL model using convolutional neural networks produced a DL-score. A hybrid model integrating Rad-score, DL-score, and clinical predictors was constructed. Diagnostic performance of models was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). In the prospective validation set, six radiologists interpreted cases with and without hybrid model assistance. Diagnostic differences were assessed using McNemar's χ² test, and inter-reader agreement by Cohen's kappa. Results The hybrid model demonstrated good performance with AUCs of 0.88 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.82-0.93) and 0.86 (95% CI: 0.78-0.92) in the prospective and external validation sets. Model assistance significantly improved accuracy and specificity across all readers (p < 0.05), with inter-reader agreement improving from kappa 0.49 to 0.73. The model stratified lesions into low-risk (4a) and high-risk (4b) subcategories with consistently distinct malignancy rates across all datasets (4a: 4.5%-16.1%; 4b: 75.4%-97.1%). Conclusion The hybrid model demonstrated good performance for risk stratification of O-RADS 4 adnexal masses and improved radiologist performance across experience levels.

The model stratified lesions into low-risk (4a) and high-risk (4b) subcategories with consistently distinct malignancy rates across all datasets (4a: 4.5%-16.1%; 4b: 75.4%-97.1%).

Conclusion

The hybrid model demonstrated good performance for risk stratification of O-RADS 4 adnexal masses and improved radiologist performance across experience levels.

title: Deep Learning Super-Resolution CT Versus Ultra-High-Resolution CT: A Direct Comparison in Cadaveric Human Lungs.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Deep learning-based high-resolution computed tomography (CT) of the lung parenchyma has not been directly compared with ultra-high-resolution CT (UHR-CT). We compared image quality between deep learning-based super-resolution CT and UHR-CT using identical cadaveric human lungs. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 10 cadaveric human lungs scanned using conventional CT and UHR-CT at two dose levels (9 mGy, 2 mGy). Five reconstruction methods were evaluated, including deep learning-based synthetic super-resolution CT (CCT-1024-PIQE) and UHR-CT-derived high-resolution images reconstructed using a deep learning-based denoising algorithm (UHR-1024-AiCE). Two radiologists independently assessed the bronchioles, seven abnormal findings, and overall image quality using a 5-point scale. The objective image noise was also quantified. Statistical comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Results At 9 mGy, no significant differences were observed in the bronchioles, whereas UHR-1024-AiCE demonstrated higher scores than CCT-1024-PIQE for ground-glass opacities and intralobular reticulation (all P ≤ 0.007). At 2 mGy, CCT-1024-PIQE showed no significant differences from UHR-1024-AiCE for most findings. Compared with the 512-matrix reconstructions, CCT-1024-PIQE achieved consistently higher visual scores at both dose levels (most comparisons, P < 0.05). Image noise increased at 2 mGy across all methods, while PIQE-based reconstructions showed lower noise (P < 0.001). Conclusion Deep learning-based super-resolution CT showed no significant differences from UHR-CT in many pulmonary findings, particularly under low-dose conditions, while improving visualization compared to conventional 512-matrix reconstructions.
