title: Molecular surveillance of adenovirus and coronavirus in Procellariiformes, Brazil: Detection of new divergent adenoviruses.
abstract: Adenoviruses are widespread DNA viruses that infect a broad range of vertebrate hosts and are recognized for their long-term host coevolution, remarkable genetic diversity, and broad pathogenic potential. Coronaviruses circulate among wild birds due to their evolutionary potential and are relevant to animal and public health. However, the diversity and ecological role of these viruses in pelagic seabirds remain poorly understood. This study provides the first molecular survey of adenoviruses and coronaviruses in Procellariiformes from the South Atlantic. Fifty stranded individuals representing 12 Procellariiformes species were collected along the southeastern Brazilian coast, between 2017 and 2023. Adenovirus and coronavirus survey were performed using nested PCR protocols, followed by sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and histopathology of positive cases. Adenovirus was detected in seven individuals (14%; 95% CI: 5.8-26.7%) from three species: Southern Giant Petrels (Macronectes giganteus), Cory's Shearwaters (Calonectris borealis), and Black-browed Albatrosses (Thalassarche melanophris). Five sequence types were identified, including similar variants in Southern Giant Petrels and distinct adenoviruses in Cory's Shearwaters and Black-browed Albatrosses. All viruses clustered within a divergent lineage with adenoviruses previously detected in New Zealand seabirds and a Chimney Swift from the USA. No intranuclear inclusion bodies were found in histopathological analysis. All specimens were coronavirus-negative. This first molecular detection of adenoviruses in Procellariiformes expands the known diversity and host range of seabird adenoviruses and suggests circulation of genetically distinct viruses across oceanic regions, highlighting the need for genomic and epidemiological studies of their evolution, transmission, and health impacts.

title: Intraoperative endoscopy in colorectal surgery in Spain: Results of a national survey.
abstract: Introduction Anastomotic leakage remains one of the most feared complications in colorectal surgery. Intraoperative colonoscopy (IOC) enables direct assessment of anastomotic integrity and allows immediate therapeutic intervention. The aim of this study is to describe the implementation of intraoperative endoscopy in colorectal surgery in Spain, analysing available resources, training, utilization patterns, and impact on intraoperative decision-making. Methods Observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study based on an online survey distributed through the Asociación Española de Cirugía. The questionnaire, validated by a panel of experts, comprised 26 questions grouped into five domains: professional profile, infrastructure, technique and protocols, perceived outcomes, and training. The survey was active for 46 days. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed using absolute frequencies and percentages. Results A total of 122 complete responses were obtained from 92 hospitals across 16 autonomous communities (completion rate: 31.7%). Flexible endoscopy was used by 55.7% of respondents, and 36.1% performed IOC routinely. Surgeons performed the procedures in 61.5% of cases. IOC was also used for localisation of lesions by 54.9% of respondents. In 61.8% of surgeons, the surgical approach was modified in up to 20% of patients. Indocyanine green fluorescence angiography was available in 85.2% of centres. Overall, 86.1% considered IOC a fundamental tool, and complications were virtually absent. Conclusions IOC is highly regarded in Spain, yet its systematic integration remains heterogeneous. Deficits in structured training, therapeutic methods, and equipment persist. A joint effort from scientific societies, hospital management, and surgical teams is required to ensure uniform implementation and improve anastomotic safety.

title: Modern multidisciplinary management of brain metastasis.
abstract: Brain metastases (BrM) are no longer considered to be a uniform end-stage complication of cancer, but as a biologically and clinically heterogeneous disease requiring coordinated management. This article synthesises the fundamentals of BrM diagnosis and treatment, relevant to primary and urgent care settings. Treatment sequencing should account for acuity of neurologic symptoms, anticipated intracranial response, extracranial disease tempo, steroid requirements, and risks of local therapy. Focal radiotherapy is now the dominant local modality for limited BrM. Surgery remains central for large, symptomatic, diagnostically uncertain, or mass-effect-producing lesions. Postoperative stereotactic radiosurgery is favoured over whole-brain radiotherapy. Novel CNS-active targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors can permit deferral of radiotherapy in carefully selected asymptomatic patients with certain molecularly defined cancers. Follow-up, based on longitudinal MRI, requires multi-disciplinary surveillance and decision-making. Optimal care combines integrated multi-disciplinary management and risk-adapted sequencing to jointly achieve preservation of neurologic function while maintaining durable systemic control.

title: Evaluating skeletal muscle in chronic liver disease: remaining challenges.
abstract: Skeletal muscle alterations are increasingly recognized as determinants of prognosis in chronic liver disease, and computed tomography (CT) has made their assessment widely accessible. However, interpretation of these measurements raises several challenges. First, myosteatosis is usually inferred from low CT muscle attenuation, which has not been validated against intramuscular fat content in cirrhosis. Second, muscle alterations may differ according to the aetiology of liver disease, and studies pooling aetiologies may obscure aetiology-specific patterns. Third, "sarcopenia" is frequently incorrectly used for low muscle mass alone, whereas incorporating muscle function, better predicts adverse outcomes in chronic liver disease. Addressing these issues is necessary before muscle quality can become a reliable clinical biomarker.

title: A multimodal MRI radiomics sonata for differentiating small renal masses: a two-center retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurately distinguishing benign from malignant small renal masses (SRMs) is crucial to avoid unnecessary surgeries, yet reliable preoperative diagnostic tools remain limited. Methods A total of 189 patients with SRMs from two hospitals (2018-2022) were enrolled. Clinical data and MRI features were analyzed by two radiologists. Radiomics features were automatically extracted from manually segmented ROIs using dedicated software. Significant features were selected via univariate analysis, multivariate regression, and Lasso to develop three models: radiomics, clinical, and combined nomogram. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the Area Under the receiver operating characteristic Curve (AUC). Results The radiomics-clinical nomogram was constructed using T2WI signal intensity (p < 0.001), pseudocapsule (p = 0.001), and radiomics score (Rad-score, p = 0.001) via multivariate logistic regression. In the training set, the nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.962 (95% CI: 0.931-0.993), outperforming both the radiomics model (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.862-0.974) and the clinical model (AUC = 0.856, 95% CI: 0.780-0.933). Favorable performance was observed in the internal validation set (nomogram: AUC = 0.981, 95% CI: 0.944-1.000; radiomics model: AUC = 0.912, 95% CI: 0.750-1.000; clinical model: AUC = 0.844, 95% CI: 0.578-1.000) and external validation set (nomogram: AUC = 0.971, 95% CI: 0.886-1.000; radiomics model: AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.841-0.989; clinical model: AUC = 0.916,95% CI: 0.760-0.976). Conclusion All three models enable effective and non-invasive preoperative differentiation of benign from malignant SRMs, with the radiomics-clinical nomogram exhibiting the highest diagnostic accuracy, supporting its potential as a valuable clinical tool.

title: Pretreatment FDG-PET Biomarkers Predict Regional and Distant Failure but Not Local Recurrence Following Modern Use of Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy for Early-Stage Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Background Quantitative fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) biomarkers are associated with prognosis following stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (ES-NSCLC); however, their relationship with patterns of failure remains poorly defined. We evaluated the prognostic significance of pretreatment metabolic PET parameters following definitive SBRT. Patients and methods Patients with T1-3N0M0 ES-NSCLC treated with SBRT between January 2010 and December 2024 were identified from a prospectively maintained institutional database. Pretreatment FDG-PET metrics including maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), mean standardized uptake value (SUVmean), metabolic tumor volume (MTV), and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) were stratified into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups. Overall survival (OS); cancer-specific survival; and local, regional, and distant failure were analyzed using competing-risk methods and multivariable Fine-Gray regression. Results A total of 168 patients were included (median age, 77 years; median follow-up, 34.6 months). Local, regional, and distant failure occurred in 3.6%, 10.1%, and 15.5% of patients, respectively. Increasing TLG, SUVmax, SUVmean, and MTV were associated with inferior OS on univariable analysis, while high-risk TLG (HR, 2.26; P = .014) and SUVmean (HR, 2.72; P = .008) remained independent predictors of worse OS. No PET biomarker predicted local failure. Conversely, high-risk TLG and MTV independently predicted regional recurrence, while high-risk TLG, SUVmax, and SUVmean independently predicted distant metastasis. Conclusion Pretreatment FDG-PET metabolic biomarkers identify patients at increased risk of regional and distant recurrence following SBRT for ES-NSCLC but do not predict local failure after modern ablative radiotherapy. TLG demonstrated the most consistent prognostic performance and may represent a clinically useful biomarker for risk-adapted staging, surveillance, and future treatment intensification strategies.

title: Preoperative respiratory muscle strength, muscle mass, and respiratory sarcopenia as predictors of postoperative pulmonary complications after thoracic and cardiac surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background & aims Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after thoracic, upper abdominal, and cardiac surgery and are associated with adverse outcomes. Respiratory sarcopenia (RS), characterized by coexisting reductions in respiratory muscle mass and strength, may represent a clinically relevant prognostic phenotype, but its prognostic value remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess whether low preoperative respiratory muscle mass, reduced strength, or their coexistence as RS or probable RS predicts PPCs after thoracic and cardiac surgery. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from January 1990 to February 2026 for studies relating preoperative respiratory muscle mass, strength or flow, or RS to PPCs. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality In Prognosis Studies tool. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled using random-effects models after harmonizing effect directions such that ORs >1 denoted higher risk. Results Sixteen studies were included; all involved thoracic or cardiac surgery, and none included an upper abdominal cohort. Cutoff-based respiratory muscle strength or flow impairment was associated with increased odds of PPCs (OR 2.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.50-3.37; I 2 = 51.2%), with the most consistent association observed for percent-predicted peak expiratory flow (PEF) (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.43-2.90; I 2 = 0%). Continuous PEF was associated with PPCs, whereas ultrasound-based diaphragm indices showed smaller, non-significant associations. RS or probable RS was associated with PPCs (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.33-3.26; I 2 = 0%). Conclusions Preoperative functional respiratory muscle impairment, particularly reduced PEF, and RS or probable RS were associated with PPCs. Given that the evidence was limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from thoracic surgery, prospective confirmation is needed.

title: Spectral CT in Modern Radiotherapy: A Clinical Framework for Precision Treatment Planning, Adaptive Radiotherapy, and Response Assessment.
abstract: Aims To provide a clinical framework for understanding the role of spectral computed tomography (CT), including dual-energy CT (DECT) and photon-counting CT (PCCT), across the radiotherapy pathway, from simulation and treatment planning to adaptive radiotherapy (ART) and treatment response assessment. Materials and methods This review examines the clinical applications of spectral CT in radiotherapy, focusing on the translation of spectral-derived information into clinically relevant decision-making. Applications of virtual monoenergetic imaging, relative electron density (RED), effective atomic number (EAN), and stopping-power ratio (SPR) are discussed in relation to target delineation, dose calculation, and uncertainty reduction in photon and particle therapy. Emerging iodine-based and composition-sensitive biomarkers are also evaluated for tissue characterization, treatment response assessment, and biologically informed ART. Results Spectral CT offers technical advantages and potential clinical value in radiotherapy through improved tissue characterization, enhanced dose calculation, and additional quantitative information for treatment response assessment. However, routine clinical implementation remains challenging because of variability in acquisition and reconstruction protocols and limited integration with treatment planning and adaptive workflows. Prospective evidence demonstrating improvements in patient outcomes is also limited. Conclusion Spectral CT is an enabling quantitative imaging platform that complements, rather than replaces, conventional CT. Its clinical value will depend on standardized acquisition and analysis protocols and integration into established radiotherapy workflows. Prospective clinical studies are needed to determine whether spectral-derived information can improve treatment decision-making and patient outcomes.

title: Respiratory Instability-driven Cardiac Dose Deviation in Postmastectomy Deep Inspiration Breath-hold Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (DIBH VMAT): Development and External Validation of a Respiratory-informed Predictive Framework.
abstract: Aims Deep inspiration breath-hold (DIBH) reduces cardiac exposure during left-sided breast radiotherapy; however, treatment-day cardiac dose may differ from the planned dose because of variations in respiratory reproducibility and anatomy. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a framework for predicting fraction-level cardiac dose variation using routinely acquired respiratory, anatomical, and dosimetric information. Materials and methods A retrospective cohort of 150 patients treated with postmastectomy DIBH VMAT (volumetric modulated arc therapy) was analyzed. Models were developed using a 30-patient development cohort with patient-wise-nested cross-validation, externally validated in 20 independent patients using cone-beam CT-derived synthetic CT dose recalculation, and applied to a 100-patient deployment cohort. Separate models predicted deviation from planned per-fraction mean heart dose (ΔMHD) and left anterior descending coronary artery dose (ΔLADCA D0.03 cc) using treatment-day real-time position management (RPM)--derived respiratory features, planning computed tomography (CT)-derived geometric variables, and plan-derived dosimetric parameters. SHAP-based analysis was performed to identify influential predictors. Results The final Gradient Boosting model for ΔMHD achieved an internal validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.541 ± 0.035 centigray (cGy) and coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.642 ± 0.069. title: A frequency-driven method for retinal vessel segmentation.
abstract: Background and objective Retinal vessel segmentation is essential for diagnosing and monitoring ocular and systemic diseases. However, most existing deep learning methods operate predominantly in the spatial domain, limiting their ability to capture fine vessel structures and maintain topological continuity, especially for thin and low-contrast vessels. Existing frequency-aware approaches mostly rely on fixed transforms or simple feature concatenation, lacking task-adaptive spectral modeling. We developed a frequency-driven framework to address these limitations. Methods We implemented FRetinalNet, a frequency-driven encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder employs a Frequency Feature Tuning Block (FFTBlock) that parameterizes convolutional kernels in the spectral domain and adaptively modulates them with contextual cues via inverse FFT. Spatial and frequency features from parallel branches are fused using a Frequency Aware Fusion Block (FaFBlock) with cross-modality attention. The decoder includes dual-resolution branches for fine boundary recovery and global structural coherence, along with an auxiliary decoder for complementary supervision. Training proceeds in two stages: Stage 1 pretrains the encoder with original and Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform inputs using consistency loss; Stage 2 transfers weights and fine-tunes under supervised objectives. We evaluated on DRIVE, STARE, and OCTA-500 using Dice, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC. Results FRetinalNet achieved the highest Dice scores on DRIVE (0.8578) and STARE (0.8696) compared with state-of-the-art methods. On OCTA-500, it obtained the best Dice for arteries (0.8864) and veins (0.9055) on the 6mm subset, and the best arterial (0.9169) and venous (0.9101) Dice on the 3mm subset. Ablation studies confirmed that two-stage training improves Dice from 0.8390 to 0.8578, and that all proposed components provide complementary benefits. Conclusions Explicit integration of learnable spectral parameterization and cross-domain feature fusion improves delineation of fine structures and topological continuity. The two-stage training pipeline provides robust frequency-aware initialization across fundus and OCTA modalities.

title: Intrinsic dimension for evaluating and analyzing neural networks for medical image segmentation.
abstract: Background and objective Evaluating medical image segmentation models typically relies on expert annotations, which are scarce, costly, and time-consuming to obtain. Intrinsic dimension (ID), defined as the minimal number of parameters required to describe high-dimensional data, has been shown to correlate with model generalization in classification tasks, but whether this relationship extends to segmentation remains unclear. Methods In this study, we systematically investigate ID as a label-free indicator for evaluating segmentation performance, including the generalization of standard segmentation models and the adaptability of promptable foundation models (i.e., SAM-based models). We also perform a layer-wise ID analysis to characterize variations in latent representation complexity. Furthermore, we propose a novel, computation- and memory-efficient strategy for ID calculation to broaden its applications. Results We reveal the following findings: 1) For standard segmentation, lower ID values of training-sample representations are consistently associated with better generalization performance on unseen test samples, as measured by DSC. 2) For promptable segmentation, test-data ID consistently reflects model adaptability to specific target data compared to entropy, a metric commonly believed to predict performance. 3) Layer-wise ID in segmentation follows an initially increasing and then decreasing pattern, similar to that in classification. Conclusions Our findings suggest the potential of ID as a label-free indicator for assessing the generalization and adaptability of segmentation models, thereby supporting model selection in label-scarce clinical settings.

title: VAE-based synthetic volume generation for trabecular bone microarchitecture.
abstract: Background and objective Micro computed tomography (microCT) enables detailed characterization of trabecular bone microarchitecture through quantitative morphological parameters. However, trabecular bone exhibits morphological variability across species, anatomical locations, bone types, and physiological or pathological conditions. Individual microCT datasets generally represent only a limited portion of this morphological variability, which may constrain the development and validation of quantitative descriptors, image-processing pipelines, and computational models. This study presents a Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based framework for generating synthetic trabecular bone images, with the potential to support more comprehensive investigations of trabecular microarchitecture. Methods The VAE is trained on individual microCT slices and learns a three-dimensional latent space in which the ordered sequence of slices is mapped onto a continuous trajectory. Generating a synthetic volume reduces to i) defining a latent space trajectory and ii) decoding its points into 2D images ensuring inter-slice coherence without requiring any explicit 3D architecture. An interactive trajectory editor allows the user to manipulate, extend, or resample the latent path, providing full control over the morphology, length, and resolution of the synthetic volume. The reconstruction capability of the VAE was assessed by comparing the original microCT slices with their VAE-based reconstructions, and the original microCT-derived volume with the corresponding 3D volume obtained from the VAE-based reconstructed images, using 2D and 3D descriptors of trabecular microarchitecture. New sequences of synthetic images could be generated by modifying latent-space trajectories through the editor, thereby enabling the generation of multiple synthetic 3D volumes with controlled morphological variability. In this study, one such sequence was generated, and the corresponding 3D synthetic volume was characterized using microarchitectural parameters. The resulting values were then compared with those reported in the literature to assess the plausibility of the generated structure. Results Comparison of the morphological descriptors showed a high degree of similarity between the VAE-reconstructed and original microCT images. The corresponding 3D volumes also exhibited comparable morphological characteristics, indicating that the reconstruction process preserved the main structural features of the original microCT sample. Finally, the synthetic volume generated by synthetic VAE-based images exhibited microarchitectural parameter values comparable to those reported in the literature. Conclusion These results provide support for the ability of the proposed framework to generate synthetic trabecular microarchitectures with coherent structural features. Therefore, the framework can support data augmentation for deep-learning model training and more extensive investigations of trabecular microarchitecture. Future developments will focus on linking selected morphological descriptors to the three latent-space axes, thereby expanding the range of microarchitectural variability that can be generated and investigated.

title: Longitudinal CT imaging to predict radiotherapy treatment outcome in head and neck cancer: a deep learning approach.
abstract: Purpose CT images acquired at multiple time points before and during radiotherapy treatment could capture tumor temporal changes, offering valuable insights into tumor response. By modeling temporal changes in CT scans with deep learning techniques, we compared the predictive performance of multi-time point models versus single time point models, assessing the impact of incorporating temporal features to predict two-year disease-free survival in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) patients. Materials and methods A total of 202 OPSCC patients treated with (chemo)radiotherapy at the University Medical Center Groningen were included. A planning CT scan was available per patient, along with repeat CT scans (rCTs) acquired at different time points during treatment. Three training/ validation sets were created based on the data availability per patient: first two, three, or four consecutive rCTs. An independent testing set of 53 patients having all four consecutive rCTs was used to compare the performance of models trained using different inputs. Deep learning models were built using single or multiple time points as input. To model longitudinal features, self-attention mechanisms and temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) were applied to deep features extracted from the CT scans at different time points. Models were trained with 3-fold cross-validation and three feature extraction architectures. Predicted probabilities were ensembled by averaging. Finally, performance was assessed by accuracy, F1 macro, AUC score, and calibration plots. Results Self-attention demonstrated superior ability over TCNs in capturing temporal changes in multi-time points models. The top-performing model achieved 0.75 accuracy, 0.66 F1 score, 0.61 AUC, and the best overall calibration using planning CT and the first two rCTs with self-attention. Models trained on single time point CTs up to the 10th fraction generally showed slightly lower accuracy (≤0.72), similar F1 score (around 0.66), but higher AUC (≥0.70). Despite the similar discrimination performance, TCNs demonstrated poor calibration (slope values ≥1.74). Conclusion Multi-time point CT images acquired before and early in treatment showed potential in predicting disease-free survival in OPSCC. Deep learning models based on self-attention, specifically those using planning CT and the first two consecutive rCT scans, demonstrated promising clinical utility.

title: Artificial intelligence in axial spondyloarthritis imaging: a review of current evidence.
abstract: The diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) remains challenging and is frequently delayed. Imaging is central to diagnosis, but relevant inflammatory and structural abnormalities may be subtle, heterogeneous, or overlap with findings related to mechanical stress, anatomical variation, and degeneration. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is therefore being investigated to support image interpretation, lesion detection, quantification, and standardized assessment. We synthesize evidence from 12 studies applying convolutional neural networks and related architectures to magnetic resonance imaging and radiographs, automate imaging scores, and combine imaging-derived information with clinical variables. Several models achieved performance comparable to experienced human readers, including during external validation. However, performance may decline in heterogeneous real-world populations for study-specific reasons not explained solely by scanner or protocol differences. No AI tool currently has regulatory clearance for autonomous use in axSpA, and applications remain largely confined to research and clinical trials.

title: Ultrasound-controlled therapeutics for bladder cancer: Mechanisms, recent advances, and future perspectives.
abstract: Bladder cancer remains a significant clinical challenge, characterised by a high recurrence rate and substantial healthcare costs. Although advances in surgery, systemic therapy, and intravesical treatment have improved clinical outcomes, treatment-related toxicity, therapeutic resistance, and the persistently poor prognosis of advanced disease highlight the need for more effective therapeutic strategies. Ultrasound-based micro/nanotherapeutics offer a promising approach that combines deep tissue penetration with high focal precision in a non-invasive, externally controllable manner. This review summarises recent advances in ultrasound-mediated therapeutic strategies for bladder cancer, including ultrasound-mediated drug and gene delivery, sonodynamic therapy (SDT), and high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) ablation. It describes how ultrasound, often in combination with microbubbles or nanobubbles, enhances the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs and therapeutic genes through cavitation-induced permeabilisation of biological barriers. It then examines the mechanisms underlying SDT-induced reactive oxygen species generation and its integration with chemodynamic therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and imaging, alongside tumour microenvironment (TME) modulation strategies such as hypoxia relief and antioxidant depletion that augment SDT efficacy. Finally, it discusses HIFU ablation, including nanoparticle-assisted strategies that enhance tumour destruction through combined thermal and mechanical effects. The limitations of each modality and future directions for clinical translation, including standardisation of ultrasound devices and exposure parameters, optimisation of nanoplatform design, and integration of artificial intelligence-based predictive models, are also discussed.

title: Biomimetic PLGA nanoparticles-mediated low-intensity pulsed ultrasound-triggered targeted release of C646 for esophageal cancer therapy.
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is associated with high morbidity and poor clinical prognosis among the Chinese population. Conventional chemoradiotherapy is hampered by severe systemic toxic effects and inadequate tumor-targeting performance. EP300 represents a promising epigenetic therapeutic target for ESCC. Nevertheless, the small-molecule EP300 inhibitor C646 suffers from low target selectivity and substantial off-target toxicity. Herein, we constructed homotypic tumor-cell-membrane-coated, C646-loaded PLGA nanoparticles (C646/PLGA@CM NPs). This nanosystem integrates biomimetic homologous targeting, immune evasion capability, and low intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS, US)-triggered on-demand release for combinatorial therapy against ESCC. Physicochemical characterizations confirmed successful membrane coating, satisfactory colloidal stability, and US-triggered drug-release profiles. Cellular assays demonstrated that C646/PLGA@CM NPs achieve efficient homologous uptake in tumor cells and evade phagocytosis by macrophages. Quantitative analysis using SynergyFinder confirmed strong synergistic antitumor effects of the nanoparticles combined with US. In vitro assays showed that C646/PLGA@CM combined with US markedly suppressed the proliferation and migration of KYSE-140 cells by inducing G2/M-phase cell-cycle arrest and reversing epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Furthermore, results from ESCC subcutaneous xenograft mouse models revealed that C646/PLGA@CM combined with US exerted potent in-vivo antitumor efficacy with satisfactory biosafety. Transcriptomic profiling together with qRT-PCR assays indicated that the antitumor mechanism involves EP300-inhibition-mediated activation of the p53/FoxO pathway, alongside dysregulation of tumor-suppressive and oncogenic miRNAs. Collectively, this CM-coated nanoplatform combined with US offers a feasible precision-targeted therapeutic strategy for ESCC.

title: SCOPE-Med: Structure-Preserving and Contour-Oriented Pseudo-Label Reconstruction for mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation.
abstract: Mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation aims to learn segmentation models from a small labeled set in one domain and abundant unlabeled data from multiple unknown domains. Its central challenge is to construct reliable pseudo-supervision under substantial domain shift. Existing methods commonly infer pseudo-label reliability from confidence or predictive uncertainty at the sample, model, or complete-mask level, implicitly assuming uniform reliability across each prediction. Coarse anatomical support can remain relatively stable, whereas local contours and fine details are more sensitive to appearance variation and boundary ambiguity. This uneven sensitivity makes a single trust decision inadequate, because it may either retain corrupted local details or discard useful structural information. To address this issue, this paper proposes SCOPE-Med, a Structure-preserving and Contour-Oriented Pseudo-label rEconstruction framework for mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation. SCOPE-Med organizes heterogeneous teacher predictions into coarse structural components and detail-sensitive residuals through Gaussian decomposition. The structural components retain spatially coherent region-level information, while the residuals preserve local variation that may contain both useful corrections and domain-induced noise. Predictive uncertainty then regulates local residual correction and suppresses unstable detail injection in ambiguous regions. An auxiliary boundary prediction head and contour-constrained objective provide complementary geometric supervision during student optimization. Through decomposition, regulation, and reconstruction, SCOPE-Med refines pseudo-supervision at the component level instead of assigning a single confidence score to an entire prediction. Experiments are conducted on two public two-dimensional binary segmentation benchmarks. Across overlap- and boundary-sensitive metrics, SCOPE-Med achieves strong average performance under the evaluated mixed-domain settings.

title: A review of deep learning applications on histopathologic and genomic data in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
abstract: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis explains the histological pattern of injury seen through light microscopy in kidney biopsy specimens and is the end result of different injuries to podocytes. The clinical classification of patients by FSGS lesion is challenging because of a broad spectrum of etiologies, limited understanding of pathophysiology, and poor correlation among histopathology, treatment response, and clinical outcomes. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a problematic process to detect lesions, with low and late analysis of the absence of initial symptoms, and a challenging position of specific markers. However, Histopathological and genomic Data in Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) are significantly used in multiple research applications, but they face several limitations that restrict the efficiency of experimental analysis. This review systematically analyzed recent enhancements in biopsy-based analysis and deep learning models for FSGS, with specific emphasis on different mechanisms. Moreover, this review analyzed different strategies, namely kidney transplantation, pathogenesis to therapeutic approaches, transformer-based architectures, glomerular segmentation methodologies, multitasking strategy classification, and gene expression analysis for FSGS. This review analysis includes 121 research papers, which are selected and analyzed for glomerular segmentation, gene expression, clinical outcomes, lesion classification, and disease recurrence prediction. Based on the recent research frameworks, it explicitly states the performance analysis, benefits, as well as challenges of FSGS. The article presents details of a new dataset and future directions for improving the majority of nephropathology diagnoses previously available through the use of integrated approaches that utilize both histopathology and genomics, enhancing future research direction in FSGS.

title: AAC-TTA: Anti-adversarial consistency with test-time adaptation for imbalanced histopathology classification under scanner-induced domain shift.
abstract: The performance of medical image classification models can degrade at deployment because of two common real-world challenges: domain shift and class imbalance. Domain shift causes whole-slide images acquired on different scanners to exhibit substantial visual variation, while class imbalance under-represents clinically important high-grade patterns. The effect of class imbalance is not limited to training data: it can re-emerge during unsupervised test-time adaptation, further suppressing rare but diagnostically important classes even as overall performance improves. To address these coupled deployment challenges, we propose Anti-Adversarial Consistency with Test-Time Adaptation (AAC-TTA), an unsupervised test-time adaptation framework for imbalanced histopathology classification under scanner-induced domain shift. AAC-TTA probes local prediction stability using small entropy-guided adversarial and anti-adversarial perturbation views, and derives a more stable target-domain training signal from the views that pass a reliability check. It further combines agreement-based reliability gating with constrained adaptation of lightweight model components, so that adaptation is not driven by unreliable pseudo-labels. Experiments on AGGC22-derived H&E-stained prostate histopathology patches for automated Gleason grading, comprising 95,400 training and 47,700 test patches across three scanner domains (Akoya, Philips, and KFBio) show that AAC-TTA achieves the highest macro-F1 among representative test-time adaptation baselines while substantially improving recognition of the under-represented high-grade class. Rather than artificially constructing separate no-, moderate-, and high-imbalance scenarios, we evaluate the single G5-minority imbalance that arises naturally in the AGGC22 data, since G5 is both intrinsically rare and the most diagnostically critical high-grade pattern. Our results indicate that medical test-time adaptation methods should be evaluated not only by overall performance but also by their ability to preserve minority-class recognition under domain shift.

title: Multimodal visual question answering in neuro-oncology and gastroenterology: A domain-specific feasibility study.
abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) requires models to combine image content with the clinical intent expressed by a question, yet domain-specific resources and controlled analyses of modality use remain limited. This study introduces two expert-validated Med-VQA datasets for brain tumor MRI and gastrointestinal endoscopy and evaluates a dual-stream architecture that combines BERT question representations and ViT image features through Modular Co-Attention on Attention (MCAoA). The model formulates answer prediction as closed-vocabulary classification and is assessed through overall, question-type, disease-class, baseline, ablation, and usability analyses. The complete fine-tuned model with product fusion achieved accuracies of 80.86% (WUPS 81.32%) on the brain tumor dataset and 75.95% (WUPS 76.77%) on the gastrointestinal dataset. It exceeded the question-only and image-only baselines by 23.86 and 43.16 percentage points, respectively, on brain tumor MRI, and by 18.54 and 35.92 percentage points on gastrointestinal endoscopy. Product fusion provided a small but consistent advantage over concatenation, while end-to-end encoder fine-tuning improved accuracy over frozen encoders on both datasets. A complementary study with clinical experts indicated positive perceived usability in a controlled setting. These findings show that performance cannot be reproduced from either modality alone and support the complementary use of image and question information. However, the ablations establish modality-level dependence rather than spatially correct anatomical grounding, which requires targeted counterfactual and attribution-based evaluation.

title: Adaptive consistency representation learning for semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation.
abstract: Three-dimensional medical image segmentation plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and surgical planning. Semi-supervised learning provides an effective way to reduce annotation requirements; however, heterogeneous feature perturbations may induce predictions with different levels of local disagreement, making uniformly weighted consistency supervision sub-optimal. This work presents an Adaptive Consistency Representation Learning (ACRL) framework for semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation. ACRL constructs heterogeneous feature-perturbed auxiliary views and adaptively modulates the voxel-wise consistency strength according to the disagreement between each auxiliary prediction and the feature-unperturbed main prediction. A Multi-scale Feature Aggregation module and a Bottleneck Attention Module are incorporated to enhance structural representation. Experiments on the LA, Pancreas-CT, and BraTS19 datasets achieve Dice scores of 90.54%, 81.85%, and 87.51%, respectively, under the 10% labeled setting. Across the evaluated settings, ACRL shows competitive overlap accuracy and favorable boundary-distance performance relative to representative conventional and foundation-model-assisted semi-supervised baselines. Controlled ablations further show that reliability-adaptive weighting provides additional benefits over uniformly weighted multi-branch consistency.

title: De-Seg: Advancing OCTA segmentation with multi-scale feature fusion and edge refinement.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of retinal vessels in optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) is essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of ocular diseases such as diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma. However, this task remains challenging due to the presence of low-contrast microvessels, projection artifacts, and interference from fine vessel structures. To overcome these limitations, we propose De-Seg, a deep learning framework designed to enhance vessel segmentation through multi-scale feature fusion and edge refinement. The model employs a dual-branch encoder that combines a U-Net-style backbone with parallel multi-scale convolutions and a dedicated edge-aware branch utilizing Sobel operators. These branches are effectively fused via skip-connected decoder layers to maintain high spatial precision. The bottleneck is augmented with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to capture global contextual information, while a Multi-Scale Feature Extraction Block (MS Block) enlarges the receptive field to better capture faint capillaries. An Edge Block is introduced to enhance boundary clarity and mitigate interference from lesion regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that De-Seg achieves competitive performance on multiple OCTA benchmarks, yielding Dice scores of 92.13% on OCTA-3M and 94.67% on ROSSA, outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies validate the necessity of each component in improving feature representation and edge accuracy. The framework exhibits strong generalization capability, showing robust performance even under cross-domain settings. Overall, De-Seg provides a reliable and efficient solution for quantitative OCTA analysis, with potential applicability to other vascular imaging modalities.

title: Dual-state adaptive unrolled network for structure-preserving low-dose CT image restoration.
abstract: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces spatially heterogeneous noise and artifacts that can obscure subtle anatomical structures. We address post-reconstruction image-domain LDCT restoration, where degradation suppression and structure preservation impose competing demands on a single restoration trajectory. We propose DSAUNet, a Dual-State Adaptive Unrolled Network that maintains persistent anatomy- and degradation-oriented latent states across unrolled stages. Rather than acting as transient feature branches, the evolving states participate in parameterizing subsequent restoration behavior through a degradation-oriented global policy coordinate for stage-level modulation and state-derived confidence variables for spatially selective regulation. Direction-aware prior modeling and multi-scale state guidance further realize this state-parameterized restoration process. Under the reported protocols, DSAUNet achieves 40.3721 dB PSNR and 0.9642 SSIM on 2DeteCT, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.6320 dB and 0.0108, and achieves 47.4277 dB PSNR and 0.9846 SSIM under the patient-level five-fold Mayo evaluation, with a 1.0920 dB PSNR gain over the strongest PSNR baseline. On LoDoPaB-CT, it further obtains 38.5501 dB PSNR and 0.9141 SSIM, with the best PSNR, SSIM, and VIF among the compared methods. Controlled raw-state, persistent state-swapping, policy-coordinate, and confidence-map analyses support functionally differentiated state roles and active adaptive regulation. Bidirectional 2DeteCT-Mayo zero-shot experiments reveal direction-dependent transfer behavior, while unified profiling characterizes an accuracy-complexity trade-off. Together, these results support persistent dual-state controlled unrolling as a structured approach to image-domain LDCT restoration within the evaluated settings.

title: A review of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for medical image analysis.
abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace selected scalar weights or fixed activations with learnable univariate edge functions. We conducted a controlled retrospective evidence reconstruction and update of Crossref, Europe PMC, arXiv, and OpenAlex, supplemented by local full texts and citation tracking, for studies published from January 2024 to February 2026. After report-level screening and version consolidation, 138 independent medical-imaging studies met explicitly defined medical-imaging eligibility criteria (127 direct imaging inputs; 11 image-derived representations). Studies were classified by primary KAN placement - backbone, bottleneck/token, physics-informed or implicit representation, or task-specific head - and evaluated for task, modality, comparator, reported result, and evidence of a KAN-specific contribution. None met the strictest contribution-evidence standard of a complete resource-controlled factorial comparison; 48 provided moderate, 46 weak/compound, and 44 insufficient evidence for the independent KAN contribution. Whole-model results were favorable in 68 studies, mixed or trade-off in 30, unfavorable or without incremental gain in 4, and indeterminate or not comparable in 36; these labels do not isolate the effect of KAN. External validation, calibration, repeated-run stability, and deployment metrics were inconsistently reported. The evidence supports KAN chiefly as a task-dependent module for controlled testing within established convolutional, Transformer, state-space, or physics-informed pipelines, rather than as a generally superior replacement. Priorities include matched ablations, function-stability analysis, external-center evaluation, and standardized resource reporting.

title: CDPDNet: Integrating text guidance with hybrid vision encoders for medical image segmentation.
abstract: Most publicly available medical segmentation datasets are only partially labeled, with annotations provided for a subset of anatomical structures. When multiple datasets are combined for training, this incomplete annotation poses challenges, as it limits the model's ability to learn shared anatomical representations among datasets. Furthermore, vision-only frameworks often struggle to resolve semantic ambiguities between missing labels and target regions, potentially hindering discriminative performance and cross-dataset consistency. In this study, we proposed a CLIP-DINO Prompt-Driven Segmentation Network (CDPDNet), which combined a self-supervised vision transformer with CLIP-based text embedding and introduced task-specific text prompts to tackle these challenges. Specifically, the framework was constructed upon a convolutional neural network (CNN) and incorporated DINOv2 to extract both fine-grained and global visual features, which were then fused using a multi-head cross-attention module to overcome the limited long-range modeling capability of CNNs. In addition, CLIP-derived text embeddings were projected into the visual space to help model complex relationships among organs and tumors. To further address the partial label challenge and enhance inter-task discriminative capability, a Text-based Task Prompt Generation (TTPG) module that generated task-specific prompts was designed to guide the segmentation. Extensive experiments on multiple medical imaging datasets demonstrated that CDPDNet consistently outperformed existing state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Code and pretrained model are available at: https://github.com/wujiong-hub/CDPDNet.git.

title: RADMorph: A region-aware deformable registration network for organ-specific thoracic CT alignment.
abstract: Deformable image registration plays an important role in radiation therapy, supporting applications such as contour propagation, treatment planning, and motion analysis. However, accurate registration of lung CT images remains challenging in the presence of large respiratory-induced deformations. In this study, we propose RADMorph, a deep learning framework that explicitly models region-dependent motion to improve registration robustness and anatomical consistency under large deformations. RADMorph comprises two key components. The Adaptive Region Feature Encoder (ARFE) learns region-specific motion representations through feature clustering and region-conditioned filtering, while the Region-Centered Displacement Modulator (RCDM) estimates deformation fields by integrating local image similarity with inter-region distance-based modulation. We evaluated RADMorph on multi-center datasets acquired under free-breathing and deep-inspiration breath-hold conditions, as well as on four-dimensional CT datasets. Across these datasets, RADMorph showed competitive overall performance compared with convolutional and transformer-based registration methods, with improvements varying across geometric and intensity-based metrics. The proposed method improved contour propagation and boundary localization for clinically relevant structures in most evaluated settings while reducing global deformation folding. Quantitative evaluations further demonstrated accurate voxel-level correspondence across the evaluated datasets, supporting the potential use of RADMorph in applications that rely on spatial correspondence, such as dose mapping and adaptive radiotherapy. RADMorph integrates region-aware representation learning with distance-modulated deformation estimation to provide a region-informed approach for modeling complex respiratory motion. These characteristics may facilitate more reliable contour transfer and quantitative analysis of dynamic thoracic imaging.

title: Motion uncertainty visualization based on Gaussian process regression.
abstract: In the context of image-guided soft-tissue intervention and surgery navigation, soft tissue motion estimation for a deformed/registered pre-operative/pre-interventional medical image may suffer from multiple sources of uncertainty. Visualizing the uncertainty in the deformed image is of great interest because it conveys the uncertainty in the registered pre-interventional/pre-operative navigation information on deformable soft-tissue organs governing the decisions of the surgeon or intervention specialist. We address the problem of propagating the uncertainty from a Gaussian process (GP)-based motion estimation of an input image. To visualize the deformed image itself, we show its maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. To convey the overall uncertainty in the MAP deformed image estimate, we apply a spatially-varying blur (according to the uncertain motion estimate) to an image containing a grid and combine it with the MAP deformed image itself. We show 2D cross sections of the final image that convey both the deformed image and its uncertainty. We further extend our approach to local investigations of points or regions of interest (e.g., a tumor). To visualize where a point/region of interest (POI/ROI) is after deformation, we estimate marginal (i.e., per voxel) label (e.g., for being a tumor) probabilities (MLPs) based on an input probabilistic segmentation of the ROI in the non-deformed pre-interventional/pre-operative image and the input GP posterior distribution over deformation fields and show 2D cross sections of visually mapped MLPs or MLP isocontours.

title: Medical Vision Foundation Models: A comprehensive review from technical evolution to clinical translation.
abstract: Medical Vision Foundation Models (MVFMs) mark a shift from task-specific artificial intelligence (AI) toward general-purpose visual intelligence in medical imaging. However, clinical deployment remains constrained by tensions among data availability, technological development, and integration into clinical workflows. To address these issues, this review provides a systematic analysis of the field's evolution from 2019 to 2025. We introduce the Data-Technology-Translation Triad as a unifying conceptual framework to structure the progress, key factors, and challenges of MVFMs. Our analysis traces the field's development and identifies a convergence toward Transformer-based and hybrid architectures, alongside hybrid pre-training paradigms. We present a unified technical framework that covers pre-training strategies, including generative, contrastive, and hybrid learning, as well as adaptation mechanisms such as full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and prompt learning. Furthermore, we examine how data scarcity, heterogeneity, and privacy constraints in medical imaging drive the adoption of self-supervised learning and highlight domain generalization as a critical research direction. Although MVFMs demonstrate strong performance in data-efficient and multi-task settings, their clinical translation is hindered by limited generalization, insufficient interpretability, misalignment with clinical workflows, and regulatory uncertainty. In response, we propose practical directions for developing reliable general-purpose medical vision systems, with emphasis on causal reasoning, dynamic data learning, interactive human-AI collaboration, and coordinated efforts among researchers, clinicians, and regulators. This review provides a structured reference to guide MVFMs from technical validation to clinically effective, reliable, and ethically sound deployment. An updated collection of MVFM papers and related resources is available at our website https://github.com/ice-TuoShui/MVFM-Review.

title: Clinical-context guidance and hyperbolic prototype learning for long-tailed radiology report generation.
abstract: Automated radiology report generation (RRG) can reduce the reporting burden, but existing methods remain limited in their ability to integrate clinical context effectively at the feature level. They also struggle with long-tailed disease distributions, which can hinder recognition of infrequent findings. To address these issues, CSMH-RRG, a clinically guided framework that integrates clinical semantic modulation (CSM) and hyperbolic prototype-based classification (HPC), is proposed. The CSM module conditions postencoder visual representations on patient-specific clinical context through semantic injection and channel recalibration. The HPC module represents multiple disease states as learnable prototypes on the Poincaré ball and converts predicted states into disease-state tokens for report generation. Under the primary MIMIC-CXR protocol, CSMH-RRG achieved a BLEU-4 score of 0.262 and a diseasewise macro CheXbert F1 score of 0.564, achieving state-of-the-art performance on clinical factuality metrics while maintaining comparable BLEU-4 performance to the best-performing baseline. When transferred from MIMIC-CXR to IU X-ray without fine tuning, it achieved a BLEU-4 score of 0.118 and a CE F1 score of 0.289. Specifically, in the MIMIC-CXR frequency-stratified classifier analysis, CSMH-RRG increased tail-group macro F1 from 35.5% to 41.4% relative to the linear baseline. Head-group macro F1 also increased from 72.1% to 73.5%. These results indicate that CSMH-RRG supports report generation and improves frequency-sensitive disease-state prediction within the evaluated benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/tinkerbellqwq/CSMH-RRG.

title: Segment Anything Models for medical image segmentation: From native capabilities to clinical requirements.
abstract: Medical image segmentation is essential for computer-aided diagnosis and precision medicine, yet conventional supervised models depend heavily on high-quality annotations and often generalize poorly across domains. The Segment Anything Model (SAM) family offers a transferable, interactive, and extensible foundation for segmentation, but direct medical transfer remains limited by domain gaps, insufficient modeling of medical semantics and anatomy, and mismatches in high-dimensional volumetric and sequential imaging scenarios. This review critically examines the evolution and native capability boundaries of SAM, SAM 2, and SAM 3. Across generations, native capabilities expand from spatial prompting to sequential propagation and concept-level target specification, without automatically conferring medical expertise. We organize medical adaptation from three connected perspectives: model adaptation and strategy selection, task knowledge organization and utilization, and application-oriented adaptation. Cross-method analysis shows that no strategy is universally optimal; effectiveness depends on the gap between foundation-model capabilities and target-task requirements, together with data scale, domain discrepancy, imaging dimensionality, computational resources, and clinical constraints. We further identify four priorities for clinical translation: standardized evaluation for cross-study comparability, controlled continual adaptation under clinical domain drift, dynamic resource scheduling for high-dimensional and real-time workflows, and uncertainty stratification and clinical reliability control. Overall, further progress depends on accurate capability assessment, condition-matched adaptation, and explicit control of computational and prediction risks.

title: HybPromptSeg: Spatial-frequency hybrid prompting for unified multi-task medical image segmentation.
abstract: Fully automated segmentation of medical images is essential for streamlining clinical workflows and improving diagnostic efficiency. However, building a single model that jointly handles multiple segmentation tasks remains challenging because different tasks may vary not only in target structures but also in heterogeneous data distributions. Existing learnable-prompt methods encode task-specific priors, but their generalization may still be constrained by cross-task interference when the tasks have substantially different data distributions. In this study, we propose Hybrid Prompt-based Segmentation, referred to as HybPromptSeg, which is a hybrid prompt-driven, encoder-decoder-based network that unifies multiple medical image segmentation tasks within a single shared model. Concretely, we introduce a Unified Hybrid Prompt (UHP) mechanism that integrates spatial-domain and Fourier-amplitude representations within a shared learnable prompt to model task- and modality-related variations. We further design a Task-conditioned Prompt Generation (TPG) module that generates discriminative task-conditioned prompts to guide the decoder for different segmentation tasks. To evaluate HybPromptSeg, we construct two benchmarks: a single-modality multi-task (SMMT) benchmark for evaluating task discrimination under shared-modality conditions, and a multi-modality multi-task (MMMT) benchmark for evaluating robustness under cross-modality variations. Experimental results demonstrate that HybPromptSeg achieves the best performance among the evaluated unified multi-task models on both benchmarks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/nnnsjtu/HybSeg.

title: FDG-PET in Lymphoma: The Deauville Era and Beyond.
abstract: FDG-positron emission tomography (PET) has augmented lymphoma imaging from morphology-based assessment to functional metabolic evaluation. The introduction of the Deauville five-point scale and its incorporation into the Lugano classification marked the beginning of the "Deauville era" providing a standardized staging and response assessment, enabling risk adapted therapy and prognostication in FDG-avid lymphomas and detection of histologic transformation in lymphomas with low FDG uptake. Beyond visual interpretation, volumetric biomarkers such as metabolic tumor volume and total lesion glycolysis have demonstrated important prognostic value. Emerging Artificial Intelligence applications are further expanding the role of FDG-PET in lymphoma management.

title: FDG-PET in Cognitive Impairment and Dementia.
abstract: Neuroimaging is crucial in early and accurate assessment of diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy optimization in patients with declining cognitive abilities. Imaging modalities now available for clinical indications related to neurodegenerative processes include Computed Tomography (CT), MR imaging, and PET imaging with 6 positron-emitting radiotracers approved at this time by the US Food and Drug Administration. The central focus of this article is the role of FDG-PET in clinical and research applications of patients with cognitive problems, and how the derived information may be effectively integrated with information acquired from other neuroimaging modalities.

title: Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET in Myocardial Viability and Ischemic Heart Disease.
abstract: Assessment of myocardial viability remains pivotal in managing patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and left ventricular dysfunction. Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-PET is the reference standard for evaluating myocardial metabolic viability, enabling identification of dysfunctional yet salvageable myocardium that may benefit from revascularization. This review summarizes the pathophysiological basis, imaging protocols, interpretation strategies, and clinical evidence supporting FDG-PET for myocardial viability assessment. Particular emphasis is placed on recent advancements, including quantitative imaging, hybrid PET/computed tomography and PET/MR imaging systems, artificial intelligence, radiomics, and emerging molecular tracers. Future directions and ongoing challenges in viability imaging are also discussed.

title: 18 F-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET in Rheumatologic and Autoimmune Disorders.
abstract: FDG PET detects the silent inflammation of autoimmune and rheumatologic diseases even before tissue damage, as activated leukocytes overexpress glucose transporters. It has an important role in large vessel vasculitis which includes early diagnosis, disease monitoring and response assessment to treatment. In inflammatory arthritides, it quantifies synovitis and enthesitis and detects early treatment response. In connective tissue and immunoglobulin G4 related diseases, whole body imaging maps silent disease, helps exclude malignancy, and guides biopsy. It is central to cardiac sarcoidosis and an early test in fever of unknown origin.

title: 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT in Sepsis.
abstract: 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tompgraphy/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) has emerged as a valuable whole-body metabolic imaging modality in sepsis and related systemic infectious disorders. Exploiting increased glucose metabolism in activated inflammatory cells, it facilitates localization of occult infective foci, detection of septic embolization, and guidance of source control when conventional investigations are inconclusive. Evidence demonstrates high diagnostic yield and meaningful impact on clinical management, particularly in sepsis of unknown origin and high-risk bacteraemia. However, diagnostic accuracy depends on appropriate patient preparation and timing. This review summarizes current evidence, practical challenges, emerging applications, and future research priorities for integrating 18F-FDG PET/CT into sepsis care.

title: Valuable Role of Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET in Therapeutic Decision Making and Theranostics of Neurologic Disorders in Conjunction with Non-Fluorodeoxyglucose Tracers.
abstract: Brain ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) is an important functional imaging modality for evaluating glucose metabolism. Over time, it has been observed that various metabolic patterns can support diagnoses, inform prognosis, guide therapeutic decision-making, and assess treatment response. Clinical applications span seizures, brain tumors, traumatic brain injury, neuroinflammatory and infectious disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, and other chronic neurological conditions. Although FDG is not itself a theranostic radiopharmaceutical, its ability to characterize metabolism may contribute to treatment planning, particularly in molecularly targeted neuro-oncology. This chapter reviews established and investigational applications of brain FDG-PET, emphasizing disease characterization, therapeutic selection, and response assessment.

title: A decade of image-guided pleural biopsies: a multicentre retrospective study assessing diagnostic yield and complication rate.
abstract: Aim Pleural disease is common, with diagnostic options including pleural effusion cytology and pleural biopsy, either by local anaesthetic thoracoscopy (LAT) or image-guided biopsy. LAT facilitates multiregion sampling and simultaneous effusion management but may not be feasible with a loculated pleural space. Using long term local data, we assessed the diagnostic yield (DY) and complications associated with ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy (USGPB) and computed tomography-guided pleural biopsy (CTGPB). Materials and methods We performed a retrospective multicentre cohort study across 6 hospitals, retrieving data regarding USGPB and CTGPB performed in these hospitals between 01/01/13 and 31/03/23 using study code and key word searches. Patient demographics, pathology, final diagnosis (by biopsy or consensus diagnosis), and complications were recorded. Results A total of 194 CTGPBs were performed; 166/194 were diagnostic (DY 85.6%). 7/194 (3.6%) had a peri-procedural pneumothorax on CT, but none required intervention. For diagnosis of pleural malignancy, the sensitivity of CTGPB was 93.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 88.9%-97.0%), specificity 100% (89.1%-100%), positive predictive value (PPV) 100% (97.6-100%) and negative predictive value (NPV) 76.2 (63.7-85.4%). Ninty-three USGPBs were performed, all without post-procedural pneumothorax; 83/93 were diagnostic (DY: 89.2%). title: Change in left atrioventricular coupling index from acute to chronic phases for prediction of major adverse cardiac events after myocardial infarction.
abstract: Aim Previous studies confirmed the usability of the left atrioventricular coupling index (LACI) to enhance risk stratification of cardiovascular adverse events in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). We intend to study the prognostic value of the change in LACI (ΔLACI) from the acute to the chronic phases to predict major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in an AMI patient cohort. Materials and methods A total of 264 patients following AMI were included in a secondary analysis. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in the acute and chronic stages. LACI was defined by the ratio of left atrial to left ventricular end-diastolic volumes. MACE, including all-cause mortality, reinfarction, or heart failure after the follow-up examination (52 [interquartile range {IQR}: 47-61] months after AMI), was defined as the primary endpoint. Results Among the 264 participants (median age, 59 years [IQR 50-66]; 229 men), MACE occurred in 41 patients over 52 months after the first imaging. LACI was higher in patients with MACE (P< 0.001). The Youden Index identified a LACI cut-off at 24% and a ΔLACI cut-off at 0.02%/month (both P < 0.001) to classify high-risk patients. After adjusting for multivariate models, ΔLACI (model 1, hazard ratio [HR]: 0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.36-0.60; model 2, HR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.50-0.78; both P < 0.001) was an independent predictor of MACE. ΔLACI enabled further risk stratification in AMI (LACI > 24%, P < 0.001; LACI < 24%, P = 0.013). Conclusion LACI and ΔLACI provide superior prognostic value for MACE in AMI patients. ΔLACI provides incremental prognostic value beyond baseline LACI.

title: When is 4 Gy enough? Defining dose sufficiency and durable control in indolent B-cell lymphoma.
abstract: Ultra-low-dose radiotherapy, most commonly delivered as 4 Gy in two fractions (2 Gy × 2), is an established low-burden approach for radiosensitive indolent B-cell lymphoma. Its use as stand-alone definitive local therapy is constrained by a persistent gap between early tumor regression and durable local control. This review examines when 4 Gy should be considered sufficient by integrating clinical intent, lesion biology, response assessment, immune context, and emerging biomarkers. We distinguish its use as stand-alone local treatment, palliation, response-adapted de-escalation, and immune-integrated strategies. Across these settings, early response indicates radiosensitivity but does not prove lesion sterilization or equivalence to standard-dose radiotherapy. Dose sufficiency depends on durable in-field control, tumor burden, anatomical definition, reassessment reliability, feasibility of salvage, and the consequences of local failure. Immune and cellular combinations may extend the value of 4 Gy beyond local cytoreduction, but the contribution of irradiation should be tested separately from systemic or intratumoral partners. PET response, MRD, ctDNA, and immune correlates may help distinguish transient cytoreduction from durable clearance and local response from patient-level disease control. At present, these biomarkers are better suited to trial design and mechanistic validation than to routine dose selection. Future studies should move beyond response rates and define decision rules that link early response, immune modulation, biomarker dynamics, lesion-level durability, salvageability, and cumulative treatment burden.

title: Multimodal AI for early lung cancer detection: from LDCT to clinical and molecular integration.
abstract: Low‑dose computed tomography (LDCT) is the established screening backbone for lung cancer in high‑risk populations. However, its clinical value depends on a complete pathway, including eligibility assessment, image acquisition, nodule interpretation, follow‑up, referral, quality assurance, and harm reduction, and not on image detection alone. Artificial intelligence (AI), radiomics, clinical‑risk models, and blood‑ or breath‑based biomarkers are being investigated as tools to improve decisions within that pathway. This narrative, state‑of‑the‑art translational review synthesizes evidence on AI‑enabled integration of clinical risk, LDCT‑derived imaging features, radiomics, longitudinal imaging, and molecular or experimental biomarkers for early lung cancer detection and pulmonary nodule triage. AI‑enabled integration may improve defined decisions within the LDCT pathway, most plausibly pulmonary nodule triage. To distinguish genuine decision support from simple data fusion, this review applies a five‑tier framework: data aggregation, diagnostic enrichment, risk stratification, threshold‑based triage, and pathway‑level decision support across all modalities and studies. Within this framework, cell‑free DNA (cfDNA) methylation and cfDNA fragmentomics occupy a higher translational tier than autoantibodies, generic serum markers, breathomics, or metabolomics, because their signals have a coherent biological basis and they have been tested in multimodal nodule‑triage studies with external validation. AI is best understood as an integrative decision layer within LDCT‑centered pathways. Its value depends on whether it supports calibrated, fair, and actionable decisions, not on discrimination alone. The guiding question of this review is not about a general comparison between AI and biomarkers. Rather, it is about identifying which data layer most benefits each particular decision, pinpointing the exact stage of the LDCT pathway where that decision occurs, and evaluating that benefit based on rigorous evidence of calibration, safety, and net clinical benefit.

title: Drastic muscle wasting following surgery is a strong predictor of prognosis in early-stage pancreatic cancer-a Taiwanese multicenter cohort study.
abstract: Objective To clarify the impact of preoperative sarcopenia and muscle wasting postoperative on the short- and long-term outcomes following pancreatectomy in resectable pancreatic cancer (PC) patients. Summary background data Previous studies revealed that sarcopenia, defined as generalized loss of skeletal muscle mass, was a poor prognosis factor following surgery. However, research focus on postoperative muscle wasting and their influences on the prognosis in resectable PC was very limited. Methods Retrospective analysis was performed for 284 early-stage PC patients who underwent pancreatic resection in two medical centers. Preoperative psoas major area and the degree of muscle reduction postoperative 3 months were calculated by computed tomography to define sarcopenia and drastic muscle wasting. Patients were assigned to 2 groups based on the presence or absence of sarcopenia or drastic muscle wasting and compared for postoperative morbidity and survival rate. Results Sarcopenia was present in 149 of 284 patients (52.4%), and a total of 88 patients (31.0%) developed muscle wasting of over 17% postoperatively. Compared with non-sarcopenia group, patients with sarcopenia had significantly greater incidence of overall or major morbidity (P = 0.001; P = 0.038, respectively), while sarcopenia status didn't correlate with poor-long term survival (DFS, P = 0.812; OS, P = 0.238). Surprisingly, patients presented drastic muscle wasting displayed poor DFS (P < 0.001) and OS (P < 0.001) and were found to be independent predictors of unfavorable DFS (P = 0.005) and OS (P < 0.001) after adjusting for clinicopathologic parameters. Conclusions Sarcopenia preoperative is associated with higher risk of morbidity. Moreover, the concept of assessment in wasting muscle quantity following pancreatectomy is essential for accurate long-term prognosis in resectable PC patients.

title: Interpretable CT-based radiomics nomogram integrating clinical and semantic features for preoperative grading of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms: a shap-based analysis.
abstract: Preoperative grading of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) is crucial for personalized management. This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning framework based on CT imaging to predict PNENs pathological grades. We retrospectively analyzed 125 patients with pathologically confirmed PNENs, divided into training and test cohorts. A comprehensive radiomics pipeline was implemented, involving the extraction of high-dimensional features from CT images. We constructed three predictive models: a clinical model, a radiomics model, and a fusion model. To ensure methodological robustness, seven machine-learning algorithms were employed and cross-validated to identify the optimal classifier. Furthermore, the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) method was utilized to decode the "black box" of the radiomics signature. The fusion model-integrating CT radiomic signatures with semantic hallmarks-consistently outperformed the standalone clinical and radiomics models, achieving a superior AUC of 0.891 in the validation cohort. SHAP analysis revealed that microscopic texture complexity (e.g., Zone Entropy) and macro-geometric irregularity (e.g., Sphericity) were the dominant predictors, aligning with the biological aggressiveness of high-grade lesions. By integrating multi-dimensional CT features with a rigorous machine-learning consensus, our study provides a highly accurate and interpretable "virtual biopsy" tool.

title: CT-guided iodine-125 brachytherapy for advanced thymic epithelial tumors: a preliminary observational study.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to provide a preliminary description of the application of CT-guided iodine-125 ( 125 I) seed implantation, a form of brachytherapy, in patients with advanced or recurrent thymic epithelial tumors (TETs). Methods We retrospectively reviewed seven patients with advanced or recurrent TETs who underwent CT-guided 125 I seed implantation. Based on the extent of disease at presentation, one patient had widespread distant metastases, while the remaining six had localized lesions. Treatment planning was performed using a treatment planning system(TPS, Beijing Astro Technology Co., Ltd.) with a prescribed dose of 60-70 Gy. Follow-up evaluations included regular contrast-enhanced CT scans. Tumor response was assessed according to RECIST 1.1 criteria, and safety was evaluated using CTCAE v5.0. Results A total of 12 lesions were treated across seven patients. All procedures were technically successful. Over a median follow-up of 46 months (range: 9-69 months),four patients (57.1%) attained a complete response (CR) and three patients (42.9%) attained a partial response (PR) at the patient level. Patient-level response was defined by composite assessment of all target lesions. At the lesion level, six lesions (50%) demonstrated a CR and six lesions (50%) demonstrated a partial response PR. Notably, lesion-level observations are statistically non-independent given that half of treated lesions derived from a single patient. Complications included pneumothorax in three patients (one of whom required drainage) and grade 1 radiation pneumonitis in one patient; all adverse events resolved without long-term sequelae. No severe radiation-related toxicities (e.g., pericarditis) were observed. In a descriptive subgroup excluding the patient with widespread metastases, four of six patients achieved CR and two achieved PR; no local progression was documented during available follow-up, but this finding remains descriptive and non-comparative. Conclusion CT-guided ¹²⁵I radioactive seed implantation appears feasible and well-tolerated in patients with advanced or recurrent TETs. The observed objective tumour responses and toxicity profile are hypothesis-generating but must be interpreted with caution given the very small sample size, heterogeneous cohort, non-independent lesion-level data, and lack of a control group. This preliminary study cannot establish durable local control or superiority over external beam radiotherapy. Further larger, prospective studies with standardized dosimetry and time-to-event endpoints are warranted.
