title: Deep-learning histopathradiomics enables high-throughput quantification of pollutant-induced tissue injury in marine mussels.
abstract: Quantitative tissue-level biomarkers are important for assessing pollutant-induced biological effects, yet conventional histopathology remains largely manual, low-throughput, and observer-dependent. We developed a deep learning-based histopathradiomics workflow for high-throughput morphometric quantification in the marine mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis. Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) was used as a benchmark stressor to provide a biologically defined tissue-injury context for workflow evaluation. An optimized Res-UNet achieved Dice coefficients of 0.9159 ± 0.0788 for gill epithelium and 0.8687 ± 0.1612 for digestive tubule walls, enabling automated quantification of 1264 gill filaments and 1437 digestive tubules within minutes. The resulting gill epithelial area and digestive tubule wall area showed injury-related patterns consistent with semi-quantitative pathology and manual thickness-based morphometry. The current binary framework focuses on predefined structural endpoints rather than the full spectrum of histopathological lesions. Without further model optimization, application to an independent sulfamethoxazole (SMX) + BaP dataset retained comparable tissue-injury patterns across exposure scenarios and independent experimental and histological batches, supporting cross-scenario applicability. Overall, this workflow transforms established histopathological biomarkers into scalable and biologically interpretable morphometric endpoints, while reducing repeated manual delineation and providing a practical basis for standardized tissue-level effect assessment in marine sentinel organisms.

title: Contralateral piriform cortex alterations after surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy: A pilot MRI volumetry study.
abstract: Purpose Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is increasingly conceptualized as a network disorder, with the piriform cortex as an implicated region. We characterized postoperative contralateral piriform cortex-cortical amygdala (PCA) structural and perfusion-related changes in a small seizure-free TLE cohort. Methods Nine patients with drug-resistant TLE who underwent epilepsy surgery and achieved postoperative seizure freedom were included in this single-center pre-post pilot study. Bilateral PCA was manually delineated on 3D T1-weighted MRI using ITK-SNAP, and volumes were normalized to total intracranial volume derived from CAT12 segmentation. Eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal lobe regions were examined as exploratory regional-specificity comparisons. In patients with available pulsed arterial spin labeling (PASL), piriform and putaminal signal intensities were measured by region-of-interest analysis. Non-parametric paired tests were used; secondary and exploratory analyses were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Results Normalized to total intracranial volume (TIV) contralateral PCA volume decreased postoperatively (Wilcoxon Z = -2.073, exact two-tailed p = 0.039; r = 0.69). None of the eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal regions showed a significant pre-post volume change. Contralateral putamen-normalized piriform signal intensity did not change significantly (Z = -0.105, p = 0.917), and no secondary or exploratory analysis remained significant after FDR correction. Conclusions In this hypothesis-generating pilot cohort, contralateral PCA volume decreased after epilepsy surgery, whereas the PASL-derived signal-intensity measure did not show a corresponding group-level change. These observations do not establish a surgery-induced network mechanism and require confirmation in larger controlled longitudinal cohorts.

title: Using Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance to Improve Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease Risk Stratification in Individuals with Type 2 Diabetes from Primary Care and Endocrinology Settings.
abstract: Objectives Current metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) guidelines recommend fibrosis screening in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) because of their increased risk of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2). However, fibrosis risk is variable, and clinical tools to identify individuals at lower risk are lacking. We evaluated whether assessment of insulin resistance by homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) could improve risk stratification for clinically significant fibrosis. Methods We prospectively recruited 501 adults with T2D from primary care and endocrinology clinics. Participants were classified as insulin-resistant (HOMA-IR ≥2.5; n=350) or insulin-sensitive (HOMA-IR <2.5; n=151). Liver steatosis was assessed using VCTE, MRI/MRE, or liver biopsy according to the most accurate test, and the prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2) was compared between groups. Results Insulin-resistant participants had higher prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis than insulin-sensitive participants (≥F2: 10% vs. <1%; p<0.001). They also had greater hepatic steatosis, higher ALT, AST, CK-18, HbA1c, and adipose tissue insulin resistance (Adipo-IR) levels, and lower adiponectin concentrations (all p<0.001). Fibrosis was infrequent among insulin-sensitive participants and almost exclusively limited to mild fibrosis (stage F1). Among participants with steatosis, ≥F2 fibrosis was present in 1% of insulin-sensitive participants compared with 13% of insulin-resistant participants (p<0.001). Conclusions Clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2) was uncommon among insulin-sensitive individuals with T2D and largely limited to mild fibrosis (F1). HOMA-IR <2.5 identified a subgroup at very low risk for fibrosis, supporting its potential use as a simple, clinically accessible tool for MASLD risk stratification in primary care and endocrinology settings.

title: Urorectal septum malformation sequence presenting with complete penoscrotal transposition, urethral atresia, and imperforate anus: A case report.
abstract: Urorectal septum malformation sequence (URSMS) is a rare congenital anomaly featuring severe genitourinary and gastrointestinal malformations. We report a neonate with complete URSMS, characterized by complete penoscrotal transposition, a hypoplastic phallus without urethral opening, and an imperforate anus. Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum creatinine of 2.47 mg/dL. Intraoperatively, the rectum and urethra formed a common channel at the phallic base. Anoplasty and urethrostomy were performed. Postoperatively, the infant was anuric and ultrasound confirmed bilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney. Recognition of URSMS is important for accurate diagnosis, surgical planning, and counselling regarding prognosis.

title: Risk-stratified Prostate Cancer Screening in 2026: Blood- and Urine-based Biomarkers.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) encompasses a broad biological spectrum ranging from indolent to aggressive disease. Although early randomized trials generated controversy regarding the benefits versus harms of screening, contemporary evidence supports screening and early detection strategies that focus on men at the highest risk of clinically significant PCa (csPCa) or International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥2. Current guidelines from major urological associations emphasize shared decision-making, with earlier screening considerations for high-risk populations. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing is important in PCa screening, but its limited specificity necessitates adjunctive tools to reduce unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis. Risk calculators/nomograms, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), blood-based assays (including PSA derivatives and multivariable tests such as the Prostate Health Index, 4Kscore, Stockholm3, and Proclarix), and urine-based assays (including SelectMDx, MyProstateScore 2.0, ExoDx, and miR Sentinel) further refine detection. The integration of MRI and biomarkers represents modern risk-adapted screening and early detection pathways. Ongoing large-scale trials are evaluating multimodal biomarker and MRI strategies to optimize csPCa detection while minimizing harm. Overall, risk-stratified, imaging- and biomarker-driven approaches offer pragmatic and evidence-based pathways to enhance early detection of csPCa while reducing overdiagnosis and overtreatment. PATIENT SUMMARY: This short review discusses how blood and urine tests, alongside genetic risk information, can help identify the men most likely to harbor aggressive prostate cancer-enabling early detection and intervention while avoiding unnecessary biopsies and potential harm in men at low risk.

title: Machine Learning Models Combining [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET Radiomics and Clinical Features to Predict Overall Survival for Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer Treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligand Therapy.
abstract: Purpose Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains incurable despite recent therapeutic advances. [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT (lutetium-177 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy) provides meaningful clinical benefit in selected patients. However, ∼30% of the patients do not respond to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Although several baseline prognostic factors are well known, reliable pretherapeutic predictive biomarkers are still lacking. We developed and compared several predictive machine learning (ML) models integrating clinical, biochemical, and imaging data, including [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET (gallium-68 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen ligand positron emission tomography) radiomic features, to estimate overall survival (OS) in patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Methods This retrospective monocentric study included 102 patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA between January 2022 and March 2024. Five lesions per patient were segmented on their pretherapeutic [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/computed tomography (CT) scans. Radiomic features were extracted following Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative guidelines. Multimodal ML models integrating clinical, genomic, biochemical, and imaging features (including radiomics) were developed to predict OS. Results Median OS of the total cohort was 11.2 mo. Intralesional homogeneity, characterized by the second-order radiomic feature normalized inverse difference moment, was associated with shorter OS (p = 0.025). The best-performing ML model achieved a 12-mo area under the curve (AUC) of 0.778 by combining 22 clinical, biochemical, genomic, and radiomic features. The model leveraging PET data alone achieved strong performance, with an AUC comparable to the clinical model (0.715 vs 0.766). Conclusions ML models based on [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT, including radiomic features, offer a noninvasive, standardized, and widely accessible approach to predict OS in patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. This study highlights the strong predictive potential of PSMA PET imaging for patient stratification in a real-world setting.

title: The Nature of Progression on Active Surveillance for Favorable-risk Gleason Grade Group 2 Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Background Active surveillance (AS) is a recommended option for favorable-risk Gleason grade group 2 (GG2) prostate cancer (PCa), but uptake varies. Objective To describe the nature of progression of confirmed GG2 disease in a well-annotated AS cohort. Design, setting, and participants Participants at the University of California, San Francisco, were diagnosed with cT1-2N0/xM0/x, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) <20 ng/ml, core positivity ≤50%, and GG2 PCa without expansile cribriform or intraductal carcinoma (EC/IDC) at diagnosis, with two or more biopsies on AS from 2000 to 2025. Intervention Active surveillance. Outcome measurements and statistical analysis Outcomes were upgrade (GG3 or higher), volume increase to >50%, EC/IDC, disease progression (upgrade, volume increase, or EC/IDC), active treatment, recurrence (biochemical recurrence or salvage treatment) after radical prostatectomy (RP), metastasis, and PCa-specific mortality (PCSM). Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify risk factors for AS outcomes. Results and limitations A total of 329 men were included. At 5 and 10 yr of follow-up, respectively, the upgrade rate was 31% and 58%, volume increase rate was 22% and 31%, EC/IDC development rate was 10% and 41%, disease progression rate was 44% and 79%, active treatment rate was 46% and 65%, and metastasis rate was 0.80% and 3.3%. The 5-yr post-RP recurrence rate was 32%. No PCSM events were recorded within 10 yr. PSA density (PSAD) and positive baseline multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI; Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 4-5) were associated with disease progression and active treatment. Limitations include the single-institution cohort, a largely Caucasian population, and incomplete mpMRI and genomic testing. Conclusions Men with confirmed favorable-risk GG2 PCa on AS have moderate rates of disease progression requiring treatment at 10 yr. Metastasis and PCSM rates were low, but confidence intervals are wide and require external validation. Positive mpMRI and increased PSAD were associated with disease progression and can help tailor AS intensity.

title: Can We Omit Systematic Biopsies in Men with a Positive MRI During Repeat Biopsies for Active Surveillance for Prostate Cancer? Results from the PRIAS Study.
abstract: Background and objective This study evaluated the added value of systematic biopsies (SBx) in addition to targeted biopsies (TBx) for detecting upgrading during repeat biopsies on active surveillance (AS) using data from the Prostate Cancer Research International Active Surveillance study. Methods We analyzed repeat biopsies of men who underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and SBx at diagnosis, with or without TBx depending on the presence of an MRI lesion, had at least one positive (Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 3-5) follow-up MRI, and received both SBx + TBx at subsequent repeat biopsy. Upgrading compared with diagnostic biopsy was assessed for TBx only, SBx only, and both, using three definitions: any upgrading, upgrading to grade group (GG) ≥2 with cribriform growth or intraductal carcinoma (≥GG2+), and upgrading to ≥GG3. Cumulative incidences were calculated using each detection method as competing events. For upgrading ≥GG2+ detected by SBx only, the laterality relative to the MRI lesion was determined. Key findings and limitations We analyzed 650 repeat biopsies in 568 patients with a median follow-up of 3.0 yr (interquartile range = 1.8-4.3) for men still on AS. During available follow-up, any upgrading occurred in 238 biopsies (37%), of which 47 (7.2%) were detected by SBx only. Upgrading to ≥GG2+ and ≥GG3 was observed in 100 biopsies (16%) and 78 biopsies (12%), respectively, with SBx alone identifying 19 (3.0%) and 15 (2.3%) of these patients. At 6 yr, the cumulative incidence of ≥GG2+ upgrading was 27% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 21-32%), with 5.4% (95% CI = 2.9-9.1%) for upgrading detected exclusively by SBx. Three of the 19 cases with upgrading to ≥GG2+ detected by SBx only were located contralateral to the MRI lesion (0.5% of all biopsies). Limitations include the retrospective design, which may introduce selection and registration biases. Conclusions and clinical implications In men on AS who underwent diagnostic MRI with SBx (with or without TBx) and a positive follow-up MRI, SBx has limited added value during repeat biopsies, particularly for contralateral sampling, supporting a targeted and perilesional biopsy approach.

In men on AS who underwent diagnostic MRI with SBx (with or without TBx) and a positive follow-up MRI, SBx has limited added value during repeat biopsies, particularly for contralateral sampling, supporting a targeted and perilesional biopsy approach.

title: Malignant transformation of endometriosis into endometrioid ovarian carcinoma with a contralateral borderline seromucinous tumour: A rare case report.
abstract: Background Endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer is uncommon and is most often represented by endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas. Synchronous contralateral borderline ovarian tumours are uncommon and may be missed when gross intraoperative assessment is reassuring. Case A 43-year-old woman with a confirmed diagnosis of endometriosis for approximately 5 years presented with worsening pelvic pain and menstrual symptoms. A left ovarian endometrioma increased from 6.1 × 6.8 × 5.2 cm in April 2024 to 8.8 × 9 × 9.5 cm in April 2025, with subsequent MRI showing a complex mass with solid components (O-RADS MRI 5). CA-125 was 408.6 U/mL and CA 19-9 was 643.58 U/mL; RMI-I was 1225.8 (U = 3, M = 1, CA-125 = 408.6). Staging laparotomy was performed. Histopathology demonstrated grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma arising in an endometriotic cyst of the left ovary, FIGO stage IC1, while the grossly normal-appearing right ovary contained a borderline seromucinous tumour with endometrioid differentiation. The omentum, peritoneal cytology, and all 31 sampled lymph nodes were negative for malignancy. Immunohistochemistry supported endometrioid carcinoma. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of interval change and suspicious imaging features in an endometrioma, the limitations of gross intraoperative assessment of the contralateral ovary, and the value of complete histopathological examination in identifying synchronous bilateral ovarian pathology.

title: 177 Lu-Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Prior to Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy in Oligorecurrent Prostate Cancer: Secondary and Exploratory End Point Results from the Randomized Phase 2 LUNAR Trial.
abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy-free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone (n = 47) or 177 Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT (n = 45). At a median follow-up of 31.9 mo, 177 Lu-PNT2002 significantly improved PFS (median 17.6 vs 7.4 mo; hazard ratio [HR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.23-0.61; p < 0.001) and HT-FS (HR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.34-0.95; p = 0.03). Exploratory analyses demonstrated improved poly-PFS (HR 0.28, 95% CI = 0.08-1.03; p = 0.04), CRFS (HR 0.13, 95% CI = 0.02-1.10; p = 0.03), and CT-PFS (HR 0.46, 95% CI = 0.19-1.09; p = 0.07). No new safety signals were observed. With extended follow-up, neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 before SBRT produced durable improvements in PFS and HT-FS. While poly-PFS, CRFS, and CT-PFS were exploratory end points, their improvement provides hypothesis-generating evidence that the addition of radioligand therapy to SBRT may alter disease trajectory beyond delaying PSMA PET/CT-detected recurrence.

title: PSMA-PET/CT-guided Intensification of Radiation Therapy for Prostate Cancer (PSMAgRT): 5-yr Analysis of a Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Background Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET) improves lesion detection, leading to treatment intensification via PSMA-guided radiotherapy (PSMAgRT), but its impact on patient outcomes remains undefined. Objective We evaluated whether PSMAgRT improves failure-free survival (FFS). Design, setting, and participants This phase 2, two-center, open-label randomized trial enrolled patients planned for standard-of-care (SOC) radiotherapy (RT). Intervention Patients were randomized 1:1 to SOC or PSMAgRT to all detected sites across four strata: salvage post-radical prostatectomy (RP), high-risk, oligometastatic, and salvage post-RT. Between 2018 and 2021, 262 patients were randomized (253 treated/analyzed). Outcome measurements and statistical analysis The primary FFS end point (measured from RT completion) comprised prostate-specific antigen (PSA)/radiological progression, next-line therapy, or death. Secondary end points included freedom from biochemical progression (FFBP; PSA rise ≥0.2 ng/ml post-RP or ≥2 ng/ml above nadir in other strata). Prespecified analyses used a one-sided threshold of p 1 < 0.10, whereas post hoc analyses used two-sided p < 0.05 thresholds and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results and limitations Among 253 patients, median follow-up was 66 mo (range 9-91). The 5-yr primary FFS was 66% with PSMAgRT versus 62% in controls (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.80; one-sided 90% CI, upper bound 1.04; p 1 = 0.14). FFBP favored PSMAgRT: 72% versus 65% overall (subdistribution HR [sHR] 0.70, one-sided 90% CI upper bound 0.92; p 1 = 0.048), 81% versus 66% in patients with high-risk disease (sHR 0.54; p 1 = 0.07), and 80% versus 68% in patients in post-RP stratum (sHR 0.54; p 1 = 0.037). In an exploratory, post hoc analysis combining patients with high-risk disease and those in the post-RP stratum, FFBP favored PSMAgRT (sHR 0.54, 95% CI = 0.32-0.91; two-sided p = 0.02). Only one grade ≥3 event was possibly related to dose escalation. Limitations include a phase 2 design with a heterogeneous population. Conclusions Although the primary FFS end point was not met in the overall population, treatment-effect estimates favored PSMAgRT in the high-risk and post-RP strata. These findings provide a meaningful rationale for the target populations currently being evaluated in the definitive phase 3 PATRON trial. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03525288.

title: Dysregulated Retinal DPP10 Expression with Single Cell-based Next Genomic Sequencing Profiling in X-linked Juvenile Retinoschisis.
abstract: X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) is a hereditary retinal dystrophy resulting from mutations in the retinoschisin (RS1) gene, which lead to progressive structural abnormalities in the retina and consequent visual impairment. Despite this, the molecular mechanisms through which RS1 mutations induce cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling during disease progression remain inadequately elucidated. To delineate transcriptional changes associated with RS1 mutations, we conducted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered Rs1 emR209C knock-in mouse model. Integrative analysis with the Mouse Retina Cell Atlas demonstrated that rod photoreceptors exhibited the most significant transcriptional dysregulation among retinal cell types. Notably, dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 10 (DPP10) was progressively and markedly upregulated, predominantly within photoreceptors, as the disease advanced. These findings were corroborated by immunofluorescence staining, quantitative PCR, and western blot analyses, which confirmed increased retinal DPP10 expression concurrent with a gradual decline in RS1 levels. To explore the functional implications of DPP10 dysregulation, we developed Y79 retinal cell models expressing either wild-type RS1 or the XLRS-associated RS1 R209C variant. Cells expressing the RS1 R209C mutation exhibited elevated DPP10 expression alongside reduced viability. Crucially, siRNA-mediated knockdown of DPP10 partially rescued cell viability and was associated with reduced GRP78/BiP expression in RS1 R209C-expressing cells, supporting potential functional relevance between DPP10 upregulation and mutant RS1-induced cellular stress. Furthermore, circulating DPP10 concentrations were significantly increased in patients with XLRS compared to control subjects. Collectively, these results identify DPP10 as a molecular alteration associated with RS1 mutation and suggest its potential as a circulating biomarker candidate for XLRS.

title: Circulating microRNAs reflect hemorrhagic MRI markers in cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
abstract: Background Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a major cause of intracerebral hemorrhage in older individuals. Although cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) aid MRI diagnosis they offer limited pathophysiological insight. MicroRNAs (miRs) regulate microvascular function and may serve as noninvasive biomarkers for distinguishing CAA subtypes and assessing hemorrhagic risk. This study investigated circulating miR profiles in probable CAA and Dutch-type hereditary CAA and examined their relationship with hemorrhagic MRI markers. Methods Small RNA sequencing was performed on plasma from patients with probable CAA (n = 6) and symptomatic D-CAA (n = 6) compared to matched controls. Candidate miRs were validated by qPCR in a validation cohort of probable CAA patients (n = 20) and controls (n = 20). Bioinformatic analyses identified miR-mRNA interactions and pathway enrichment analysis. Correlation and receiver operating characteristic analyses evaluated the association with hemorraghic MRI-markers and the diagnostic performance of circulating plasma miRs. Results Plasma miR-26b and miR-221 were significantly increased in probable CAA. MiR-26b, miR-221, miR-223, and miR-664a correlated with micro- and macrobleeds, with miR-26b showing the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.745). Target prediction highlighted genes involved in endothelial cell function including CDKN1B, FOXO1 and PTEN, with enrichment of NPAS4- and MECP2-related transcriptional pathways. Conclusion Circulating miRs show potential as biomarkers reflecting hemorrhagic pathology in CAA.

title: Office Hysteroscopic Removal of an IUD-Myoma Composite Using an 18.5 Fr Hysteroscope and Blue Laser in a Postmenopausal Woman with Cervical Atrophy: A No-Anesthesia Approach.
abstract: Objective To study the feasibility and safety of office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an intrauterine device (IUD)-myoma complex using a blue laser in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy. Design Step-by-step video demonstration of the surgical procedure with narrated explanation. Subjects A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman (G2P2, menopause for 7 years) with a 30+ year indwelling T-shaped copper IUD. She had no postmenopausal bleeding or pelvic pain. Examination revealed severe cervical atrophy with marked stenosis. Transvaginal ultrasound (both 2D and 3D) showed the IUD encased by a myoma-like lesion, forming an IUD-myoma complex measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.8 cm. The patient declined inpatient surgery under anesthesia. Intervention Office vaginoscopic hysteroscopy was performed without anesthesia or cervical dilation using an 18.5 Fr continuous-flow hysteroscope (5 Fr working channel). Normal saline was used as the distension medium at a pressure of 100 mmHg with continuous fluid circulation. A 450 nm blue laser (30 W, continuous mode) was introduced through the working channel to vaporize the myoma-like tissue in a stepwise manner. Once the IUD was fully exposed, 5 Fr grasping forceps were used to remove the IUD together with the remaining myoma tissue en bloc. After vaporization, residual tissue fragments were retrieved for histopathological examination. Main outcome measures Successful IUD removal, operative time, pain score (Visual Analog Scale, VAS 0-10), intraoperative and postoperative complications, and follow-up ultrasound findings at one week. Results The procedure was successfully completed without conversion to general anesthesia or cervical dilation. Total operative time was 36 minutes. The patient tolerated the procedure well, reporting mild discomfort (VAS pain score 3/10). No intraoperative complications occurred. The patient experienced slight vaginal bleeding for 2 days postoperatively, which resolved spontaneously. At the one-week follow-up visit, transvaginal ultrasound revealed a normal uterine cavity with no residual IUD fragments or myoma tissue. Histopathological examination of the residual tissue fragments confirmed benign leiomyoma. Conclusion Office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an IUD-myoma complex using a blue laser is feasible and safe in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy. This technique offers a patient-centered alternative for women at high anesthesia risk or who prefer to avoid hospital admission. Objective

To study the feasibility and safety of office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an intrauterine device (IUD)-myoma complex using a blue laser in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy.

Design

Step-by-step video demonstration of the surgical procedure with narrated explanation.

Subjects

A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman (G2P2, menopause for 7 years) with a 30+ year indwelling T-shaped copper IUD. She had no postmenopausal bleeding or pelvic pain. Examination revealed severe cervical atrophy with marked stenosis. Transvaginal ultrasound (both 2D and 3D) showed the IUD encased by a myoma-like lesion, forming an IUD-myoma complex measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.8 cm. The patient declined inpatient surgery under anesthesia.

Intervention

Office vaginoscopic hysteroscopy was performed without anesthesia or cervical dilation using an 18.5 Fr continuous-flow hysteroscope (5 Fr working channel). Normal saline was used as the distension medium at a pressure of 100 mmHg with continuous fluid circulation. A 450 nm blue laser (30 W, continuous mode) was introduced through the working channel to vaporize the myoma-like tissue in a stepwise manner. Once the IUD was fully exposed, 5 Fr grasping forceps were used to remove the IUD together with the remaining myoma tissue en bloc. After vaporization, residual tissue fragments were retrieved for histopathological examination.

Successful IUD removal, operative time, pain score (Visual Analog Scale, VAS 0-10), intraoperative and postoperative complications, and follow-up ultrasound findings at one week.

The procedure was successfully completed without conversion to general anesthesia or cervical dilation. Total operative time was 36 minutes. Office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an IUD-myoma complex using a blue laser is feasible and safe in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy. title: Joint associations of endometrial thickness and pattern with live birth after fresh and frozen-thawed embryo transfer: a retrospective cohort study of 45,729 cycles.
abstract: Objective To investigate how endometrial thickness and pattern jointly relate to live birth in fresh and frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles. Design Retrospective cohort study. Subjects A total of 45,729 embryo transfer cycles performed between January 2018 and August 2022, including 16,566 fresh and 29,163 frozen-thawed cycles. Exposure Endometrial thickness and pattern were assessed by transvaginal ultrasound on the trigger day in fresh cycles and on the day of progesterone initiation in frozen-thawed cycles. Fresh and frozen-thawed cycles were analyzed separately. Main outcome measures Live birth per embryo transfer cycle. Results In both fresh and frozen-thawed cycles, restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated significant overall and nonlinear associations between endometrial thickness and live birth (all P<0.001), while non-A morphology was associated with a lower adjusted live birth risk than type A morphology in no-interaction modified Poisson models (fresh: aRR, 0.880; 95% CI, 0.832-0.930; frozen-thawed: aRR, 0.892; 95% CI, 0.863-0.923). In fresh cycles, type B/C was associated with lower live birth risk than type A within the 7.0-7.9 mm and 8.0-8.9 mm strata. In frozen-thawed cycles, live birth rates increased from 16.7% in the <7 mm B/C group to 44.7% in the ≥14 mm A group, with a significant type A advantage within strata below 10 mm. In some frozen-cycle comparisons, thinner type A endometrium significantly outperformed the adjacent thicker B/C stratum, indicating that type A morphology was associated with higher live birth rates within thinner endometrial strata. Adjusted spline curves showed that live birth risk increased most rapidly at lower thicknesses, with the slope beginning to attenuate at approximately 11-12 mm in fresh cycles and 9-10 mm in frozen-thawed cycles. Sensitivity analyses reproduced the same overall pattern. Additionally, endometrial thickness and morphology varied with ovarian stimulation protocol and gonadotropin duration in fresh cycles, and with endometrial preparation regimen in frozen-thawed cycles. Conclusion Endometrial thickness showed a nonlinear association with live birth, and trilaminar morphology was associated with higher adjusted live birth rates in both fresh and frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles. The prognostic contribution of endometrial pattern was most evident in thin-to-intermediate endometrium.

title: Ultrasound-assisted enzymatic synthesis of medium- and long-chain triacylglycerols from tricaprylin and algal oil.
abstract: Medium and long-chain triacylglycerols (MLCTs) are functional lipids, but their efficient synthesis in various systems remains challenging. An ultrasound-assisted enzymatic interesterification process was developed using tricaprylin and algal oil as substrates. The optimized enzymatic conditions were obtained by artificial neural network modeling. The structure of enzyme and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) of enzymatic process were both evaluated. The results showed that the MLCT yield reached 69.16%, with Cy-Cy-DHA as the predominant product (28.99%). Only slight structural changes were observed in the enzyme after ultrasound treatment, while the apparent reaction rate constant increased by nearly 2.8-fold and the activation energy decreased. CFD showed that ultrasound improved substrate diffusion and mixing with a lower maximum static pressure than stirring (178 vs. 259 Pa), suggesting MLCT synthesis was enhanced mainly by mass transfer intensification. This study provides valuable insights into mechanisms underlying ultrasound-enhanced enzymatic processes and guides their further scale-up and industrial application.

title: Perforated and Complicated Cholecystitis: A Narrative Review of Diagnosis, Management, and Differentiation from Gallbladder Cancer.
abstract: Introduction Perforated cholecystitis is a severe complication of gallbladder inflammation that is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis is often challenging because clinical and radiographic findings overlap with those of uncomplicated cholecystitis and, in some cases, gallbladder malignancy. This review summarizes the current evidence regarding the diagnosis, imaging, management strategies, outcomes, and differentiation of perforated cholecystitis from gallbladder cancer. Methods A comprehensive literature review was conducted using PubMed and Embase from inception to May 2026. Eligible studies included full-text articles, case reports, and original research describing perforated cholecystitis with an emphasis on diagnosis, treatment, outcomes, and gallbladder cancer mimicry. Results Gallbladder perforation results from progressive inflammation, ischemia, and mural necrosis, most commonly involving the fundus of the gallbladder. The Niemeier classification categorizes perforations into acute free perforation (Type I), localized perforation with abscess formation (Type II), and chronic perforation with fistula formation (Type III). Advanced age, male sex, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, delayed presentation, and non-operative management were identified as important risk factors. Computed tomography (CT) was the most sensitive diagnostic modality, demonstrating wall defects, pericholecystic collections, abscesses, bilomas, and extraluminal gallstones. Management includes cholecystectomy, percutaneous cholecystostomy, and interval surgery for selected high-risk patients. Evidence regarding the optimal surgical timing remains inconsistent. Chronic perforation and xanthogranulomatous inflammation may closely mimic gallbladder carcinoma on imaging and intraoperative assessment. Conclusion Perforated cholecystitis is a diagnostically challenging and potentially life-threatening condition. CT imaging is central to diagnosis, while management should be individualized according to the patient status and perforation type. Greater recognition of the features distinguishing perforation from gallbladder malignancy may facilitate earlier diagnosis and improve outcomes. When malignancy is a significant consideration, and the patient's condition permits, consider early referral to an HPB surgeon or multidisciplinary hepatobiliary team to guide further diagnostic evaluation, including tissue acquisition when appropriate, and definitive surgical planning.

title: Systems pharmacology reveals the molecular mechanisms of nerolidol against polycystic ovary syndrome through integrated transcriptomic, network pharmacology and experimental validation.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a heterogeneous endocrine and metabolic disorder marked by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, insulin resistance, chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, arising from dysregulation across several interconnected molecular pathways. Because its pathogenesis is multifactorial, therapies targeting diverse biological processes at once remain scarce. Nerolidol, a naturally occurring sesquiterpene alcohol with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective properties, has an action against PCOS whose molecular basis remains unresolved. Transcriptomic differences associated with PCOS were examined using the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE34526. Exploratory differential-expression screening identified nominally altered probes using an unadjusted P < 0.05 and |log 2 FC| > 1; however, no individual probe remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at FDR < 0.05. Functional enrichment analysis was subsequently used to investigate biological processes and pathways represented by these exploratory transcriptional signals. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG enrichment were applied to pinpoint dysregulated biological processes and signalling pathways. Computational findings were tested in a letrozole-induced PCOS rat model treated with nerolidol, with efficacy judged from oestrous cyclicity, ovarian histopathology, reproductive hormone profiles, oxidative stress biomarkers, inflammatory mediators and metabolic parameters. Transcriptomic analysis showed marked enrichment of processes related to kinase regulation, insulin secretion, intrinsic apoptotic signalling, receptor-mediated signalling and the DNA damage response, while KEGG analysis pointed to pathways governing endocrine regulation, cell signalling and metabolic homeostasis. In animal experiments, nerolidol restored oestrous cyclicity, improved ovarian morphology, corrected endocrine disturbances, and reduced oxidative stress and PCOS-related pathology. These phenotypic effects were functionally concordant with several biological processes highlighted by the computational analyses. However, because the predicted signalling molecules and pathways were not directly measured in ovarian tissue following nerolidol treatment, the proposed molecular mechanisms remain hypotheses requiring targeted experimental validation.

title: Bicentric comparison of 3-year clinical outcomes between endoscopic ultrasound-guided embolization with coil and hemostatic adjunct versus balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration for treatment of bleeding gastric varices: A propensity-score matched study.
abstract: Background and aims Endoscopic ultrasound-guided coil injection (EUS-COIL) and balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) performed by interventional radiology (IR) are both effective obliterative procedures to treat gastric varices. Comparative studies are lacking. Our aim was to assess clinical outcomes for EUS-COIL versus BRTO for treatment of acute gastric variceal bleeding. Methods This retrospective cohort study included all patients admitted to two tertiary care centers between 2009-2024 who underwent either EUS-COIL or BRTO for bleeding gastric varices. The primary outcomes were technical/clinical success and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included transfusions, reintervention, length of hospital stay, further hepatic decompensation (esophageal variceal hemorrhage, new ascites, or new hepatic encephalopathy (HE)), and all-cause mortality. Subgroup analyses were performed in patients with cirrhosis, including with propensity score matching (PSM) which was conducted 1:1 for age, sex, Child-Pugh classification, MELD-Na score, and hemoglobin level on admission. Outcomes over the 36-months post-intervention were assessed using time-to-event analysis. Results A total of 94 patients were included (48 EUS-COIL, 46 BRTO), of whom 60 patients with cirrhosis (30 per group) were analyzed after propensity score matching. In the matched cohort, technical success was 100% in both groups and clinical success was 100% versus 93.3% (p=0.49). The EUS-COIL group experienced significantly fewer adverse events (3% vs 37%; p=0.003) and had a longer time-to-reintervention (65 ± 52 days vs 10 ± 9.6 days; p=0.022) over a median follow-up 900 ± 790 days. The incidence of further hepatic decompensation was lower in the EUS-COIL group (10% vs 40%; p=0.007), as was the likelihood of further hepatic decompensation (HR 0.28 (95%CI: 0.08-0.984), p = 0.047) compared to BRTO. No significant differences were observed with regard to post-procedural transfusion requirements, rates of reintervention, length of hospital stay, and mortality in cirrhosis patients. In the unmatched cohort, technical (100% vs 80%; p=0.001) and clinical (100% vs 89%; p=0.03) success were higher with EUS-COIL than BRTO. Conclusions In patients with gastric variceal hemorrhage, EUS-COIL demonstrated higher rates of technical/clinical success and lower rates of adverse events (both peri-procedural and on long-term follow-up) compared to BRTO. EUS-COIL had significantly lower rates of further hepatic decompensation. While larger prospective studies are required, these data suggest that EUS-COIL, when available, may be the preferred initial therapy for bleeding gastric varices as part of a step-up strategy.

title: Incidence and Follow-Up of Extracardiac Findings on Cardiac Computed Tomography: A Single Tertiary Centre Experience.
abstract: Background Extracardiac findings (ECF) are frequently detected on cardiac computed tomography (CT), yet their clinical follow-up in contemporary practice is variable. We sought to describe their incidence and assess whether clinically significant findings were associated with documented follow-up or further investigation. Method We conducted a retrospective observational study of consecutive patients undergoing cardiac CT, including CT coronary angiograms (CTCA) and CT left atrial mapping (CTLA), at a single tertiary centre between January 2021 and December 2022. ECF data were extracted from formal reports. For patients with clinically significant findings, electronic medical records were reviewed to determine whether findings were documented as acknowledged and whether further investigation or follow-up was recorded. Results A total of 402 patients underwent cardiac CT. Most ECF were low risk, including hiatus hernia (39.8%) and small pulmonary nodules <6 mm (13.4%). Clinically significant ECF were identified in 41 patients (10.2%), including pulmonary nodules measuring 6-8 mm (2.7%), pulmonary nodules >8 mm (2.5%), indeterminate liver lesions (1.5%), other mass lesions (1.5%), and pulmonary emboli (1.2%). Twenty-two patients (5.5%) met criteria for Fleischner guideline-directed surveillance, of whom 15 had documented follow-up, including one subsequent diagnosis of malignancy. Overall, 12 patients (29.2%) with clinically significant ECF had no documented follow-up. Clinically significant ECF were more frequently observed in patients undergoing CTLA (odds ratio 2.4; 95% confidence interval 1.1-5.1; p=0.03) and were associated with higher odds of lacking documented follow-up compared with CTCA (odds ratio 4.8; 95% confidence interval 1.1-21.2; p=0.05). Missed clinically significant ECF predominantly occurred in the outpatient setting. Conclusions ECF on cardiac CT are common, and approximately 10% represent clinically significant abnormalities. In this cohort, clinically significant findings identified on CT left atrial mapping were associated with lower rates of documented follow-up compared with CTCA. These findings suggest a potential vulnerability in outpatient CTLA mapping pathways and support consideration of strategies to reduce unacknowledged ECF.

Clinically significant ECF were more frequently observed in patients undergoing CTLA (odds ratio 2.4; 95% confidence interval 1.1-5.1; p=0.03) and were associated with higher odds of lacking documented follow-up compared with CTCA (odds ratio 4.8; 95% confidence interval 1.1-21.2; p=0.05). Missed clinically significant ECF predominantly occurred in the outpatient setting.

Conclusions

ECF on cardiac CT are common, and approximately 10% represent clinically significant abnormalities. In this cohort, clinically significant findings identified on CT left atrial mapping were associated with lower rates of documented follow-up compared with CTCA. These findings suggest a potential vulnerability in outpatient CTLA mapping pathways and support consideration of strategies to reduce unacknowledged ECF.

title: Impact of hepatocellular carcinoma proximity to the hepato-caval confluence on the recurrence risk after hepatectomy.
abstract: Background The prognostic impact of HCC proximity to major hepatic veins is unclear. We studied whether tumour distance to the inferior vena cava (IVC) or suprahepatic veins (SHV) influences recurrence and survival after resection. Methods Retrospective single-centre cohort of consecutive HCC resections (2012-2021). To limit confounding, 70 patients with moderately aggressive tumours (AFP < 1000 ng/mL), size < 150 mm, no preoperative macrovascular invasion and R0 resection were analysed. Distance to vessel (DTV) on preoperative CT scan (minimum HCC-IVC/SHV) classified patients as DTV ≤ 10 mm or > 10 mm. Primary endpoint disease-free survival (DFS); secondary: overall survival (OS). Cox models adjusted for covariates. Results Baseline characteristics were similar between the two groups, with a median follow-up of 56 months. Median DFS was shorter in DTV ≤ 10 mm: 28 vs 40 months (p = 0.04). In multivariable analysis, DTV ≤ 10 mm (HR 1.88; p = 0.028) and higher preoperative MELD (HR 1.25; p = 0.0001) independently predicted poorer DFS. Median OS tended to be lower with DTV ≤ 10 mm (70 vs 117 months; p = 0.06). Conclusion HCC proximity ≤ 10 mm to SHV/IVC is associated with higher recurrence risk and a trend to worse OS after R0 resection. Prospective validation is warranted.

title: Temporal Changes in LGE-CMR Enhancement After Monopolar Biphasic Focal Pulsed Field Ablation for Pulmonary Vein Isolation.
abstract: Background Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a novel non-thermal ablation modality for pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) in atrial fibrillation (AF). While chronic lesion formation after PFA has been described, data regarding acute lesion characteristics and lesion maturation remain limited. Objective To characterize acute and chronic lesion formation following focal point-by-point PFA for PVI using serial late-gadolinium-enhancement cardiovascular-magnetic-resonance-imaging (LGE-CMR). Methods Six consecutive patients with symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF underwent index PFA-guided PVI using the CENTAURI system and a focal point-by-point lesion delivery strategy. LGE-CMR was performed 1 day and 90±10 days after ablation. Quantitative assessment of regional and global left atrial (LA) enhancement was performed using a standardized segmentation protocol. Changes in enhancement burden and LA dimensions were analyzed between imaging timepoints. Results Among six patients at mean age 65±7 years, five patients (83%) had paroxysmal AF. Acute PVI was achieved in all patients without procedural complications. Serial LGE-CMR demonstrated substantial temporal changes between acute and chronic imaging. Enhancement within the right pulmonary vein (PV) region decreased from 3.3±2.2% to 0.8±0.8%(p=0.030), while the proportion of enhanced tissue decreased from 24.1±13.5% to 5.7±5.8%(p=0.017). Similar reductions were observed around the left PVs (4.4±3.1%vs.1.4±1.2%, p=0.064). Posterior wall enhancement decreased from 2.4±1.1% to 0.3±0.3%(p=0.007) and global LA enhancement from 12.8±6.2% to 3.3±1.6%(p=0.013), while LA volume remained unchanged. Conclusion Serial LGE-CMR demonstrated substantial enhancement reduction of acute lesions following focal point-by-point PFA for PVI, which remained largely confined to the PV antra and adjacent posterior wall, providing novel in-human insights into lesion maturation following focal PFA delivery.

title: The triglyceride-glucose index and intramyocardial hemorrhage identify a high-risk phenotype in STEMI.
abstract: Aims The prognostic value of combining the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index and intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) in STEMI is unclear. We assessed their individual and combined association with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Methods This retrospective study included 456 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. TyG index was calculated from admission blood samples; IMH was assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance. The primary outcome was MACE (median follow-up 4 years). Multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, incremental prognostic assessment (C-index, NRI, IDI), and interaction testing were performed. Results MACE increased across TyG tertiles (15.79% → 27.63% → 43.42%). The highest tertile remained independently associated with MACE (adjusted HR 1.86; 95% CI 1.09-3.20). Patients with high TyG (≥8.66) plus IMH had the worst prognosis (HR 4.00; 95% CI 2.49-6.39; P < 0.001), far exceeding either factor alone. Adding the combined variable to a base model improved discrimination and reclassification (C-index 0.640 → 0.658; NRI = 0.216, P = 0.020; IDI = 0.025, P = 0.008). Neither additive nor multiplicative interaction was significant, and results were consistent in diabetic and non-diabetic patients. A significant interaction was observed between TyG index and infarct location (P for interaction = 0.037), with a stronger effect in anterior (HR 1.59) than non-anterior infarction (HR 0.75). Conclusions The TyG index independently predicts long-term MACE in STEMI. Combining high TyG with IMH identifies a high-risk phenotype with a 4.0-fold higher MACE risk and incremental prognostic value. The TyG effect is stronger in anterior infarction, suggesting infarct location should be considered in metabolic risk stratification.

title: Radiotherapy and brachytherapy capacity, treatment timelines, and barriers to guideline-concordant curative care for cervical cancer in Latin America: the LATAM-CxRT study.
abstract: Objective To describe national radiotherapy and brachytherapy capacity, treatment delivery, and barriers to guideline-concordant curative treatment among women with cervical cancer requiring definitive or adjuvant radiotherapy in Latin America. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of national radiation oncology coordinators from 14 Latin American countries using a standardized Research Electronic Data Capture questionnaire covering institutional mix, radiotherapy and brachytherapy infrastructure, imaging capacity, cervical cancer caseloads, external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy practice, treatment timelines, and barriers and needs as perceived by coordinators. Data were cross-checked against International Atomic Energy Agency and vendor data where available. Results Fourteen countries contributed data: all completed general characteristics, 13 completed the resources and workforce module, and 12 completed the full equipment and timelines module. Among these 12 countries, the median number of linear accelerators was 33.5 per country (interquartile range 9 to 101.75), reflecting a right skew driven by Brazil. The median annual caseload was 680.5 patients for International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics stages I to II disease and 800 patients for stages III to IV disease. Nearly all countries reported intensity-modulated radiotherapy, image-guided radiotherapy, and volumetric-modulated arc therapy capabilities. Gynecologic high-dose-rate brachytherapy was available in all 12 countries, although several reported insufficient coverage, with services concentrated in reference centers; magnetic resonance imaging-guided brachytherapy, interstitial techniques, and anesthesia support were available in only a subset. Half of countries reported 91% to 100% brachytherapy completion among women initiating curative chemoradiation, but overall treatment time from external beam radiotherapy start to brachytherapy completion exceeded 56 days in most countries. Coordinators identified limited brachytherapy and imaging capacity, workforce shortages, anesthesia constraints, and financial barriers as key impediments. These findings describe installed capacity and self-reported practice rather than direct measures of patient-level access. Conclusions This 14-country survey demonstrates that, despite widespread availability of advanced external beam radiotherapy, cervical cancer care in Latin America remains constrained by heterogeneous and often insufficient brachytherapy and imaging resources and by treatment delays exceeding guideline recommendations. Targeted investment, workforce development, service organization, and financing reforms are needed to deliver guideline-concordant chemoradiation for women with cervical cancer in the region.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Triage in Primary Care: A Scoping Review of Clinical Applicability.
abstract: Aim To map artificial intelligence (AI) systems developed for triage in primary care and describe their characteristics, performance and clinical applicability. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, MEDLINE (via Ovid), Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL (via EBSCOhost), IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library were searched until March 14th 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data on system characteristics, triage function, performance, validation, safety, equity and implementation. Each system was charted by triage function and by whether it was patient-facing, clinician-facing or fully automated. Results Seventeen studies were included, published between 2013 and 2026 across 12 countries (14/17 high-income). Most were clinician-facing decision support (14/17), three had a patient-facing component and none were autonomous. Diagnostic or screening triage was the most common function (n = 7), followed by prioritisation (n = 4) and referral routing (n = 4). Only two performed urgency classification or self-triage. As a clinician aid, AI improved performance (fundus accuracy 82.8 % to 91.1 %; dermoscopy management sensitivity 72.9 % to 94.2 %), but standalone models sometimes fell below clinicians. Reported accuracy ranged from 41.2 % to 98.28 % and AUROC from 0.65 to 0.90, on heterogeneous outcomes. Validation was mostly internal (11/17), external in four. None reported a prospective randomised comparison or measured patient outcomes. Conclusion AI triage in primary care is concentrated on clinician-facing diagnostic and referral tasks and is most valuable for augmenting clinician workflows, particularly non-specialists. The evidence base remains immature, constrained by internal validation, unreliable reference standards, sparse equity assessment and absent prospective outcome data. Future work should prioritise prospective, outcome-anchored evaluation, with attention to safety and equity.

Results

Seventeen studies were included, published between 2013 and 2026 across 12 countries (14/17 high-income). Most were clinician-facing decision support (14/17), three had a patient-facing component and none were autonomous. Diagnostic or screening triage was the most common function (n = 7), followed by prioritisation (n = 4) and referral routing (n = 4). Only two performed urgency classification or self-triage. As a clinician aid, AI improved performance (fundus accuracy 82.8 % to 91.1 %; dermoscopy management sensitivity 72.9 % to 94.2 %), but standalone models sometimes fell below clinicians. Reported accuracy ranged from 41.2 % to 98.28 % and AUROC from 0.65 to 0.90, on heterogeneous outcomes. Validation was mostly internal (11/17), external in four. None reported a prospective randomised comparison or measured patient outcomes.

Conclusion

AI triage in primary care is concentrated on clinician-facing diagnostic and referral tasks and is most valuable for augmenting clinician workflows, particularly non-specialists. The evidence base remains immature, constrained by internal validation, unreliable reference standards, sparse equity assessment and absent prospective outcome data. Future work should prioritise prospective, outcome-anchored evaluation, with attention to safety and equity.
